en: The Great Exploits (Mahāvastu Avadāna), Volume Two: The Great Exploits.

Then, at the time of his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, the Bodhisattva performs four great observations: namely, the observation of the time, the observation of the place, the observation of the continent, and the observation of the family. Bodhisattvas are born into two types of families: either a kṣatriya family or a brāhmaṇa family. When the earth is ruled by kṣatriyas, they are born into a kṣatriya family; when the earth is ruled by brāhmaṇas, they are born into a brāhmaṇa family. Monks, the family into which Bodhisattvas are born is endowed with sixty qualities. What are these sixty? It is well-known; it is not of low conduct; it is perfect in birth; it is perfect in lineage; it is perfect in its succession of male ancestors; it is perfect in the succession of its renowned male ancestors; it has many women and many men; it is not fickle; it is not deficient; it is not base; it is not depressed; it is possessed of wisdom; it is possessed of virtue; it does not look for honor; that family enjoys great wealth; that family has firm friends; that family is grateful and knows the proper rites; that family does not act out of mere whim. That family does not act out of anger, does not act out of delusion, and does not act out of fear; it fears blame; it gives abundant alms; it possesses the resolve for manly effort; it has firm prowess, excellent prowess, and supreme prowess; it honors shrines, honors the deities, and honors former friends; it is devoted to duty, devoted to generosity, and mindful of its own past and future. It is renowned for its fame and renowned for its divine renown; it is the eldest of its clan.

And that family is preeminent, excellent, superior, well-established in its lineage, of great renown, possessing a large retinue, a tireless retinue, a devoted retinue, and an inseparable retinue; it is respectful toward mothers and fathers, observant of the duties of ascetics and brahmins, honoring the elders of the clan, and abundant in wealth and grain, with vast treasuries and storehouses, many elephants, horses, goats, and sheep, and numerous female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and that family is invincible against others who are adversaries or enemies. The family in which Bodhisattvas are born is endowed with these sixty qualities. Those beings who are thus perfected in their family—beings such as these—attain great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). At the time of his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, the Bodhisattva makes a great preparation. At the time of the Bodhisattva’s descent, thousands of gods, beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, all belonging to the realm of desire, assemble in the Tuṣita heaven. Bimbisāra and others were told: “Be reborn in Rājagṛha. When you are disciplined, a great multitude of people will follow the path of discipline. Likewise, Sahasodgata, the caravan leader Abhaya, and other wealthy householders and wealthy brahmins [were told]. Udayana, the King of Vatsa, was told: “Be reborn in Kauśāmbī. When you are disciplined, a great multitude of people will follow the path of discipline. Ghoṣila the householder and likewise other wealthy kṣatriyas and wealthy householders [were told]. By this method, thousands of sons of gods—who had been companions to the Blessed One as he wandered through *saṃsāra*—are reborn in Jambudvīpa within the sixteen great provinces, in families of wealthy kṣatriyas, wealthy brahmins, and wealthy householders. “Without doubt, when you are disciplined, a great multitude of people will follow the path of discipline. The Bodhisattva considers: “Where shall I be reborn? This King Śuddhodana is a suitable father for me. He seeks a mother who would be gracious, of noble birth, pure of body, having little passion, and short-lived—one whose remaining lifespan is exactly ten months plus seven nights.
After giving birth to the Supreme among Men, the mother of all Bodhisattvas relinquishes her life on the final seventh day.
What is the reason for this, that even the mothers of the All-Knowing One, having given birth to the Best of Men, quickly abandon their lives?
While dwelling in the Tuṣita realm, the Bodhisattva, through his pure karma, maintains this mindfulness as he examines prospective mothers.
If a woman should have a remnant of life remaining here,
she shall live for seven days and ten months beyond that.
For what reason? Because it is improper for one such as me to engage in sexual intercourse after having maintained the supreme state at a later time.
Even if they were to indulge in sensual pleasures with the mother of the Sugata,
that would not cause the father of the hosts of gods to be one of broken conduct.
The Blessed One indeed constantly speaks of the faults of sensual desires;
yet the mother of the Lord of the World indulges in sensual desires.
And those jewel caskets that exist within the palaces of kings—
the jewels, the best of men, the vessels, and the mothers of awakening.

While searching the earth for one of short lifespan, the Bodhisattva saw the chief queen of Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu—gracious, of noble birth, pure of limb, and possessing little passion—who was of short lifespan; of her, only ten months plus seven nights remained of her allotted span of life. This thought occurred to the Bodhisattva: "She is a suitable mother for you."
While surveying the world, he beheld in the harem of Śuddhodana a woman resembling the consort of an immortal, like a flash of lightning, like Māyā herself.
Having observed his mother, he addressed her: "I shall descend from the Maruts;
entering my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the happiness of gods and men."
To him, the assembly of gods—wearing exquisite ornaments and with palms joined in reverence—spoke:
"O Supreme Person of undiminished virtue and beauty, may your vow be fulfilled!"
This world as well, for the benefit of the world, having renounced many delightful pleasures of the senses,
shall dwell in the human realm for the sake of honoring you, O blameless one.
They will rain down a shower of large, beautiful-colored mandārava flowers from the sky.
With uplifted minds, they released [their voices], praising him with sweet words.
That you behold the realm of Yama— delightful in its tranquility yet intermingled with grief and suffering—
and that you neither dwell upon nor indulge in sensual desires, this is truly marvelous in you.
That you, having surpassed the host of gods, illuminate the ten directions with a radiance like a mountain of gold from the Jambu river— O Bull among Suras, this too is a marvel.

You surpass the hosts of gods, including Maheśvara and the Dānavas, as well as the assemblies of Māra and the hosts of stars moving through the sky; O one of immeasurable intelligence, this too is a marvel.
O Teacher of the multitude of beings, although we do not desire separation from you,
nevertheless, O lotus-eyed one, you shall become the refuge for humans and gods.
Then, at the time of his passing away, the hosts of gods, filled with joy, proclaimed it from all directions to him whose eyes were like pure hundred-petaled lotuses.
While this conversation was taking place in the Tuṣita heaven, that peerless Māyā,
the queen of Śuddhodana, approached the king and said this:
Māyā, with eyes like those of a young deer, resembling a pure Gandharva maiden, and of youthful dark complexion,
spoke these very sweet words to Śuddhodana.
O Joy of the Śākyas, my arms are stiffened by ornaments and I wear exquisite garments; together with my companions, my desire is to pass this night without you.
O best of men, ascend to the highest floor of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s excellent palace,
where there is a preeminent couch, stainless and resembling a garment of white water-lilies.
Pleased by those words so agreeable to the queen, Śuddhodana,
that best of men with exalted resolve, addressed his retinue.
Let them quickly inform me that Dhṛtarāṣṭra has been strewn with excellent flowers;
make it covered with *kuntaka* blossoms, like a celestial palace in heaven.
And let Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with its fluttering silk streamers, shine forth in its agility,
covered by a net of excellent gold and resembling the peak of the noble Sumeru.
And let this fourfold army, variegated with spears, iron arrows, and javelins,
swiftly protect Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possesses a charming assembly.
As soon as the command was issued by the king, they prepared everything and, having performed all that was skillfully required, approached the king and said this:
O protector of the earth, may you protect your subjects for no less than a thousand years;
this excellent celestial palace stands ready, inspiring joy within you.
Then Māyā, resembling a celestial nymph, rose from her excellent seat and spoke to the son of the lord of the earth just as the sun had set.
This I undertake: non-violence toward living beings, celibacy, and I also abstain from taking what is not given, from intoxicants, and from idle speech.
O best of men, I likewise desist from all idle chatter and from slander;
O lord of men, I desist from harsh speech—this is my resolve.
May I not conceive envy toward the desires of others, nor even malice; may I give rise to no perverted views regarding living beings, and may I abandon such distorted thoughts.
"O Protector of the Earth, I shall practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night;
such is my resolve."
O protector of the earth, let there not indeed be a thought of desire toward me, nor let you look upon me with hostility;
do not send me away, lest demerit accrue to me, a woman living the holy life.
"I shall fulfill all your intentions," the king said.
"Take your pleasure within this excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your disposal."
Accompanied by her full retinue of thousands of women, she immediately ascended that excellent celestial palace and sat down there, her heart's desire completely fulfilled.
For some time, she spent that period upon her bed— which resembled snow, the white water-lily, and the lotus— in silence, delighting in tranquility and self-restraint.
Then she lay down on her right side,
having entwined her excellent body around the bed like a flowering creeper around a noble tree.
Then, beholding the queen lying upon her bed, resembling a celestial nymph in form,
the hosts of gods descended from the Tuṣita abode and took their positions upon the roof of the palace.
All those immortals, with heads bowed and joyful hands joined in *añjali*,
paid homage at the bedside to Māyā, the mother of the Jina, who possessed vast merit.
Then, filled with great curiosity and wearing pure garlands, many daughters of the gods,
desiring to see the Mother of the Jina, ascended to the top of the palace.
Having approached and beheld Māyā reclining upon her bed, radiant like a flash of excellent lightning,
he conceived vast joy and bliss, and then rained down celestial flowers.
Even among humans, such a form as this is indeed well-born and marvelous;
may you remain here for some time, for no woman of the gods shall be equal to you.
Listen, O friends, to the playful charm of this woman, which is so appropriate;
reclining on her bed, she captivates the mind and shines forth like the very essence of gold.
Since she shall bear a Great Man who delights in ultimate generosity, self-restraint, and virtue,
and who is stainless and brings an end to all outflows— O Queen, what is lacking for you?
In this beautiful belly, measured by the palm of the hand and adorned with a wondrous line of hair,
he of infinite intelligence shall dwell, forever unstained by the impure and pure.

For her who shall uphold this sūtra of infinite qualities, there is vast and supreme wholesome merit, accumulated over a very long night, the power of which has been gathered through virtue for a long time.
You are a worthy woman, most excellent; he is indeed a preeminent man, a son free from craving and stainless. O queen of kings, what is lacking for you?
Then the Rākṣasas, assuming various forms, were swiftly commanded in the sky:
"O you who bear excellent weapons, stay alert on all sides and leave no direction unguarded!"
Immediately following them, hosts of double-tongued serpents stood in all directions for the sake of protection;
even at the sound of a mere breeze stirring, they would spring up in fury like blazing fires.
Standing immediately behind them were stationed yakṣas with blazing crests and distorted forms;
they, with malicious intent, were to ward [the enemies] off, saying, "Do not commit the slaughter of anyone at all."
Standing immediately behind them were many hosts of Gandharvas bearing beautiful forms,
holding auspicious bows for the sake of protection at the moment of the passing of the one possessed of stainless wisdom.
The four Lords of the World also stood in the sky together with their own retinues;
today, it is said, the Blessed One will descend, he who increases the welfare and happiness of the world.
Standing in the sky together with the thirty-three gods, the foremost of the thirty-three, the bearer of the excellent wheel,
will before long undergo his final passing, desiring incomparable bliss.
With their ten fingers joined at the base of their palms, the vast hosts of gods bow toward him;
gazing up at the Jina in Tuṣita, they utter sweet words.
O you whose power of merit is accumulated through purification, this is the time; enter into your final existence.
Your mother is still waiting for you; now show compassion toward the suffering people.
"I am passing away"—uttering these words, he spoke this auspicious speech;
then, at that very moment, the Conqueror beheld the dream, the fruit of excellent maturation.

Resembling snow and silver, with six tusks, beautiful feet and lovely limbs, and a deep red head— this preeminent elephant, moving with graceful gait and possessing faultless joints of the body, has entered my womb.

Indeed, Bodhisattvas do not descend into their mother’s womb during the dark fortnight; rather, it is on the full moon night, when the moon is in conjunction with the Puṣya constellation, that Bodhisattvas enter their mother’s womb. U-

When the supreme woman is observing the *poṣadha* vows, joyful, free from embarrassment, not of base conduct, gracious, pure of limb, with little passion, perfected in birth, perfected in family, perfected in form, perfected in complexion, perfected in name, perfected in stature, perfected in girth, articulate, having reached the full bloom of the prime of youth, renowned, wise, mindful, self-possessed, with a favorable mind, perfected in every aspect, and complete in every way—such is the supreme woman into whose mother’s womb Bodhisattvas descend. A radiance is emitted by the Bodhisattva, by which radiance the entire Buddha-field is illuminated. One son of the gods asks another son of the gods:
For what reason has the excellent deity released this radiance,
cooler than the rays of the moon and as pure as gold,
by which the hosts of lords of asuras and lords of men [have been affected]?
And the hells, which were like blazing fires, were completely gladdened.
Then he said:
To those of great renown who, in various places, protect the people trapped in the cage of saṃsāra and overcome by passion, [I pay homage] by means of bringing about their liberation.
A radiance was emitted by the Sinless One for the purpose of addressing him.
The Bodhisattva said:
"O immortals, do not abandon the cities; this is surely not the time for joy.
Now is the time to shatter the city of old age and death with the blow of wisdom."
Mindful, clearly comprehending, and with a favorable mind, the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb.
Thus, having let out a lion’s roar like a lion among men at the time of his passing away,
he vanished and was reborn in an instant within the palace of the king.
I pay homage to that most excellent Jina, who illuminates the Tuṣita realm with his radiant complexion and who is now descending from the city of the gods.
Together with Brahmā, the world, and all beings including recluses and brahmins, he—
the unsurpassed light of the world— illuminates them all with his radiance.
Behold this wonder and marvel: how the Teacher, endowed with great supernormal power, mindful and clearly comprehending, has descended into his mother’s womb.
And for as long as that best of men, endowed with the supreme marks,
remained within his mother’s womb, he was mindful, possessed of awareness, and fully conscious.

Immediately upon the Bodhisattva’s descent, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways; it shook in a manner that was thrilling, gladdening, exhilarating, indescribable, worthy of being gazed upon, enchanting, not disagreeable, joyous, serene, free from agitation, and free from terror. And even as it shook, it did no harm to any living being, whether moving or stationary.
Then this earth, together with its oceans and Mount Meru, shook in six ways;
the worlds were made stainless and delightful.
By the splendor of him who dispels the great darkness.
As many as there were king-serpents and lords of serpents, they all became intent upon providing protection, defense, and guardianship.
Even the four world-protectors performed protection for the Lord of the World,
lest anyone seeking harm should injure him who crushes the power of Namuci.

Śakra, the lord of the gods; Suyāma, the son of the gods; Saṃtuṣita, the son of the gods; Sunirmita, the son of the gods; Vaśavartin, the son of the gods; Mahābrahmā; and the Śuddhāvāsa gods—all became intent upon providing protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb.
Then thousands of millions of gods, being well-pleased, approached Kapilāhvaya to protect the one of excellent wisdom.
The supreme city of Kapila shines resplendent with hosts of immortals who have entered it as if into the city of the gods, moving with the stride and gait of those whose power is mind-made.
Having surrounded Māyā, thousands of the hosts of Maheśvara,
their stains quickly vanished and entirely purified, took their seats in the sky.
Now, behind them, many thousands of Indras with stainless crests sat down for the sake of guarding the one of manifold virtues.
Now, behind those lords of gods,
thousands of myriads of gods belonging to the realm of desire were seated in the sky, without support.
Behind the hosts of gods were the asuras, and behind the asuras sat the multitudes of double-tongued serpents,
along with yakṣas of deformed appearance and throngs of rākṣasas.
By this rite, the glorious sky was filled with hundreds of thousands of immortals;
indeed, through the Giver of Boons, exceedingly pure merit was accumulated.
Thus, he of great majesty and mindfulness, having passed away from the Tuṣita heaven,
assumed the form of an elephant with six tusks, resembling a white boar.
While she was lying on her heroic bed, observing the *poṣadha* vow and dressed in pure garments,
he— skilled in mindfulness and clear comprehension— descended into his mother’s womb.
And at the break of day, she told it to her beloved husband:
"O best of kings, a white royal elephant has entered my womb."
Having heard that, the king spoke to the assembled fortune-tellers:
"Tell me the true result and ripening of all these dreams."
There, when questioned by the king himself, the soothsayers declared:
"One bearing the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
Be joyful, O best of men, for he has appeared within your lineage—
he who upholds the earth, the hero-womb, the incomparable being, the Great Being.
O tiger among heroes, just as I have personally acquired from the ancient teachers, there are two paths for him that are not otherwise.

If they shall dwell in a house, he becomes a lord of the earth, possessing the seven treasures and great supernatural power; ever accompanied by victory, he has a retinue of hundreds of thousands of kings.
Then indeed, having renounced the earth consisting of the four continents, he will go forth;
he will become a Buddha, one who is not led by others, a leader of men and gods.
The Śākyan lady also related her dream to her beloved husband:
"A white lordly elephant, having burst through my side, has entered my womb."
Having heard this, the king spoke to the assembled fortune-tellers:
"Tell me everything that occurred in his dream, along with its true result and ripening."
There, when questioned by the king himself, the soothsayers declared:
"One bearing the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
If, however, he dwells in the midst of a household, he will conquer the entire earth;
he shall obtain a thousand sons who are brave and such heroic men.
Then, having cast aside the earth filled with infinite jewels, he went forth.
"He will become a Buddha in the world, omniscient and all-seeing.
Thus spoke Mahābrahmā.
In a dream, a woman saw the sun entering her womb from the sky;
she shall give birth to a fortunate jewel among women.
The lord of this [world] becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The woman who in a dream beheld the moon entering her womb from the sky shall give birth to a son who is a god among men.
He becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch of power.
The woman who, in her dream, beheld the sun entering her womb from the sky,
shall give birth to one whose limbs are marked with excellence.
Thus he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch of power.
The woman who in her dream beheld a white elephant entering her womb shall give birth to one endowed with the essence of an elephant's strength.
Thus he becomes a Buddha, one who has awakened to the Dharma that is the goal.
The queen was asked: "What do you carry? She replied: "A universal monarch."
I bear within my womb a universal monarch, a supreme man, a tiger among kings, whose golden body illuminates the interior and who is endowed with the most excellent marks.
The gods in the sky raised their voices, saying: "He will become a Buddha, not a universal monarch (cakravartin). Then Mahābrahmā spoke this verse:
You are the elephant, the most excellent of jewels, who removes the force of passion and power;
you are the lamp of the world that dispels the darkness, gloom, and delusion;
you are the treasury of virtues, the bearer of an immeasurable mine of gems.
You uphold the royal seer Samaruci, whose wheel is unimpeded.
The goddess said:
Just as passion and hatred do not overcome me upon perceiving the womb of the Lord of Men,
there is no doubt that he will be of equal splendor, just as these words issue forth.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the mother moves with ease, stands with ease, sits with ease, and lies down with ease, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, no weapon can penetrate the body of the Bodhisattva’s mother; neither poison, nor fire, nor lightning can prevail against her, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, celestial maidens keep watch over the Bodhisattva’s mother with divine ointments, massages, and perfumes, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother has her body clothed in divine garments and wears divine ornaments, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the mother comes to possess divine fragrances, divine garlands, divine unguents, and divine foods, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb...

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, those who constitute her inner circle consider it most essential to listen to and place their trust in her, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Through the power of the Bodhisattva alone, they invite her with whatever needs to be done. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, no one passes above the Bodhisattva’s mother, not even a bird; she remains free from illness and free from suffering. She possesses a balanced digestive faculty, neither too cold nor too hot, due to the seasonal transformation brought about by the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes a recipient of exquisite foods and drinks, of the finest flavors, the highest flavors, attained flavors, and freshly prepared flavors, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes free from passion; she practices a celibate life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, pure, and complete. Not even a thought of passion arises in that supreme woman toward any man, not even toward King Śuddhodana himself, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother observes the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), and these remain perfectly undertaken from before, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, all those Naga kings and lords of Nagas—whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth—all approach the residence and scatter divine sandalwood powder, divine *tamāla* leaf powder, scatter divine *agaru* powder, scatter divine *kesara* powder, and scatter divine flowers. They honor her with perfect worship and they honored her with complete worship. Having scattered divine sandalwood powder, they scatter divine *agaru* powder, divine *kesara* powder, and divine *tamāla* powder. Having scattered divine loose flowers, they [honored her] for its completion.

Having honored her for the sake of worship and having honored her for the sake of complete worship, they circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, all the kings of gold and lords of gold, as well as the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika realms—all of them approached the residence, scattered divine sandalwood powder, scattered divine aloe-wood powder, scattered divine tamāla-leaf powder, and scattered divine loose flowers; and having honored her for the sake of completion, having honored her for the sake of perfect worship, and having honored her for the sake of pure worship, they circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain too low, nor does he remain too high; he does not remain with his face downward, nor with his face upward, nor on his left side, nor in a squatting position. Rather, he remains on his right side, sitting cross-legged. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he remains unsullied and pure, not defiled by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other impurity. Indeed, the Bodhisattva remains in his mother’s womb with his limbs cleansed, bathed, and radiant. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he sees his mother, and the Bodhisattva’s mother also sees him as he dwells within her womb like a figure of refined gold; and having seen him illuminating her womb like a figure of refined gold, she becomes joyful.
Just as if a beryl gem were placed in a crystal casket upon her hip and lap, even so does the mother behold the Bodhisattva,
illuminating her womb like a statue of refined gold.

The hosts of gods come with joyful minds to inquire whether the Bodhisattva has had a pleasant night and a pleasant day; and the Bodhisattva greets those inquiring hosts of gods by raising his right hand, yet he does not distress his mother. While the Bodhisattva remains in his mother’s womb, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, maruts, rākṣasas, and piśācas do not leave him, day or night. Furthermore, no talk of attachment is spoken there—neither talk associated with sensual desires nor any other untruthful speech. On the contrary, they speak only of the excellence of the Bodhisattva: in terms of form, essence, power, color, fame, and roots of merit. The honoring of the Bodhisattva while he is in his mother’s womb never ceases: there are divine musical instruments, divine aloe-wood incense, a divine rain of flowers, and a divine rain of powders. Thousands of apsarases sing and dance nearby. The mother of the Bodhisattva shares laughter and conversation with thousands of celestial maidens. And when the mother of the Bodhisattva is fast asleep, the celestial maidens gently fan her with garlands of mandārava flowers, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself. Moreover, this is the unsurpassed perfection of the descent into the womb within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
And behold now another marvel in that assembly of gods:
how vast was the discourse that arose, generating supreme rapture!
For them there is no talk of sensual pleasures, nor talk of apsarases, nor talk of song;
for them there is no talk of instrumental music, nor talk of food, nor talk of drink.
No talk of ornaments arises among them, nor does any talk of clothing;
even the thought of vehicles or gardens does not occur to their minds.
Excellent! The splendor of the Guide, who possesses the power of merit, outshines the world including the gods; this story flourishes there.
"How excellent is the descent into the womb, corresponding to his past deeds, for one who has reached the further shore!"—
thus were various kinds of expanded discourses uttered in the midst of that assembly.
"Excellent!"—with such disinterested expressions they pass that time;
even this discourse of the one of supreme intelligence blossoms in the midst of the assembly.
Thus, speaking many kinds of discourse, the hosts of gods take delight,
conversing about their form, complexion, splendor, excellence, and heroic conduct.

The mother of all Bodhisattvas gives birth when the tenth month is complete. Śākyan Subhūti sent word to the king: "Let the Queen come here; she will give birth here. The king replied: "She shall come, and we will erect a Salabhañjaka pillar."
Make the Lumbinī grove very beautiful, cleared of grass, stumps, leaves, and refuse; fill it with heaps of excellent fragrant flowers and make it sweet-smelling with scented water.
And in the Lumbinī grove, let the winds blow, their bodies perfumed with the scent of *tāla* leaves;
let them carry the fragrance of nectar and cause intoxication to arise.
May clouds from the sky, laden with the fragrance of the finest aloeswood incense,
descend and cover that Lumbinī grove, which is strewn with the finest powders and fragrant juices.
And fashion for each one an excellent cloistered walk with fine linen, silk, wool, and *kauśika* silk, just like those of the preeminent gods in heaven from the wish-fulfilling trees.
The gods and goddesses, taking perfumes and garlands, came to the Lumbinī grove.
Wearing earrings of crystal jewels, with garments slipping off and long strings of pearls hanging down,
they take up perfumes and garlands and fly forth along the path of the sky.
One [goddess] was carrying a grove of mandārava flowers, another was holding saṅgerī blossoms; one carried yellow sandalwood, and another, celestial garments from the wish-fulfilling tree.
Taking garlands grown on land and in water, as well as jewels and ornaments, the Apsarases, with joyful hearts, turned their faces toward Jambudvīpa.
Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, carrying parasols made of gold and jewels, flew through the sky.
The atmosphere was filled with variegated crystal, maṇi, and musāragalva stones resembling gabled chambers,
and with hundreds of banners raised high upon silk cloths.
Resembling the breath of an elephant, the autumn clouds shine in the path of the birds,
fragrant with the scent of excellent, sweet-smelling flowers, intermingled with lotuses, water-lilies, and campaka blossoms.
The lords of serpents, greatly delighted, showered the city with clouds laden with fragrant water; there were hundreds of other such wonders as well.
Having entered that excellent forest, the Mother of the Victor, accompanied by her illusory friends,
wanders in her chariot of the mind like a celestial nymph skilled in the arts of love.
Having approached for the sake of sport and grasped a branch of a *pilakṣa* tree with her arm,
she gracefully stretched out at the time of the birth of that illustrious one.
Then ninety thousand daughters of the gods quickly assembled;
with palms joined in reverence and pure intentions, they spoke these words.
Today you shall give birth to one who will destroy old age and disease— one as delicate as the offspring of the immortals,
honored in heaven and on earth, the benefactor and well-wisher of both humans and gods.
Do not indeed give way to despondency; we shall perform your preparatory rites. Speak whatever must be done, and let it all be seen as already accomplished.
Then the four world-protectors, together with their retinues, quickly assembled;
with divine fly-whisks in their hands, they approached the Goddess from the right side.
All the hosts of gods, having enjoyed the illusory display, stood in the sky;
with garlands and perfumes in their hands, they shone together with their retinues.

Furthermore, the mother of a bodhisattva does not give birth to the bodhisattva while lying down or sitting, as other women do; rather, the mother of the bodhisattva gives birth to the bodhisattva while standing. Mindful and clearly conscious, the bodhisattva emerges from her right side without causing her any pain.
For it is from the right side that the best of men are born;
all those tigers among men become dwellers in this place.
Why was her side not pierced, and why did no pain arise for that mother of the Conqueror after she had given birth to the Supreme among Men?
The Tathāgatas manifest in a mind-made form;
thus, the side is not broken, nor does pain arise.
The Bodhisattva, weary from dwelling in the womb, takes seven steps.
As soon as he was born, he took seven strides upon the earth;
he gazed at the directions and let out a great laugh.
What is the reason stated here that one traverses seven steps, neither eight nor six? Listen now to the traditional teaching on this matter.
Exhausted by his dwelling in the womb, the Sage, who is the benefactor of the entire world,
then proceeded with speed toward this final dwelling in a womb.
But when he had taken seven steps, the hosts of gods descended;
suddenly, from the guardians of the world, the Sage was held upon their laps.
Then there arose a rain of divine flower droplets,
strewn with the finest mandārava blossoms and thick with celestial sandalwood.
For a long time, the foremost of the gods released intense and sublime incense for the sake of adorning him of supreme intelligence.
And for whatever purpose the Peerless One gazes upon the directions,
regarding that as well, I shall declare the authoritative tradition and the delightful instruction.
Among beings, whether among gods or humans, there exists no one for whom such an occurrence takes place,
nor even the descent into the womb.
When the side of the Mother of the Victors becomes radiant like a firefly or gold,
then the Omniscient One is born in his final existence.
As soon as he was born, that mind arose in the Preeminent Speaker:
"Is there anyone of equal intelligence to me who can turn back this reasoning?"
Some suffer through wandering in saṃsāra just as I do;
for this purpose, the Sun-like Person gazes upon all directions.
Then, looking toward the directions, the best of speakers beheld thousands of millions of deities; at that, he let out a laugh.
As soon as I was born, the deities belonging to the host of Māra said to me:
"You shall become a universal monarch with a great treasury over the four continents."
Then a smile arose within him: "Beings do not understand me;
I shall become an omniscient one, all-seeing, the supreme among men."
Thus do the teachers of the instructions praise this ripening;
for in such a way has the teaching of the lions among men been well-proclaimed.
I pay homage to that most excellent Jina, who, while standing amidst well-flowered *śāla* trees, was supported by his mother as she gave birth to the Hero.
As soon as he was born, the Sugata stood upon the earth with level feet;
he took seven steps and gazed toward all directions.
And as he was walking, a fan and a parasol followed him,
so that gadflies and mosquitoes might not fall upon the body of the Knower of the Best.
Immediately upon the birth of the Sugata, the gods first received the Conqueror; afterwards, humans held him, who is unsurpassed, in their arms.
The gods received the Sugata, who was endowed with the thirty-two marks;
afterwards, humans carried him, who is unsurpassed, upon their laps.
The lamps of men were extinguished, for the world had been illumined by the Sugata, who was born like a torch-bearing banner for gods and humans.
When the Sugata was born, his kinsmen ran about seeking water;
then, even before them, wells full to the brim overflowed from their mouths.
Two streams of water welled up— one cool, one warm—
to bathe the Sugata there as if he were an image of refined gold.

Furthermore, when the Sugata was born, the Bodhisattva’s mother remained unharmed and uninjured, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself; her womb remained full yet not distended. Moreover, immediately upon the birth of the Bodhisattva, in the midst of four hundred million continents, a preeminent *aśvattha* tree-staff appeared on the central circle of the earth. In the intermediate island, a sandalwood grove appeared, which served for the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment and use, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself. There, thousands of sons of gods and thousands of apsarases arrived, bringing perfumes and garlands for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva. One son of a god asked another son of a god: "Where are you going? He replied:
This supreme consort of the lord of men shall give birth to that excellent child, whose womb is as fair as a blossomed, choice lotus;
he who shall attain the highest goal upon the circle of the earth.
Having slain Māra together with his army, I approach that Hero.
His limbs were unstained by the impurities of the womb,
like a supreme lotus born in the water;
his body was radiant, shining like the rising sun.
He overcomes the gods together with Brahmā.
Then, as soon as he was born into the family of the Śākyas,
the steadfast one took seven steps here;
having surveyed the directions, he uttered a lion’s roar.
"This is now my final existence," he thought;
and in the sky there appeared a brilliantly shining parasol, adorned with the finest jewels and pearls, outshining all others in its splendor.
Many sons of the gods held aloft in the sky a canopy of shaken mandārava flowers.
They held aloft in the sky an excellent golden parasol, its color resembling the sun, a conch shell, or a lotus;
then, fans were released and began to wave.
Having grasped the Victor with their hands, they fanned him.
Then there arose a fragrant, pleasantly warm, abundant, light, lovely, and beneficial breeze for human beings—
a propitious, delightful, and cool breeze.
Two streams of water rose up from the sky.
Then, from the peak of Mount Meru, various kinds of upper garments were released and spread out on all sides;
they were thoroughly perfumed by scents wafting in every direction.
They caused the firm earth, consisting of six layers, to tremble.
In palaces made of gold, silver, and beautiful jewels, the gods, accompanied by music,
proclaimed the birth of the Conqueror born of noble lineage as they gazed upon him.
They beautified the sky, including the moon, the sun, and the stars.
This great seer, having crossed over the great flood of the world— including its gods, nāgas, and yakṣas—
will thereafter reach the secure state in the one direction.
The gods, being greatly delighted, proclaimed this in the sky.

Immediately upon the birth of the Bodhisattva, five hundred Śākya youths headed by Sundarananda appeared; five hundred maidens headed by Yaśodharā; five hundred servants headed by Chandaka; five hundred horses headed by Kaṇṭhaka; five hundred young elephants headed by the young elephant Candana; and five hundred treasures manifested themselves. Five hundred kings were sent forth to celebrate his victory and prosperity.

King Śuddhodana gave the command: "Turn the Queen back from this very place; someone else shall carry the Bodhisattva. The divine son Viśvakarman fashioned a palanquin made of jewels. [The King asked: "Who will carry this palanquin? The Four Great Kings presented themselves, saying, "We shall carry the Essence of Beings. Then the Bodhisattva, together with his mother Māyā, ascended the palanquin. Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā cleared the way.

King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers: "Lead the prince, the Increaser of the Śākyas, from this very place to the temple of the gods to pay homage at the feet of Queen Abhayā. At the king's word, those ministers led the prince, the Increaser of the Śākyas, from there to the temple of the gods to pay homage at the feet of Queen Abhayā. Now, thinking, "We shall have him bow his head at her feet," the prince’s feet appeared before Queen Abhayā; Queen Abhayā then bowed her head at the prince’s feet.
When the Great Lord of the World, the Teacher of the lords of men, entered the shrines without desire,
and they caused him to be saluted with their heads, then his feet would manifest from that [place].
Then the goddess Abhayā said: "It is not fitting for him to pay homage to me;
if he were to offer salutation to another, his head would surely split into seven pieces."

As soon as the prince was born, all beings down to the Avīci hell became prosperous and happy. The gods offered him homage, and the fearless queen, greatly rejoiced, paid him obeisance. [These are] the verses for the raising up.
Since all matters were favorable for the king upon the birth of the preeminent leader of the world,
he was given the name Sarvārthasiddha, "Accomplisher of All Aims."
When the prince had entered the royal palace, the king said to the domestic priest:
"Quickly seek out brahmins who are skilled in the qualities and rules for discerning marks."
And having understood this, the gods named Maheśvaras, who have mastery over their own minds,
[will protect you] so that the assemblies of twice-born ones, possessing unskillful characteristics, shall not form false conceptualizations.
Free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, eight thousand excellent Maheśvaras approached the Teacher of gods and men who had just been born, with their hands joined in reverence.
Clad in pure garments and standing at the gate of the royal palace, they addressed the silent door-keeper with voices as sweet as the song of the kalaviṅka bird:
"Approach Śuddhodana and say this: 'We are experts in the rules governing the marks and qualities [of a great man].'"
Eight thousand remain; they would enter if it is approved by you.
Having assented with "So be it," the king's doorkeeper entered the royal palace and,
with palms joined in reverence and a joyful heart, spoke to the protector of the earth.
Rule for a long time, O conqueror of enemies, a kingdom with incomparable, excellent, and radiant glory;
at your gate stand those like unto the gods, desiring to enter.
Those with perfectly full and stainless eyes, possessing sweet voices and the gait of an elephant in rut—of them I have no doubt; they are not human beings, but sons of gods.
As they walk back and forth, the dust of the earth does not touch their noble feet, nor does it show their footprints upon the ground; this too is a marvel.
With profound and steady gestures, noble appearance, and tranquil gaze,
they produce vast joy in the people who behold them.
And another marvel occurred: no shadow of their bodies was seen, nor was any sound of their joints heard as they walked.
O lord of the best of men, you have undoubtedly come to see the excellent son;
rejoice and pay homage, and behold the gods who are not born from a womb.
O excellent Maruts, you are undoubtedly like Śrī herself— holding choice garlands and perfumes in your hands, graceful in your gestures, with bodies enchanting to the mind, and shining with splendor.
Having heard these words, Śuddhodana, his body trembling with joy, said: "Speak quickly! Let them enter the magnificent palace."
For what reason? Such characteristics do not belong to ordinary persons;
nor does such supernatural power as you describe exist among human beings.
Then that door-keeper, having approached Maheśvara, spoke these words,
bowing low with palms joined in reverence, joyful and delighted in heart.
The king rejoices: "May you enter the palace of the bull among kings, which is like a celestial city, having been authorized by the lord of men."
Having heard these words, eight thousand of the most excellent Maheśvaras entered the royal palace of that foremost leader of an unconquered lineage.
King Śuddhodana, too, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose with his retinue, his body moved by the power of reverence.
The bull among kings said to them: "Welcome; may there be affection for all of you.
We are pleased by the sight of you and by your power of tranquility and self-control."
"We have these excellent seats available; please remain here, sirs, out of favor toward us."
Then, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, you whose actions are irreproachable, sit down upon those seats with feet variegated and purified by many jewels.
Having waited for some time, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty hear the purpose for which we have come here."
O Lord of Men, a son has indeed been born to you, whose every limb is faultless, who is the beauty of the world, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks.
We too are skilled in marks and capable of discerning the characteristics of virtues and faults,
were it not that we perceive in you the gravity of one who possesses the form of a Great Man.
He said: "Come, behold my son, who brings joy to gods and men, whose renown is secure, and who has reached the perfection of the marks and qualities."
Then, having taken Guṇadhara in a soft Kācalindika woolen blanket,
he placed the Moon of Orators upon his hip before the best of gods.
Beholding from afar the prowess of the One Possessing Ten Powers,
the Great Lords are seen falling to the surface of the earth with their crowns slipping from their heads.

They then informed the king: "It is a gain for you, Great King, a great blessing for you, that such a Great Man has been born in your family, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. They are as follows:"
Even, joyful, long, and extended, with the fifth being the cleft of the thighs;
like that of an antelope, broad-based, with a sheathed [penis], and like a nyagrodha tree—these are the ten.
The webbed fingers and toes are soft and fully developed; the hands and feet have a single mark with upward-pointing tips;
the skin is smooth; there is a space between the fingers like that of a swan; and the body has seven prominent elevations—these are the ten.
The mark of a beautiful torso, the golden-hued lion-like chest, and the fifth, the even white [teeth];
the even, abundant [tongue], the Brahma-voice, and the eyelashes like those of a blue bull—these are the ten;
together with the hair-tuft and the cranial protuberance on the head, the Protector possesses the thirty-two marks.

In the southern region, there was another young brahmin, the son of a wealthy brahmin from Ujjayinī, who was dark and black in complexion, wise, skillful, and intelligent. He had studied the Vedas, the mantras, and the treatises under his teacher. Having completed his studies of the Vedas, he departed from his home, went to the Vindhya Mountains, and entered the life of a wandering ascetic (*ṛṣipravrajyā*). Subsisting on roots, fruits, and leaves, he lived a life of austerity. Thereupon, having established a hermitage on the Vindhya Mountains, through diligent application, exertion, and effort along the path of practice, he accomplished the four *dhyānas* and realized the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). Having attained the four *dhyānas*, possessing the five superknowledges, being highly learned and a master of the Vedas, the sage Asita became renowned and well-known for his equanimity. The sage Asita was celebrated throughout the heavens, a traveler of the sky, possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*). Together with about five hundred disciples, he resided at that hermitage in Nālaka. Seeing the earthquake that occurred at the moment of the Bodhisattva’s birth, seeing the great radiance, hearing the delightful and non-human sounds of singing and instrumental music, seeing divine showers of flowers falling, and seeing thousands of millions of gods and thousands of *apsarases* flying through the air toward the east with celestial garlands and perfumes in their hands, as well as hundreds of other wonders, his hair stood on end with joy. "What is this today in Jambudvīpa? By whose power is the earth [shaking] today?"

A hundred wonders appeared and the earth trembled. Then that seer (*ṛṣi*) surveyed the whole of Jambudvīpa with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). "Whose is this power and majesty? From where do such delightful sounds of song and instrumental music issue forth? Why are hundreds of divine musical instruments heard? Why are gods and celestial maidens (*devakanyā*) seen? Why do showers of divine flowers rain down? And why are thousands of moons and suns visible? Why does the fire not blaze in the thousands of hells? And why have beings become endowed with exclusive happiness? Thus he saw with his divine eye: "In the city of Kapilavastu to the east, a son has been born to King Śuddhodana—one who has performed merit, who is illustrious and of great majesty, by whose power and majesty hundreds of such wonders have appeared in Jambudvīpa. At the proper time and place, I shall see the prince. Then, knowing the right time and occasion, surrounded by many disciples, he traveled through the air by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and arrived at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s inner apartments in Kapilavastu. When the ministers and the doorkeeper saw the seer, they rose up and asked: "What does the Blessed One command? For what purpose has he come? What is the reason for his visit? The seer said: "Announce to Śuddhodana: 'The seer Asita desires an audience. The doorkeeper informed the king: "The seer Asita desires an audience. Upon hearing of the arrival of the renowned, famous, and highly fortunate seer Asita, King Śuddhodana said to the doorkeeper: "Let the seer enter. The doorkeeper ran out and announced to the seer: "May your honor enter."

The seer entered. Upon seeing the seer, the king, together with his harem, rose to meet him. "We pay homage to the Blessed One; may the Blessed One be seated. The seer, having caused the king to prosper with cries of victory, sat down. The king asked, "What, Blessed One, is the purpose of your visit? The seer said, "I wish to see your son. At that time, the prince had entered a certain peaceful meditative absorption (*śāntasamādhi*). It occurred to them, "The prince is asleep. Then the king said to the seer, "Blessed One, wait a moment; the prince has just now fallen asleep. The seer said, "Great King, the prince is not sleeping. [The king looked at] the prince...

Clinging to the root, he saw the prince awake. The king was amazed at the seer’s great fortune. The king commanded, "Bring the prince to the seer. Taking the prince in a fine deerskin rug, he was brought before the seer. Even from afar, the seer beheld the marks of a Great Man upon the prince's body; placing his joined palms to his head, he stood in attendance. Having paid homage, the prince was received by the seer. The seer then examined the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the prince.

And there in the royal palace, the seer heard the title "Universal Monarch" being applied to the prince. The fortune-tellers had prophesied that the prince would become a Universal Monarch. The seer thought to himself: "He will not become a Universal Monarch; he will become a Buddha in the world. Having observed those marks, [he realized]: "These are not the marks of a Universal Monarch; such are the marks of Buddhas. He will become a Buddha in the world. And before long I shall pass away; I shall not see this jewel, I shall not hear his Dharma, and I shall not behold his supreme assembly. The seer wept and shed tears. King Śuddhodana, seeing the seer Asita weeping, became distressed along with his harem. "Why do you weep upon seeing the blessed prince? Do you foresee some misfortune for the prince? "When the prince was just born, the earth shook in six ways, a radiance appeared in the world, he was honored by thousands of gods, celestial rains of flowers fell, and thousands of divine musical instruments resounded, their sounds issuing forth. When the prince was born, five hundred boys were born in Kapilavastu, five hundred girls, five hundred male slaves, five hundred female slaves, five hundred young elephants, five hundred horses, and five hundred treasures appeared. Five hundred kings sent greetings of victory and prosperity, and many other wonders and marvels occurred. Yet the Blessed One weeps upon seeing the prince! O Blessed One, tell me this: do you foresee some misfortune for the prince? The seer replied: "Great King..."

"I see no misfortune whatsoever for the prince. O Great King, such great beings appear in the world only once in a long while. This great being has appeared; he will become a Buddha in the world. Yet I am old and shall not see it. He will teach the Dharma that leads to peace, to the noble state, and to Nirvana, but I shall not hear it. I shall not see his excellent assembly, nor shall I see the miraculous transformations of a Buddha. Therefore, O Great King, seeing this great misfortune of my own, I weep. Having thus definitively prophesied that the Bodhisattva would become a Buddha in the world for four reasons, the seer departed.
Having abandoned the hindrances, listen to me with a one-pointed mind,
just as Asita did when lamentation arose for the Śākya prince.
There was a great seer named Asita who dwelt in the region of the Vindhya mountains;
he was a high-souled one of fixed resolve, a great Kapila with excellent body-hair.
Skilled in the forest scriptures and possessing the five superknowledges,
he dwells on the peak of Mount Kailāsa like Dhanapati, the lord of the Guhyakas.
Thus he dwelt at the head of the forest, subsisting on a harsh livelihood of uncultivated roots and fruits,
together with his disciple Nālaka and many others.
Practicing the ten wholesome deeds, delighting in tranquility and self-control, he instructs others;
having reached the perfection of divine qualities, the seer is endowed with supreme virtue.
A vast radiance appeared, and supramundane joy arose without confusion;
beings experienced absolute happiness, and the earth trembled.
Seated there, he saw mandārava flowers and divine kalpa-flowers fallen upon the surface of the earth.
Asita saw hundreds of ornaments scattered in the sky,
and thousands of celestial maidens rushing through the expanse of the heavens.
He hears the sweet songs of the kinnarīs in the mountain caves,
and he calms the mountain rivers flowing along their banks, whose currents are filled with blossoms.
And he beholds a vast radiance all around in the ten directions,
suddenly surging forth like the rays of the young sun.
Having seen these and many other such wonders,
Asita’s hair stood on end and his mind became filled with thought.
But indeed, the great earth trembled, and drums resounded in the vault of heaven;
the world was illuminated, and showers of flowers rained down.
The moon and sun do not shine; the salt waters, their depths turned black, are agitated;
and the floods of water, filled with flowers, appear with lotuses for their upper garments.
All these excellent trees, covered with untimely blossoms, are today laden with fruit and flowers; fragrant scents waft abroad.
Yet the fires do not blaze today throughout the thousands of hells;
nor do the beings perishing in the intermediate spaces of the world experience suffering.
Furthermore, neither hunger nor thirst arises in my body as it did before;
my heart is gladdened, yet what indeed will happen today?
Why indeed, with such exceedingly powerful and exuberant laughter, do these celestial maidens run toward the eastern quarter, carrying sandalwood powder?
Who indeed has arisen today in Jambudvīpa with such great majesty? By whose fame has this great glory come to one so renowned?
Such a sign as this occurs in the world for whomever it may be;
such are the portents that appear upon the arising of the Buddhas.
He hears the hosts of immortals in the sky as they descend toward the earth:
"A Lord of the World has appeared; he shall become a Buddha, one who cannot be led astray."
Then, with a joyful mind, having heard the hosts of gods in the expanse of the sky, he thought:
"Today, a Buddha—the essence of the heroes among men—has appeared in the world."
The seer surveyed the whole of Jambudvīpa with his divine eyes and saw him who was born in the clan of the Śākyas, the son of Śuddhodana.
Having seen this, a great report concerning his awakening has arisen in all directions;
there the word "Buddha" circulates, and I shall see him in due time.
And they too, with axes in hand, wearing well-made black antelope skins as upper garments and clad in robes of bark and rags, arrived bringing fruits and water.
In the sky, without support, along the path of the wind... the seer proceeded;
having manifested supernatural power, he arrived at Kapilavastu in an instant.
At the foot of the Himavat mountains, he beheld a delightful city protected by the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha),
unassailable by enemy foes and as exceedingly beautiful as the city of the thirty gods.
The seer entered the city of the gods for the purpose of seeing the Śākyas.
He entered the city, which was filled with people intent on buying and selling in the marketplaces,
and crowded with joyful crowds of men and throngs of delighted horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry.
Approaching with his mind, he entered the gate into the inner apartments... the residence of Śuddhodana, which was like the abode of the king of the gods.
He beholds that palace-tower, awakened by its excellent windows, lattices, and balconies,
shining in the sky like a mountain peak that has fallen there.
In that preeminent celestial palace, the gabled chambers possess the splendor of silver;
their cornices shine like the blazing flames of a sacrificial fire.
The beautiful inner chambers, resembling pure conch shells and necklaces of pearls,
shine like the sun in its stainless brilliance, fashioned as if they were moons.
There they are seen, set upon well-crafted slabs of beryl,
with rows of house-pins that have the colors of lightning-charged clouds.
They see archways made of gold, resembling flames of fire;
they shine like moons fashioned from the radiance of the stainless sun.
In some places, those resembling dark clouds of the rainy season seem to pour forth water;
in other places, resembling the sun, they emerge together with stars as if resting upon it.
In some places, flocks of cats suddenly swoop down there;
and in other places, they are terrified by peacocks as they fly together.
In various places, cuckoos in their cages warble sweetly; here and there, parrots and mainas are distracted by the tinkling of their ornaments.
Pure, square, and fashioned in the ten directions,
it is well-constructed and impregnable to enemies, having been thoroughly prepared by the master of the cord.
In this place filled with heaps of many kinds of jewels, upon ground composed of various multicolored masses, the lion sits; he trembles at the rising sun.
Accompanied by female attendants and courtesans, and provided with vehicles and carriages,
he entered [the city], which was filled with eunuchs and marked by the variegated colors of saffron robes.
Having reached the palace gate, which was crowded with hundreds of servants and vehicles, filled with noble people, pure and fragrant, and free from obstruction, the matted-haired ascetic entered.
And in the assembly hall, the woman was seen standing in agitation,
her hand grasping a sword, yet speaking with words of exceeding sweetness and beauty.
"He is dark-complexioned, distinguished, profound, and well-versed in the proper methods of all the scriptures;
inform the King of the Śākyas that he has arrived. He spoke thus to the doorkeeper.
I am known as Kāla; by lineage, I am Bhāradvāja. I was born in the noble region of Ārya, and I dwell upon the peak of the Vindhya mountains.
"Very well, noble sir," the Śrutadhara replied, and having heard those words of the king in their entirety, he brought them [to the queen] and caused her to enter.
Having been granted leave, he entered the celestial abode of Siṃhahanu,
which was crowded with throngs of apsarases, like Indra gone to the Nandana grove.
Asita by name caused [the king] to celebrate with cries of victory and presented him with fruits;
the King accepted them and said, "Welcome, Blessed One!"
Then, having been invited, he sat down upon that excellent seat which had been prepared— made of gold with eight legs, covered with a most variegated rug, and adorned with jewels.
Seated upon his couch, the seer of great supernatural power, possessed of the five super-knowledges,
was invited for a meal by King Śuddhodana himself.
"A great meal has been prepared; please accept it, O Blessed One, and may you be free from ailment.
We wish to see your son, if it should be agreeable to you."
Welcome and well-disposed are you; the lovely prince has been sleeping for some time. Once he has awakened, you shall behold him like a statue of refined gold.

And when the prince had awakened, they presented him with a fine woollen blanket adorned with eight auspicious signs, just as one might present the sun appearing through a rift in the clouds to his mother.
Seeing him placed upon the fine woolen blanket like a pair of earrings, the best of sages rose quickly and received the prince in his arms.
Taking him on his hip and observing that he was endowed with the thirty-two marks as well as the secondary characteristics, he, equal to Indra, wept.
To him, whose eyes were filled with tears, King Śuddhodana said this:
"Why now, having seen the prince, has dejection arisen in you?"
O Brahmin, having seen him who, on the very day of his birth, took seven steps facing toward the unsurpassed, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
On the day he was born, those who stood in the sky holding a parasol and a fan— having seen this, O Brahmā, why do you weep?
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him by whose birth on that day the entire world was illuminated.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose day of birth two wells sprang up from the sky.
O Brahmin, having seen him on whose birth day the gods held up a parasol in the sky, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, having seen him on whose birth day the gods scattered mandārava flowers, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, having seen him on whose day of birth the unconscious earth itself trembled, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing that on the day he was born, the salt-water ocean with its dark depths was agitated.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him on whose day of birth the celestial drums resounded in the sky.
On the day he was born, five hundred sons of the Śākyas were also born;
having seen this, O Brahmin, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
On the day he was born, five hundred Śākya maidens were also born;
having seen this, O Brahmin, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, five hundred slaves were born to me; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, five hundred of my slave-girls were also born; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred horses were born for me; having seen this, why do you weep? I wish to hear the reason.
O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred young elephants were also born; having seen this, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, five hundred treasures revealed their mouths; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, the kings of the mandalas bowed down before me; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, whose royal preceptors come to visit him.
O Brahmin, having seen what it is that people become joyful, happy, and elated, why do you weep upon seeing it? I wish to hear [the reason].
"O Brahmin, dispel your grief; become joyful in mind and obtain happiness!
This one shall become a king, a protector of the earth possessed of the seven treasures."
When this had been said, Asita, having called out "Sita," spoke these words while wiping away his tears: "He has been prophesied by the seers..."
That lion among men, resembling a mass of fire and the rising sun, will not remain a king or a ruler of men;
he will become an unsurpassed Teacher.
For he has leaped across the three realms of existence in three strides without remainder,
like a great parasol in the rainy season. Such is the benefit when the Dharma is well-practiced.
One who practices the Dharma does not go to an evil rebirth.
For whatever destination a heedless man who practices unrighteousness goes,
that very unrighteousness practiced by him destroys him, like a black snake caught in one's own hand.
For neither dharma nor adharma both have an equal ripening;
adharma leads to hell, while dharma attains the heavenly realm.
For indeed, dharma protects the practitioner of dharma,
just as a great umbrella [protects] during the rainy season;
protected by dharma, I am a guardian of dharma.
The prince is well; he has [recovered] the bones of another.

Having fed that brahmin along with his retinue, he was dismissed by the brahmin Brahmāyu. That brahmin then went to the hermitage and saw the young student Dharmapāla there at the hermitage. Then they were all amazed, thinking, "The family priest has truly understood well."

The Blessed One said: "It may be, monks, that you might think the brahmin named Brahmāyus at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Because, monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the brahmin named Brahmāyus. It may be, monks, that you might think the son of the brahmin Brahmāyus named Dharmapāla at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. For at that time and on that occasion, he was Rāhula."
Hmāyu had a son named Dharmapāla; even then he was known by me, and now too I have discovered the long-lost Śākyamustī.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the illustrious Dharmapāla.

The monks said to the Blessed One, "The arrow discharged by the Blessed One has gone a great distance. The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have discharged an arrow a great distance; at another time as well, monks. [They asked], "At another time too, Blessed One? The Blessed One said, "Indeed, monks, at another time as well."

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king who ruled with great power, a vast treasury, and many vehicles; he was one who had performed meritorious deeds and possessed great majesty. His kingdom was now so extensive that his commands reached as far as Takṣaśilā. Having established his younger brother on the throne, he came from Vārāṇasī to Takṣaśilā. He then resided in Takṣaśilā. Meanwhile, another king surrounded the ruler of Vārāṇasī with a fourfold army. That brother sent a messenger from Vārāṇasī to Takṣaśilā, saying: "Come! I am besieged by this foreign army. When the king staying in Takṣaśilā heard this from the messengers, he wrote the name of the king who surrounded Vārāṇasī upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrja*). He wrapped that birch-bark around an arrow, bound it securely with thread, and shot it toward Vārāṇasī. That arrow struck the feet of the king of Vārāṇasī and shattered his foot-armor into pieces. The king was amazed at that man’s feat: "Oh, what energy and skillful aim! While standing in Vārāṇasī, he has shot an arrow here. It has traveled such a great distance and fallen at my feet; thus, I have not been killed by him. Then the king removed the birch-bark from the arrow and read it. On that very birch-bark, it was written as follows: [The message follows].
This fragment of a footstool stands for you in Takṣaśilā;
if you do not wish to die, withdraw from my kingdom.

Then, becoming even more terrified and alarmed, he thought, "I know that this arrow has come from Vārāṇasī; therefore, I have been filled with wonder, for it was shot while [the archer] was standing in Takṣaśilā. Right there at that spot, he built a shrine for the divine arrow, enshrined the arrow within the shrine, performed worship and honor, and then departed.

The Blessed One said: "It might be, monks, that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, the King of Kāśī was someone else who, while staying at Takṣaśilā, shot an arrow at Vārāṇasī. But it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that? Monks, at that time, on that occasion, I was the King of Kāśī. At that time too, I shot an arrow a great distance; even now, I have shot an arrow a great distance."
Thus ends the illustrious *Śarakṣepaṇajātaka*.

The monks said to the Blessed One, "How was Yaśodharā won by the Blessed One through his skill? The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was won by me through my skill; at another time as well, Yaśodharā was won by me through my skill. The monks said, "Was there another time, Blessed One? The Blessed One said, "There was another time, monks."

Long ago, monks, in the past, half a yojana from Mithilā there was a village named Yavakacchaka. Outside that village of Yavakacchaka was a village of smiths. There, the daughter of the head of the smith-village was named Amarā; she was gracious, beautiful to behold, wise, and endowed with eloquence. The son of the head of the village of Yavakacchaka was named Mahauṣadha; he was gracious, beautiful to behold, meritorious, and of great renown. While he was wandering through the fields and forests, he saw Amarā, the smith’s daughter, going along carrying food. He [gazed upon] her...

Mahauṣadha asked: "Bhadre, what is your name? What is your name? Amarā said: "That which is called the Tathāgata. Mahauṣadha said: "Bhadre, to whom do you belong? She said: "I belong to those who shall hear [this]. Mahauṣadha said: "Bhadre, by what means do you go? She said: "By that which is the parasol, I go. Mahauṣadha said: "Bhadre, where are you going? Amarā said: "I am going to that place where the One who has taken refuge has come. Then Mahauṣadha, the supreme scholar, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
"O immortals, you must surely be the daughter of a blacksmith;
for with your mind you truly know the field that lies in the direction of the south, where the sacrificial gift is given."
Now that girl had her head, eyes, and garments adorned, and she held a bowl of thin gruel in her hand. Then Mahauṣadha, the foremost of the wise, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, in verse:
By whom has your head been anointed and your eyes adorned?
By whom have your garments been purified, and by whom was this thin gruel prepared for you?
Then the smith’s daughter Amarā addressed the greatly wise Mahauṣadha with a verse:
Anointing the head with oil, the *lāsaka* massage,
nakedness while wearing clothes, the *śuddhā*, the *kṣudrā*, and the *nodakā* [are forms of *nagnikā*].
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
If indeed that oil and collyrium were for you out of greed,
and those festive garments were but few, yet the rain has been sent down by the King.
Then that smith’s daughter was going along, carrying a vessel of savory broth covered with a white cloth during the rain. Thereupon, the wise Mahauṣadha addressed the smith’s daughter Amarā in verse:
Since you carry this well covered with snow, frost, and dust for the sake of life,
I ask you, O immortal one, about this matter.
Whose food do you take away, O charming one?
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha Mahāprāpta with a verse:
...I take away the food from the tree.
Then, indeed, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
"Your father was thirty years old when he became a *nelāyaka*, and your grandfather was likewise;
you yourself are ten years old by birth—thus do I understand it, girl."
Mahauṣadha said:
When he has gone forth, his mother becomes sorrowful and dejected;
she searches for him, asking, "Where has he gone, my immortal one?"
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
Where those who have died breathe again, where the burnt is not burnt again,
and where a kinsman is slain by his own kin— there my father has gone.
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
The bellows of the smith blow; the charcoal burns again;
he hammers iron with iron; the father has gone to the smithy.
"Being asked for the way, tell us, O blessed lady, of the secure, straight, and direct path that is free from thorns; by it I shall go to Yavakacchaka."
Then, monks, the smith’s daughter addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
By whom trees with seven branches and double-layered leaves were made to wither, by him you have not been overcome; nor has he been overcome by you.
"This is the path to Yavakacchaka; if you are wise, you should know it. Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with this verse:
Since the barley-grass, the kadamba, and the kovidāra trees are in full bloom,
I shall take the left-hand path and go to Yavakacchaka.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
"Go, brahmin, by the path; you shall eat that devotee.
Sons are perfected by their fathers; in a month, you shall eat them."
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
Dry fuel such as bamboo and bamboo shoots can be prepared there;
having eaten of these for a month, I shall go to your home.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
Dwell, O Brahmin, in my house;
there a sacrifice will take place, for my mother will perform a great sacrifice with the King of the Gods.
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
"Whichever sacrifice your mother, the Queen of the Gods, has performed or will perform—that sacrifice I shall attend; I am now going to your home."
Then, monks, the wise Mahauṣadha requested the maiden Amarā from her parents for the sake of marriage. Her parents said to Amarā: "We will not give our daughter to a non-smith."

Monks, Mahauṣadha was greatly wise and proficient in all arts. It occurred to him: "What is the entire range of work for smiths? Needles. A smith who is able to make even a needle is a master craftsman. Mahauṣadha made a needle placed inside a sheath; within a single sheath, seven needles were inserted. All those eight needles became one needle, and that one needle also became eight needles. Taking that needle, Mahauṣadha went to that village of smiths to sell it. Passing along the road of the village headman of the smiths, he cried out: "A needle is for sale; let whoever has need of it buy it!"
A round needle with a well-fashioned, sharp point and its casing removed—I sell this in the village of smiths; buy it from me!
Hearing the voice of Mahauṣadha, that girl ran out; she addressed Mahauṣadha with a verse:
Here spears are being fashioned, as well as iron arrows and javelins;
right here they are being made, along with needles and fish-hooks.
You are a madman, O man, or perhaps you are deranged,
you who wish to buy a needle in a village of smiths.
Then indeed, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
A needle should be sold in a village of smiths by one who knows;
for only the masters know whether a task is easy or difficult to perform.
If, O blessed lady, my father should know that the needle was made by me,
he would either choose it for himself or bestow a boon upon you.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed her father in verse:
Listen to this, dear father, as the artisan speaks:
the skilled and expert smith and the clever needle-maker.
Then, monks, the father of Amarā, the smith’s daughter, was filled with wonder upon seeing that needle. Taking his daughter with him, he addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, in verse:
"Never before have I heard of or seen such a needle;
I am pleased by this work, and I give this maiden to you."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the one named Mahauṣadha, the greatly wise, was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. And why? Monks, at that time, on that occasion, I myself was the one named Mahauṣadha. Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the headman of the smith-village was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. And why? Monks, this Śākyan Mahānāma was, at that time, on that occasion, the headman of the smith-village. Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the daughter of the headman of the smith-village named Amarā was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. And why? Monks, this Yaśodharā was, at that time, on that occasion, the daughter of the smith. Even then she was won by me through my craft; even now she has been won by me through my craft."
The Jātaka of Amarā, the smith’s daughter, is completed.

The monks said to the Blessed One: "By means of his vigor, the Blessed One obtained Yaśodharā. The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was obtained by me through vigor; on another occasion as well, she was obtained by me through vigor. The monks said to the Blessed One: "Was there another occasion, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: "There was another occasion, monks."
