Monks, once in the past, in the city of Vāravālī, there was a brahmin who had mastered the three Vedas, along with the glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), the *Kaṭha* texts, and the histories as the fifth; he was skilled in phonology, word analysis, and grammar. As a teacher of the brahmanical Vedas, he instructed five hundred young students (*māṇavaka*) in the Vedas and mantras. Now, that brahmin had a daughter named Śirī, who was gracious, beautiful to behold, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion and loveliness.

He had departed. Now, while that brahmin was having a sacrifice performed at Samudrapaṭṭana, he sent a message to his teacher: "Either come yourself or send someone; I will give you whatever wealth you require. He said to those five hundred young students: "Who among you is able to go to Samudrapaṭṭana to the presence of such-and-such a caravan leader? To whoever goes, I shall give my daughter Śirikā Māṇavikā. Among them, there was a young student who was wise, industrious, and energetic. He felt an exceeding love for Śirikā. He volunteered, saying, "Teacher, I will go. The teacher gave him a letter, and having boarded a ship, he was dispatched.

Thus, he arrived in due course at a seaport. He presented that letter to the caravan leader. After the caravan leader had read the teacher’s letter and given him jewels, silver, and gold, he was sent on his way. Then, when the time came for the ship to set sail from that seaport for Vāravālī, he arrived at Vāravālī by means of that vessel. Now, as he was about to board a small boat from that ship, and while there was a great crowd, that bundle fell into the ocean. The thought occurred to that young man: "After bringing this with such great effort from the seaport, it has fallen into the ocean just as I was boarding the small boat here. What means might there be by which I could recover this wealth? There is no other means except that I shall bale out this ocean. Taking a metal shovel, he went to the shore of the ocean. Having set down the shovel at the edge of the sea, he tied his loincloth. And the deity of the ocean, approaching in the guise of a brahmin, said: "What is this? The young man replied: "U—"
"I shall empty the great ocean. The brahmin said, "The great waters will not be able to be emptied. The young man said:
For one who is diligent and heedful, even for as long as a Brahmā’s day and night— or indeed for that much longer— glory is not difficult to attain.
Listen to the heroism, the strength, the power, and the prowess of the Supreme Person,
who even as a young man in former births—
For his sake, he descended into the ocean.
At that time, his jewel had been lost; he said, "Exhaust the ocean!
Make an effort so that I may recover the jewel."
Do not be indifferent, lest you become miserable.
The golden nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas who dwell within the midst of the ocean became terrified,
just as if the clouds were agitated.
They emit a resounding roar.
Then a deity emerged from the ocean;
terrified, she looked out toward the four directions.
She saw the young man exerting himself.
To scoop up and to exhaust the ocean.
Having emerged, she spoke to him from the front:
"What do you seek from the ocean, young man?
Tell us, and we too shall [follow]."
We shall give it when we have fallen into misfortune and are being struck down.
"O deity, my jewel has been lost here;
I am searching for it in the great ocean.
Having exhausted the waters, may I find the jewel."
He drained the great ocean of its water.
Many fools wander in the world,
utterly deluded regarding both material wealth and the true Dharma;
you too, O youth of supreme intelligence, [are among them].
That which is difficult to find in the world, you seek.
Eighty leagues and four waters flow out from it, yet even by that [water] it is not known;
and below the water, its base is infinite.
But how do you venture to exhaust it?
Infinite rains fall into the ocean,
which serves as the dwelling place for those of great supernatural power;
how then could the Dharma-scripture ever be exhausted?
Since you, being evil-minded, perform improper actions even though your limbs are weary, before long you will come to ruin;
you are not even able to hold back a mere pond.
But this is not at all appropriate for you, young man.
O deity, regarding that which you have reproached and censured, I see therein your ocean of thought;
one should not dig a channel, nor should one uproot the root.
But there is no intermediate state from which one might not cross to the further shore.
I am not indolent; I would not abandon my own jewel.
Having seized wealth, I shall exert my vigor.
Let all beings here carry out my word.
I would speak thus; I would not speak otherwise.
I would not bow before a blazing fire; I would overturn the earth together with its moon and stars.
That deity reflected there:
"I must give that jewel to the young man, so that he does not exhaust the ocean."
And having taken this excellent jewel, young man, go as one whose vessel is successful.
Everywhere the energetic person fares well, while the lazy person lives in misery;
for by the power of his energy, he goes forth taking wealth with him.
Recalling his former residence and a previous birth, the Blessed One, the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
Referring to those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases,
as well as the self, the Blessed One explained this matter.
In the beginningless and endless cycle of existence where I formerly dwelt,
I was then a young brahmin and Śirī was Yaśodharā.
Having understood this matter, you should thus remember this Jātaka.

Thus, free from fever, free from fear, and free from sorrow, the Blessed One recounted this ancient *jātaka*—immeasurable and full of much suffering, involving conduct both high and low—in the midst of the community of monks. The Blessed One said: "It might be, monks, that you think the young brahmin to whom that wealth fell into the great ocean at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I myself was that young brahmin. It might be, monks, that you think the daughter of the brahmin named Śiri in the city of Vāravālī at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Monks, she who was the daughter of the brahmin named Śiri in the city of Vāravālī at that time and on that occasion was Yaśodharā. Even then she was won by me through my vigor; even now she has been won by me through my vigor."
Thus ends the glorious Śrījātaka.

The monks said to the Blessed One, "By the Blessed One, Yaśodharā was obtained with great hardship. The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was obtained by me with hardship; on another occasion as well, she was obtained by me with great hardship, great exertion, and great vigor. The monks asked, "Was it so on another occasion too, Blessed One? The Blessed One said, "On another occasion too, monks."

Long ago, monks, in the past, in Hastināpura there was a king named Subāhu who ruled his kingdom; he was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, great strength, a great treasury, and great vehicles, and he governed sixty thousand cities.

He had a son, a prince named Sudhanu, who was an only child, gracious, handsome, beautiful, meritorious, illustrious, virtuous, and filial toward his mother and father. He had been established as the crown prince by his father, Subāhu. Together with his ministers, he governed those thousands of cities inherited from his father. King Subāhu, having laid down the burden of royal duties, sat at ease, retired and secluded in the upper story of his excellent palace. Now, King Subāhu had a close friend and neighboring king named Sucandrima, who ruled in the city of Siṃhapura. He was meritorious, illustrious, possessed of great power, a great treasury, and many mounts. Now, for King Sucandrima, a sacrifice to all beings (*sarvabhūta-yajña*) had presented itself. "I shall perform a sacrifice with all kinds of living beings," he thought. He gave an order to all the hunters dwelling within his realm: "I shall perform a sacrifice with all beings. Bring together every species of creature that lives on land—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed. The Niṣādas were also commanded: "Bring whatever creatures live in the water; I shall perform a sacrifice with all beings."
"By means of the mind for the gods, by speech for kings,
not long [in time] for the wealthy, and by action for the poor."

At the mere word of the king, hunters and fishermen brought together all species of living beings, both those that move in water and those that move on land; having constructed a large enclosure, they confined there those species of land-dwelling creatures. Having also brought together those that move in water, they confined them in a lotus pond. Every species of living being was assembled, with the exception of the kinnarī.

Then, when King Sucandrima’s sacrificial enclosure had been prepared with all necessary provisions, he bathed his head, put on fresh garments, and went up to the top of his excellent palace. Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having extended his joined palms in salutation toward the four directions—the eastern, southern, western, and northern—he [turned] toward where the Blessed Ones were in those directions.

"I invite those seers who have attained the four dhyānas, possess the five super-knowledges (*abhijñā*), are endowed with miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*), are of great majesty, and roam through the intermediate space, to this sacrificial enclosure. Then, those seers who had attained the four dhyānas, possessed the five super-knowledges, were of great miraculous power and great majesty, reflected upon this and went to the sacrificial enclosure by means of their supernatural power through the air. When King Sucandrima saw those seers arrive at the sacrificial enclosure, he was delighted; filled with joy and gladness, he prostrated at their feet and said: "May the Blessed Ones inspect the sacrificial enclosure to see whether it is complete or not. The seers, having inspected it, said to King Sucandrima: "Great King, the entire sacrificial enclosure is complete, lacking only one thing. The king asked: "By what thing is it lacking? The seers replied: "Your Majesty, it is lacking a *kinnarī*. Then King Sucandrima spoke to his hunters: "Those Blessed Seers require a *kinnarī* at the sacrificial enclosure. Go and exert yourselves so that you may bring a *kinnarī* to me. Now, among those thousands of hunters, there was a hunter who was the most preeminent in valor, strength, and manliness. He was encouraged by the entire group of hunters: "You are capable and competent to bring back a *kinnarī*. Encouraged by the group and by King Sucandrima, that hunter took up his bow and quiver and entered the Himalayas.

There, he saw a certain delightful hermitage of a seer (*ṛṣi*) in the Himalayas, provided with roots, leaves, and fruits. He approached that seer, paid homage at his feet, and stood there. The seer addressed him, saying, "Come, welcome; you are welcome. Sit down on this couch. The seer then performed the hospitable rites for the hunter; according to the custom of seers, he offered him fruit and water. Having eaten the fruit and drunk the water, he sat there. And at the foot of the seer, he heard the sound of sweet singing such as he had never heard before. He asked the seer: "Venerable sir, whose is this charming sound of singing?"

[Thinking,] "Is this the song of the daughters of the gods or the daughters of the *nāgas*? the seer said, "This is not the song of the daughters of the gods, nor is it the song of the daughters of the *nāgas*; this is the song of the *kinnarīs*. Then he asked that seer, "Venerable sir, this sound of singing is heard, yet they are not seen. Where are they singing? The seer said, "On the northern side of this hermitage there is a great lotus pond (*mahāpadminī*). There, in all seasons and at all times, grow blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), red lotuses (*paduma*), white water lilies (*puṇḍarīka*), and fragrant lotuses (*saugandhika*). From Mount Kailāsa, the daughter of Druma, the king of the *kinnaras*, named Manoharā, comes to this lotus pond for the sake of sport, surrounded by many *kinnaras* and *kinnarīs*. That wise hunter questioned the seer with a stratagem, saying, "Venerable sir, it is heard that there are some humans who sport and dally with *kinnarīs*. How do those humans come to have the *kinnarīs* under their control? The seer said, "They are bound by a word of truth; they are unable to vanish. And because the seer spoke out of his straightforwardness without having reflected on the matter, he did not realize that the *kinnarī* was interested in him.

Then that hunter, having paid homage to the seer, went to that lotus pond where Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*, had a daughter who was playing. At that time, those *kiṃnarīs* were absorbed in singing and splashing in the water, and they did not see the hunter. And there, Manoharā was the most preeminent of all in beauty and voice. Standing within earshot, the hunter bound that Manoharā with a truthful utterance.
"You are the illustrious daughter of Druma, the king of the Kinnaras;
by this word of truth, remain—you are bound, O Kinnarī!"
Just as you are the daughter of the king of trees, raised by King Druma,
so, O blessed Manoharā, do not set foot [on this path] by virtue of your truthful word.
Then Manoharā, bound by that hunter’s word of truth, was unable to vanish; all those other kinnaras and kinnarīs, however, disappeared entirely.

Then that Manoharā was brought by the hunter to Siṃhapura; she was introduced there into the sacrificial enclosure. Upon seeing the Kinnarī, King Sucandrima and the great multitude of people became filled with joy toward the hunter. The hunter received a vast reward. She, bound with snares, was brought to Sucandrima in Siṃhapura, which had become a city of Brahmins, and led into the sacrificial enclosure. King Sucandrima, having prepared the requisites for the sacrifice, dispatched a messenger to Hastināpura to King Subāhu: “I shall perform a great sacrifice for all beings; come here and rejoice in it. King Subāhu sent his son, Prince Sudhanu, saying: “Go to Siṃhapura; King Sucandrima will perform a sacrifice; go and rejoice in it.”

Prince Sudhana arrived at Siṃhapura along with many hundreds of other kings. Among them all, Prince Sudhana was preeminent in beauty, majesty, retinue, and fragrance. Surrounded by hundreds of kings, Prince Sudhana entered that sacrificial enclosure (*yajñavāṭa*). There in the sacrificial enclosure, he saw those many thousands of living beings, both terrestrial and aquatic, and he also saw that Kinnarī. As Prince Sudhana gazed upon her, a noble love fell for the Kinnarī, and a love for Prince Sudhana also fell upon the Kinnarī. As it has been said by the Blessed One in the words of a Sūtra:
Whether through former association or through present benefit,
affection arises toward everyone, just as a lotus grows in water.

Thus, by the mere sight of one another, affection arose among them. Prince Sudhana asked King Sucandrima: "For what reason have these many thousands of living beings been confined here at the site of the sacrifice? The king replied: "I shall perform a sacrifice with these, and with this abundant food and drink. The prince [continued]:

He asked: "What is the fruit of this sacrifice? What is its accomplishment through merit? Of what kind will he accomplish the merit of this sacrifice by committing such slaughter of living beings? The king said: "All these various kinds of living beings that will be killed in this sacrifice shall all go to heaven. And I, for as many times as these living beings are killed here in the sacrifice, shall be reborn in heaven for that many turns. The prince said: "Great King, it is not so. This is a false view; non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the supreme Dharma. Taking life is unrighteousness (*adharma*); abstaining from taking life is righteousness (*dharma*). Taking what is not given is unrighteousness; abstaining from taking what is not given is righteousness. Sexual misconduct is unrighteousness; abstaining from sexual misconduct is righteousness. Drinking fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants is unrighteousness; abstaining from drinking fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants is righteousness. False speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from false speech is righteousness. Divisive speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from divisive speech is righteousness. Frivolous chatter is unrighteousness; abstaining from frivolous chatter is righteousness. Ignorance is unrighteousness; abstaining from ignorance is righteousness. Malice is unrighteousness; abstaining from malice is righteousness. False view is unrighteousness; right view is righteousness. O Great King, the ten unwholesome paths of action are unrighteousness; beings endowed with the ten unwholesome paths of action are reborn in the hells. Beings endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action are reborn in the heavens. Thus, O Great King, you have not taken the path to the heavens; you have taken the path leading to the hells. Having heard this Dharma teaching of Prince Sudhanu, King Sucandrima, all those kings, and the entire great multitude were delighted. Having heard the Dharma teaching of Prince Sudhanu, King Sucandrima released all those species of living beings—both those that move in water and those that move on land.

The Kinnarī Manoharā was won by Prince Sudhanu; and because of his love for her, the entire realm of the Kinnaras no longer occupied his mind. Likewise, because of her love for him, no other pleasures or diversions occupied Manoharā’s mind. King Sucandrima performed a flawless and blameless sacrifice, exactly as instructed by Prince Sudhanu. Many thousands of ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and beggars were satisfied with food and drink and clothed in garments. When the sacrifice was completed, Prince Sudhanu, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant together with Manoharā, departed from Siṃhapura for Hastināpura with a great retinue, in great prosperity, with great pomp, and in great splendor.

As Prince Sudhana was entering the city of Hastināpura, the city of Hastināpura was adorned: canopies were spread, it was draped with variegated cloths, bundles of silk ribbons and garlands were suspended, it was sprinkled and swept, perfumed with incense, and strewn with loose flowers; here and there were actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, and jugglers. Thus, Prince Sudhana, with great prosperity and a vast retinue, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant together with Manoharā, entered Hastināpura. All the king’s daughters were dismissed by that prince, who sported only with Manoharā. Because of the prince, King Subāhu’s affairs in sixty thousand cities fell into neglect, and many thousands of duties were abandoned. The merchants and countryfolk petitioned King Subāhu: "Great King, Prince Sudhana is infatuated with the Kinnarī Manoharā; he no longer attends to his duties and the royal affairs are falling into neglect; in sixty thousand cities, many thousands of tasks have been abandoned. King Subāhu summoned Prince Sudhana and said: "Son, the countryfolk are crying out! You do not attend to your duties as you did before; you dwell infatuated with the Kinnarī Manoharā. Son, dismiss this Kinnarī! "No, Father," replied the prince. "I cannot dismiss her. Why? Because she is my wife. "Son, if you will not dismiss her, then go to the forest and live there. "If that is the case, Father, I shall go. Having said this, he took leave of his father and departed for the forest. There he built a leaf hut and lived on roots and fruits. After some time, the Kinnarīs came to him and said: "Prince, come and enjoy yourself with us. He replied: "Sisters, I am not permitted to go. My father has commanded me to stay in the forest. They said: "Prince, we will go to your father and speak to him. They went to King Subāhu and said: "Great King, your son is suffering greatly in the forest. Please grant him permission to return. The king said: "If he comes, I shall give him whatever he desires. The Kinnarīs returned to the prince and said: "Prince, the king says that if you come, he will grant you whatever you desire. The prince thought: "I shall go and see my father. He went to the king and said: "Father, please grant me permission to return from the forest. The king said: "Son, what do you desire? "Father, I desire to rule over the kingdom. The king said: "Son, if you wish to rule the kingdom, then marry the daughter of King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī. "Father, I shall go and ask her. He went to Vārāṇasī and saw King Brahmadatta. He approached the king and said: "Great King, I am Prince Sudhana, son of King Subāhu of Hastināpura. I have come to ask for your daughter's hand. The king said: "Prince, I have a daughter named Śyāmāvatī. She is beautiful, possessing the most excellent marks and signs, and is beloved by all people. But she is devoted to the ascetic life and does not wish to marry. The prince said: "Great King, even if she is devoted to the ascetic life, I shall take her by force. The king said: "Prince, you may take her as you wish. Then the prince took Śyāmāvatī and returned to Hastināpura. He informed his father: "Father, I have obtained the daughter of King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī. The king was delighted and said: "Son, you have done well. I shall perform the marriage ceremony for you. Then the prince married Śyāmāvatī and lived happily with her. After some time, the Kinnarīs came to him again and said: "Prince, come and enjoy yourself with us. He replied: "Sisters, I am bound by my duty to my father-in-law and cannot go. They said: "Prince, we will go to your father-in-law and speak to him. They went to King Brahmadatta and said: "Great King, your son-in-law is suffering greatly in the forest. Please grant him permission to return. The king said: "If he comes, I shall give him whatever he desires. The Kinnarīs returned to the prince and said: "Prince, the king says that if you come, he will grant you whatever you desire. The prince thought: "I shall go and see my father-in-law. He went to King Brahmadatta and said: "Great King, please grant me permission to return from the forest. The king said: "Son, what do you desire? "Great King, I desire to rule over the kingdom. The king said: "Son, if you wish to rule the kingdom, then marry the daughter of King Mahendrasena of Roruka. "Great King, I shall go and ask her. He went to Roruka and saw King Mahendrasena. He approached the king and said: "Great King, I am Prince Sudhana, son of King Subāhu of Hastināpura. I have come to ask for your daughter's hand. The king said: "Prince, I have a daughter named Anupamā. She is beautiful, possessing the most excellent marks and signs, and is beloved by all people. But she is devoted to the ascetic life and does not wish to marry. The prince said: "Great King, even if she is devoted to the ascetic life, I shall take her by force. The king said: "Prince, you may take her as you wish. Then the prince took Anupamā and returned to Hastināpura. He informed his father-in-law: "Father-in-law, I have obtained the daughter of King Mahendrasena of Roruka. The king was delighted and said: "Son, you have done well. I shall perform the marriage ceremony for you. Then the prince married Anupamā and lived happily with her. After some time, the Kinnarīs came to him again and said: "Prince, come and enjoy yourself with us. He replied: "Sisters, I am bound by my duty to my two fathers-in-law and cannot go. They said: "Prince, we will go to your two fathers-in-law and speak to them. They went to Kings Subāhu and Brahmadatta and said: "Great Kings, your son-in-law is suffering greatly in the forest. Please grant him permission to return. The two kings said: "If he comes, we shall give him whatever he desires. The Kinnarīs returned to the prince and said: "Prince, the two kings say that if you come, they will grant you whatever you desire. The prince thought: "I shall go and see my two fathers-in-law. He went to both kings and said: "Great Kings, please grant me permission to return from the forest. The two kings said: "Son, what do you desire? "Great Kings, I desire to rule over the kingdom. The two kings said: "Son, if you wish to rule the kingdom, then marry the daughter of King Siṃhahanu of Kapilavastu. "Great Kings, I shall go and ask her. He went to Kapilavastu and saw King Siṃhahanu. He approached the king and said: "Great King, I am Prince Sudhana, son of King Subāhu of Hastināpura. I have come to ask for your daughter's hand. The king said: "Prince, I have a daughter named Yaśodharā. She is beautiful, possessing the most excellent marks and signs, and is beloved by all people. But she is devoted to the ascetic life and does not wish to marry. The prince said: "Great King, even if she is devoted to the ascetic life, I shall take her by force. The king said: "Prince, you may take her as you wish. Then the prince took Yaśodharā and returned to Hastināpura. He informed his three fathers-in-law: "Fathers-in-law, I have obtained the daughter of King Siṃhahanu of Kapilavastu. The three kings were delighted and said: "Son, you have done well. We shall perform the marriage ceremony for you. Then the prince married Yaśodharā and lived happily with her. After some time, the Kinnarīs came to him again and said: "Prince, come and enjoy yourself with us. He replied: "Sisters, I am bound by my duty to my three fathers-in-law and cannot go. They said: "Prince, we will go to your three fathers-in-law and speak to them. They went to Kings Subāhu, Brahmadatta, and Mahendrasena and said: "Great Kings, your son-in-law is suffering greatly in the forest. Please grant him permission to return. The three kings said: "If he comes, we shall give him whatever he desires. The Kinnarīs returned to the prince and said: "Prince, the three kings say that if you come, they will grant you whatever you desire. The prince thought: "I shall go and see my three fathers-in-law. He went to all three kings and said: "

"Know that he intends to depart. That prince, bound by the net of craving for Manoharā, would not grant her leave. His father spoke to him again and again: "Son, release this Kinnarī. I will bring you as many other princesses as you wish to name. Though the prince was told repeatedly by his father, he still did not release her. The ministers reported this again and again to King Subāhu: "Great King, Prince Sudhana is distracted by the Kinnarī Manoharā; he does not attend to his royal duties, and many state affairs are falling into neglect. The king then commanded the ministers: "Confine the prince! By the king's command, the prince was confined. Once the prince was confined, his home became a place of misfortune, and all prosperity vanished. Manoharā herself was granted permission by Subāhu to go to her own city of the Kinnaras, Nirati. "Manoharā, go; you have my leave. Depart for the pleasant and cool forests to the presence of your parents."

Then, adorned with all her ornaments, she descended from that palace. As she was descending, many thousands of women wept out of grief for Manoharā at the side of Sudhanu. There was no space left in the city of Hastināpura, whether to the left or right, as Manoharā was departing from Hastināpura. Receiving thousands of salutations with joined palms from the left and right, being honored with perfumes and garlands, and followed by thousands of women and a great multitude of people, she then departed from Hastināpura. Having dismissed the crowd of people, she turned northward toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains, and proceeded in that direction; yet, looking back toward Hastināpura, she gazed upon Sudhanu. And there, on the bank of the river Śatadru in the Himalayan foothills, two sons of hunters were hunting deer. One of the sons of hunters—

The second son of the hunter was named Utpalaka, and the other was named Mālaka. From afar, they saw the Kinnarī Manoharā approaching, adorned with every ornament, anointed with exquisite unguents, and wearing fragrant garlands; she came looking back again and again over her shoulder. They recognized that Kinnarī and, bowing down with palms joined in reverence, they asked:
"You go and you look back; you look back and you go. Why, noble lady, do you look back? Where will you go?"
Manoharā said:
I long for both... the city of Kiṃpuruṣa;
I behold Sudhanu and I long for Nirati.
Then those sons of hunters said:
Prince Sudhanu has women among the Kurus and Pañcālas;
sporting with them, he will not remember you.
Manoharā said:
"O Sudhanu, by my mere glance and my smile, I shall bring him here;
whether he be some old man or an elephant, he will come under my control."

She placed a ring worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and a garland of *tālīsa* wood into the hands of those sons of hunters, saying: "If Prince Sudhana should come after me, searching for me, you must give him this token and, in my name, offer him greetings. You should say to him: 'Depart from here; beyond this point it is difficult for humans to traverse. Separation from humans is certain for me. Having thus instructed the sons of the hunters, Manoharā crossed the Śatadru river without touching the water with the soles of her feet.

When King Subāhu knew that Manoharā had departed, he summoned Prince Sudhana and seated him on his lap, as well as on the lap of his mother. [The King said: "My son, do not remember the Kinnarī. Your harem is extensive, with many thousands of maidens; I shall summon others for you. Play, delight, and enjoy yourself with them. What use have you for the Kinnarī? You are a human being. The King consoled the prince, and the ministers were commanded: "Have the prince’s residence decorated. An order was given to the harem: "Entertain the prince so thoroughly that he does not even recall Manoharā. At the mere word of the King, the prince’s residence was decorated like a celestial palace (*vimāna*), furnished with every conceivable thing. In the seven gate-halls, jars of fine powder were placed, unbroken grains of rice were set out, and whatever other auspicious items are esteemed by the world were all provided. Thousands of Brahmins were stationed at the prince’s gate, as was the rest of the populace, waiting upon the prince. Having been consoled by his father, Prince Sudhana was dismissed: "Go, attend to your home; bathe, anoint yourself, wear garlands and ornaments, play, delight, and enjoy yourself; and attend to your royal duties. Having been thus instructed by his father, Prince Sudhana was sent away.

Having now departed from the royal palace together with his single attendant Vasantaka, who was devoted to him, he left the city of Hastināpura and set out toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains, for the sake of Manoharā. Those sixty thousand paternal cities of the prince—prosperous with their towns and districts—and his vast harem no longer occupied his mind; he grieved only for the Kinnarī Manoharā and remembered her constantly.
At that very moment, having abandoned the entire kingdom upon seeing the king’s lamentation,
he departed, taking with him an unwashed, soiled garment.
Having taken with him a single attendant whose disposition was one of devoted affection,
he set out toward the Himalayas, facing the king of mountains.
Before long, Sudhanu went to the Himalayas, the delightful slopes of that mountain;
there he saw two hunters, Uppalaka and Mālaka.
And he beholds the river Śatadrū, which is constantly radiant with pure and stainless crystal;
it is auspicious, its waters cool, flowing forth, soft, fresh, and well-formed; that river, with its lush meadows and swirling currents, carries hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs.
Siddhārtha said: "O hunters, did you see a certain woman—dark-complexioned, anointed with excellent unguents, wearing unfading garlands and perfumes—who was walking with a bold stride?"
The son of the hunter said: "She about whom you ask has been gone from here for a long time;
having crossed the river, she has by this time reached the Himalayas."
For she, named Sudhanu, spoke thus behind my back:
"If the son of the hunter comes, you must give him this token of recognition."
"O son of a hunter, give me this ring and this tālīsa-scented garland; you shall be my husband, my lord, and my master."
And at my word, O hunters, you should say to my master:
"Return to Hastināpura; our meeting was destined, yet our separation is certain."
Rejoicing, he accepted the garland and took up the ring;
"I would even accept death for the sake of union with Manoharā."
Those hunters said to him: "O Sudhanu, turn back from this very place!
Who would provide you with food in the city of Hastināpura?"
That did not enter his heart, nor did he listen to their words;
he was resolved only to go, and he crossed the great river Śatadru.
The hunters were also stationed there, thinking, "The king will be incensed with us if we abandon Sudhana while he is in such a predicament."
They too have descended into that river, which resounds with the cries of packs of tigers, lions, and herds of elephants;
it is followed by deer and birds, enchanting with the calls of ruddy geese.
At that very moment, they crossed the great river— resounding with the cries of swans and cranes,
filled with networks of waterfalls, frequented by beasts of prey and kinnaras, and exceedingly beautiful.

Then the prince, Vasantaka the attendant, Utpalaka the son of a hunter, and Mālaka the son of a hunter, having thus resolved, entered the Himavat, the king of mountains, following on the footsteps of Manoharā.

Manoharā also went along, hanging and binding together various colored, choice flowers that were trailing down. Then, seeing those flowers behind them, they followed after her, thinking: "Having rested here, Śyāmā has gone from here; she stayed for a moment here. In various places they saw heaps of flowers and beautiful garlands she had made, as well as discarded flower-ornaments belonging to her who wore choice flowers as ear-ornaments; seeing these, they knew: "Śyāmā has gone this way," and so they proceeded. They saw ornaments of many kinds fallen on the path, caught in the branches of the forest trees, and they saw other signs as well. And the further they entered the Himavat mountains, the more they saw many jewels and precious gems. They saw mountains with golden peaks, they saw mountains with silver peaks, they saw mountains of iron, they saw mountains of copper, they saw mountains of brass, they saw mountains of tin, they saw mountains of antimony, and they saw mountains of realgar. They saw pairs of kinnaras sporting about. They saw hundreds of other wonders and marvels. In various places they heard the sounds of kinnarīs singing, and they heard the roars of lions, the roars of tigers, and the cries of leopards. They heard the calls of deer of various colors, and they heard the cries of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and they heard the cries of piśācas and kumbhāṇḍas. They saw thousands of various kinds of medicinal herbs, and they saw vidyādharas.

As they were traveling, they saw the hermitage of the seer Kāśyapa, which was endowed with many roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, covered by thousands of trees, and well-supplied with water. They then entered that hermitage and saw there, in the hermitage, the aged and illustrious seer Kāśyapa sitting nearby with his retinue. They [then] approached the seer—

Having played [the lute], she stood before him and his retinue. It occurred to the seer: "This youth who has entered this hermitage must be a great-souled one, one who has performed meritorious deeds and is possessed of merit; he has not reached this region by mere chance. The seer welcomed the youth: "Welcome, O youth! Be seated; here are these seats. The youth sat down with his retinue. The seer offered him fruits resembling small honeycombs and water. When the youth had finished eating the fruits and drinking the water, the seer asked him: "What is the purpose of your coming here, O youth, you who have been raised in such luxury? The youth said: "O Blessed One, did you see a certain woman of such a kind passing by? The seer said: "Yes, I saw her. She came to this hermitage of mine, paid homage at my feet, and departed along the slopes of the Great Mountain. Therefore, let the youth turn back from this very hermitage. A difficult task has been undertaken by the youth in traveling this far; how much more so if he goes further beyond? It is inaccessible to humans. Turn back from this hermitage! The youth said: "I cannot turn back, Blessed One. Wherever that Manoharā went, I shall go by that very same path. The seer said: "The way of the Kinnarīs is one thing, and the way of humans is another. Even birds cannot reach the way of the Kinnaras, much less humans. Even birds can somehow reach that region, but where the Kinnaras go rejoicing and experiencing their pleasure-gardens—that is inaccessible to humans on foot. Turn back from this hermitage! Is your father not the lord of sixty thousand cities? Surely the youth should sport, enjoy himself, and experience life with noble luxuries. This place is inaccessible; you cannot go there. The youth said: "Blessed One, I must either see death or see her."

The highly fortunate seer, dwelling in great loving-kindness and being compassionate, thought to himself: "If this prince goes to a place that is inaccessible, his body may perish. The seer said: "Prince, spend this night here in the hermitage. In this region there dwell monkeys; their leader is devoted to me and comes every day to pay homage at my feet, bringing fruits resembling small honeycombs. I shall entreat that king of the monkeys, and he will lead you to the city of the Kinnaras called Nirati, belonging to Druma, the king of the Kinnaras. At the word of the seer, the prince stayed that night in the hermitage. When the night had turned to dawn, the prince heard a sound like that of a lion emerging from its lair. The prince asked the young seers: "Whose sound is this, emerging from its lair? The young seer replied: "That is the sound of the lord of the monkeys as he emerges. Every day at this hour, bringing fruits resembling small honeycombs, he emerges and moves from tree to tree, coming to pay homage at the feet of our preceptor. Then, out of curiosity, the prince rose and looked toward the direction from which the sound of the emerging monkey came. He saw the king of the monkeys coming, moving from tree to tree. When the king of the monkeys arrived at the hermitage, he set down the fruits resembling small honeycombs before the seer and sat down. The seer said: "King of the monkeys, perform a service for me. The king of the monkeys said: "Venerable sir, I shall do it. Command me. The seer said: "Take this prince, as the fourth person, to the Kinnara city named Nirati, belonging to Druma, the king of the Kinnaras. The monkey said: "Venerable sir, I am going."

Then that lord of monkeys, having mounted the prince as the fourth person on his back right there at the hermitage, proceeded from mountain peak to mountain peak and from tree to tree; and before long, he reached a hollowed-out tree—

King Rara arrived at the summit of Mount Kailāsa. And there, upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa, he beheld the city of the *kinnara* king Druma, named Nirati. It was fashioned entirely of gold and auspicious craftsmanship, adorned with thousands of parks, and graced with lotus ponds and lakes made of every kind of jewel. These were provided with embankments made of jewels, featuring stairs made of beryl slabs and surrounded by railings of the seven precious gems. They were covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, white lotuses, and fragrant lilies, and were joined by jewel-encrusted terraces. There floated boats variegated with various gems, as well as spring-colored vessels and many other kinds of rafts drifting about. The place was overspread with thousands of trees laden with various flowers, leaves, and fruits, and it was further beautified by *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *sumana*, *navamālikā*, and *yūthikā* flowers. Here and there they saw thousands of *kinnara* couples sporting; some were playing the *jaladardaraka* drums, some were playing various kinds of musical instruments, and others were singing enchanting songs in sweet voices. Within the city, they heard the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments and the sounds of sweet singing.

Then, while standing in the grove outside that city of the *kiṃnaras*, many *kiṃnarīs*—gracious, beautiful, adorned and bedecked with ornaments, carrying golden pitchers in their hands—were seen approaching that lotus pond where Sudhanu stood fetching water. Sudhanu asked them: "What festival is there in this city such that there is such great rejoicing? They replied: "Today is neither a festival nor a celebration. However, King Druma’s daughter, named Manoharā, was carried off by humans; after many years, she has now returned. Upon her arrival, King Druma the *kiṃnara* [prepared] everything..."

And the city was joyful; such was the fragrance there. Sudhanu asked, "Where will this water be taken? They replied, "That Manoharā shall bathe in it; it will remove her human scent. The prince dropped his ring into the last water-jar so that it would not be seen by those Kinnarīs. As Manoharā was bathing, the ring fell from that jar onto her lap as she bathed. When Manoharā saw the ring, she recognized it. This thought occurred to her: "Prince Sudhanu has come for my sake! How has Prince Sukāra come to this inaccessible region? She then hurriedly put on her clothes, and with tears in her throat and a weeping face, she prostrated herself before her parents and said, "He who is my husband in Jambudvīpa has arrived—the prince named Sudhanu, the only son of King Subāhu. Druma, the king of the Kinnaras, did not believe it. "Daughter, it is impossible for humans to come to this region. Manoharā said, "It is certainly true, father, he has come. Druma, the king of the Kinnaras, asked, "Was he seen by you yourself, or was he heard of from another? She said, "I did not see him myself, nor was I told by another; however, while I was bathing, Sudhanu’s ring fell onto my lap."

Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*, summoned the water-carriers. Having summoned them, he questioned them: "While you were going to fetch water, did you see any man? They replied, "Your Majesty, we saw a handsome and beautiful *kiṃnara* youth, the fourth person [in the group], on the bank of the lotus pond. The thought occurred to him: "This must be that very youth [who came with] Manoharā. He wondered, "How could he have come to this region? Then he asked his daughter: "Manoharā, let Prince Sudhanu enter this royal palace. She said, "Father, let him enter; he has come here out of love for me."

"Because of me, my father has suffered much unpleasantness and disrespect; because of me, he has experienced the suffering of imprisonment and execution, yet I have never once abandoned him. Therefore, Prince Sudhanu was imprisoned by his father Subāhu, and I was sent away. Now that he is released, he has come after me. King Druma, the Kinnara king, commanded his ministers: "Quickly have the city decorated, from the royal palace to the Asura Pond. Have canopies spread, have it strewn with variegated flowers, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, sprinkled and swept clean, scattered with loose blossoms, and drenched with all kinds of fragrant water. Let all the leading men in my city and the entire fourfold army go out to meet my son-in-law, taking along parasols, banners, and flags. At the mere word of the ministers, everything was prepared, and they went out to meet him with great magnificence. Manoharā too, dressed in costly garments and adorned with every ornament, surrounded by many thousands of Kinnaras and accompanied by the sounding of thousands of musical instruments, went out to meet him. Upon seeing Sudhanu, she fell at his feet with her head, and she stroked his feet with her face and her hair. Thus, with great splendor and great magnificence, Sudhanu was led into the city of King Druma, the Kinnara king, as far as the royal palace. There he was welcomed by King Druma, who took him onto his lap, comforted him, and said: "This is your city, made entirely of gold and adorned with thousands of gardens; it is infinitely auspicious. Here, with my daughter Manoharā, play, enjoy yourself, and take your pleasure."

Then Sudhanu, having lived for many years in the city of the Kinnaras, playing, delighting, and enjoying himself, and having experienced all the pleasures appropriate to the pleasure gardens, addressed Manoharā: "Manoharā, you know how I am the beloved and dear only son of my parents; out of love for you, I have been..."

"Having taken leave of my parents and having abandoned everything, I have come here of my own accord; it has been many years since I first arrived and have been living here. Therefore, bid farewell to my parents, for I shall go to Hastināpura. Manoharā informed her parents [of this]. Then King Druma asked Sudhanu: "Prince, will you go to the presence of your parents? The prince said: "If it is your wish, Father, then I shall go. Druma said: "I shall send you off. The *yambhaka* yakṣas are the executors of the commands of the *kiṃnaras*. The king commanded the *yambhaka* yakṣas: "Take my son-in-law, together with his retinue and Manoharā, to Hastināpura, and bring back abundant precious jewels. Those [yakṣas] lifted up Prince Sudhanu, along with his retinue and Manoharā, while she was still lying on her bed, and brought them from the *kiṃnara* city to Hastināpura. Having brought the abundant precious jewels as well, they placed them in the royal park. When the night had turned to dawn, Prince Sudhanu woke up and heard the sound of drums and the noise of people in Hastināpura. The thought occurred to him: "Where have I been brought to Hastināpura? He saw that royal park, those jeweled couches arranged just as they were, Manoharā, his threefold retinue, and the abundant jewels. The prince became joyful, thinking: "I have returned to my own city, just as I desired."

When the prince had departed from Hastināpura, King Subāhu caused a search for him to be made with great effort. At the time when the king did not receive any news of the prince, he thought: "The prince must have died while searching for Manoharā. Therefore, the king had the funeral rites for the deceased Sudhanu performed. It became known throughout the entire city: "Sudhanu is dead. Then, at the main gate of the royal park, the park-keepers ran out to raise banners in the park.

They went and arrived at the park, where they saw Sudhanu, Manoharā, and that retinue consisting of the three groups, as well as the couches made of jewels, the great heap of gems, and having seen these, they ran back and entered Hastināpura. A great crowd of people asked, "Is all well? They replied, "All is well, for Prince Sudhanu has indeed returned! He himself was filled with joy. Those park-keepers went to the royal palace and informed King Subāhu: "Great King, there is divine prosperity! Prince Sudhanu has arrived. At the mere report of this, the king and the entire royal household became joyful. A vast reward was given to those park-keepers. King Subāhu, together with his ministers and attendants, the queen—the mother of Sudhanu—and the whole of the harem rushed out to the park to see the prince; and the entire city, upon hearing the news of Prince Sudhanu’s arrival and that of Manoharā, was without any space left between its inhabitants as they rushed from Hastināpura to the park to see the prince and Manoharā. When Sudhanu saw his parents, he prostrated himself with his head at their feet; and when Manoharā saw her mother-in-law and father-in-law, she also prostrated herself with her head at their feet. The prince, together with his father Subāhu, mounted a noble elephant adorned with gold and covered with a golden net. With great royal majesty, great royal power, a grand procession, and great splendor, he was conducted into Hastināpura.
In this way may all beings be reunited with all their loved ones until they have abandoned the state of non-enlightenment,
just as Sudhanu was reunited with the Kinnarī at that time.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the prince named Sudhanu was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Monks, at that time, on that occasion, I myself was the prince named Sudhanu. It should not be viewed that the king named Subāhu at that time, on that occasion, was someone else. Why is that? Monks, this King Śuddhodana himself was the king named Subāhu at that time, on that occasion."

"Monks, she who was Sudhanu’s mother at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Queen Māyā was Sudhanu’s mother at that time and on that occasion. Furthermore, monks, you might think that he who was Sudhanu’s attendant named Vasantaka at that time and on that occasion was someone else. It should not be viewed thus. Why is that? Monks, this Chandaka was Sudhanu’s attendant at that time and on that occasion. He who was the hunter’s son named Utpalaka at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Rāhula was the hunter’s son named Utpalaka at that time and on that occasion. He who was the hunter’s son named Mālaka at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Elder Ānanda was the hunter’s son named Mālaka at that time and on that occasion. He who was the seer named Kāśyapa at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Elder Mahākāśyapa was the seer of the Kāśyapa clan living in the foothills of the Himalayas at that time and on that occasion. He who was the king of the monkeys in the foothills of the Himalayas at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Kaṇṭhaka, the king of horses, was the king of the monkeys in the foothills of the Himalayas at that time and on that occasion. He who was the Kinnara king named Druma on the summit of Mount Kailāsa at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Mahānāma the Śākya was the Kinnara king Druma at that time and on that occasion. She who was Manoharā’s mother at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Yaśodharā was Manoharā’s mother at that time and on that occasion. She who was the Kinnarī Manoharā at that time and on that occasion—do not think it was anyone else. Why is that? Monks, this Yaśodharā was the Kinnarī Manoharā at that time and on that occasion. Even then, she was obtained by me with great effort."
One who delivers diverse and profound discourses, is deeply learned,
destroys the afflictions, and crushes the arguments of opponents—
that monk shall shine within the teaching of the Self-Existent One.
Like the moon with its full orb in the sky.
Thus ends the Śrī Kinnarī Jātaka.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having realized the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Śrāvastī as a teacher of gods and humans. Having established the introductory narrative in detail, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who am delicate, my Śākya father had three palaces built—for the winter, the summer, and the rainy season—for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for enjoyment. Monks, I am delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who am delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father had gabled chambers built within those palaces—plastered and whitewashed, with doors that could be opened to the breeze and windows closed against the wind, perfumed with incense, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and streamers, and strewn with loose flowers—for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for enjoyment. Monks, I am delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who am delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father had couches made within those gabled chambers—of gold, of silver, and of jewels, spread with sixteen-fold woolen rugs, cotton coverlets, variegated rugs, and silk rugs, with pillows at both ends, red cushions, and white counter-spreads—for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for enjoyment. Monks, I am delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who am delicate..."

“Monks, for me who was so delicate, my Śākya father had canopies made over those couches so that dust and dirt would not settle upon me, for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided various ointments, such as aloe-wood, sandalwood, *kālānusāri*, and *tamālapatra*—all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided various garments, such as fine cloth from Kāśī and fine woolen blankets, for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided various garlands, such as *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *vārṣika*, *vātuṣkāri*, blue lotus, *damanaka*, and celestial flowers—all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided various foods, such as rice of various colors and black rice, accompanied by many soups and condiments—all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father, immediately after I had finished eating, would offer me a garland fit for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), such as dancing, singing, instrumental music, orchestral performances, and women—all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate. For me, monks, who was delicate and most delicate, my Śākya father provided various vehicles, such as elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, boat-vehicles, and palanquin-vehicles—all for the sake of my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment. Monks, I was delicate, most delicate...”

Māra said: “Monks, for me—who was delicate, supremely delicate—my Śākya father would have had various rugs prepared, bordered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins, covered with white woolen blankets, making a joyful sound, and adorned with victory banners, all for my own amusement, pleasure, and diversion. Monks, I was delicate, supremely delicate. Monks, for me—who was delicate, supremely delicate—my Śākya father would have had an umbrella held over me as I went out, lest the sun’s heat, dust, or grime should scorch my body, all for my own amusement, pleasure, and diversion. Monks, I was delicate, supremely delicate. Monks, for me—who was delicate, supremely delicate—my Śākya father would have had gardens constructed in the four directions for my own amusement, pleasure, and diversion. Monks, I was delicate, supremely delicate. Monks, for me—who was delicate, supremely delicate—my Śākya father would have had lotus ponds constructed in those gardens in the four directions, covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and fragrant water lilies, all for my own amusement, pleasure, and diversion. Monks, I was delicate, supremely delicate. Monks, for me—who was delicate, supremely delicate—my Śākya father would have had palaces constructed in those gardens in the four directions, lofty, vast, and magnificent, all for my own amusement, pleasure, and diversion.”

"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. To me, monks, being so delicate and exceedingly delicate, this thought occurred: 'Household life is crowded, whereas the life of renunciation is open space. It is not possible for one dwelling in the midst of a home to practice the holy life that is completely refined, completely blameless, pure, and bright. What if I were now to go forth from the home into homelessness? Then, monks, against the wishes of my parents—who were choked with tears and weeping-faced—I abandoned my comfortable home and the sovereignty of a universal monarch as if it were a mere handful of grass, and went forth from the home into homelessness. Having gone forth, I proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī and arrived there."

At that time, monks, in the great city of Vaiśālī there lived Ārāḍa Kālāma, who was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by three hundred disciples. He taught the Dharma to the disciples of the Jina for the sake of attaining a state of practice accompanied by doubt. He said to the disciples of the Jina: "Behold! Behold! Abandon! Abandon! And those disciples replied to him: "We behold! We behold! We abandon! We abandon!—both we and others. Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "What if I were now to lead the holy life under Ārāḍa? So, monks, having approached where Ārāḍa Kālāma was, I said to Ārāḍa Kālāma: "I wish, venerable Ārāḍa, to lead the holy life under the Blessed One. When this was said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma said this: "Practice it, O Gautama! Such is this Dharma and Vinaya wherein a faithful son of good family may lead the holy life, and while practicing, may attain wholesome states. Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: "I too have the desire, the strength, and the vigor; what if I, for the sake of attaining and realizing this very Dharma, were to dwell alone, diligent, ardent, resolute, and secluded? Before long, I attained and realized that Dharma. Then, monks, having approached where Ārāḍa Kālāma was, I said to Ārāḍa Kālāma: "Is this the extent of the Dharma that has been attained, realized, taught, and proclaimed by the Blessed One Ārāḍa? When this was said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma said this: "It is so, Gautama; this is the extent of the Dharma that has been attained, realized, taught, and proclaimed by me. When this was said, monks, I said to Ārāḍa Kālāma: "In that case, O Ārāḍa, this Dharma has also been attained and realized by me. When this was said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma said this to me: "In that case, O Gautama..."

"The Dharma that I know, Master Gautama knows it; the Dharma that Master Gautama knows, I know it. Therefore, let us both lead the community of disciples together. Thus, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma honored me with the highest honor and praised me with the highest praise. However, he did not establish an equal vision for the sake of equality in purpose. Then, monks, this occurred to me: "This Dharma of Ārāḍa does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering. Suppose I were to search further? Monks, being thus inclined toward further investigation, I set out for the city of Rājagṛha and arrived there. I stayed right there in the city of Rājagṛha.

Now at that time, Udraka Rāmaputra was residing in Rājagṛha; he was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by seven hundred disciples. He taught the Dharma to the disciples of the Conqueror for the sake of practicing together in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He spoke thus to the disciples of the Conqueror: "Behold! Behold! Abandon! Abandon! And those disciples replied: "We behold! We behold! We abandon! We abandon!—both we and others. Then, monks, this occurred to me: "What if I were now to lead the holy life under Udraka Rāmaputra? Monks, I approached where Udraka Rāmaputra was and said this to him: "Venerable Udraka, I wish to lead the holy life under you; may the venerable Udraka allow me to do so. When this was said, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra said this: "In that case, Gautama, practice it; stay, Gautama. Such is this Dharma and Discipline that a faithful son of good family [may find fulfillment]."

"Let me practice the holy life; while practicing it, let me further accomplish wholesome states. Monks, this occurred to me: "I indeed have the desire, I have the strength, I have the energy. What if I were to dwell alone, diligent, ardent, resolute, secluded, for the sake of attaining and realizing this very Dharma? Monks, dwelling alone, diligent, ardent, resolute, and secluded for the sake of attaining and realizing that very Dharma, before long I attained and realized that Dharma. Then, monks, I went to Udraka Rāmaputra and said to him: "Master Udraka, is this the extent of the Dharma that you, the venerable Rāma, have attained, realized, taught, and proclaimed—that which is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)? When this was said, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra replied: "This is the extent of what the venerable Rāma has attained, realized, and proclaimed—that which here is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, monks, I said to Udraka Rāmaputra: "Indeed, Udraka, I too have attained and realized this Dharma. When this was said, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra replied: "In that case, Gautama, whatever Dharma the venerable Rāma knew, that Dharma the venerable Gautama knows. Therefore, let the venerable Gautama now lead the community of disciples. Thus, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra honored me with the highest honor and praised me with the highest praise; he regarded me as his equal and placed me in the position of a teacher. Then, monks, this occurred to me: "This Dharma of Rāma does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering. What if I were to seek a higher path? Monks, because I did not find satisfaction in that view, I set out for the city of Gayā. Having arrived there, I dwelt right there.

She spoke to the prince: "O best of men, do not turn back today! O you whose face is like the full moon, do not go; let the people everywhere be forever yours. For my eyes, O hero, are insatiate as they gaze upon you. Why indeed, O you of beautiful stride, handsome features, and wearer of excellent ornaments, do you depart while I am unsatisfied, leaving my heart in total darkness? She heard the voices of the deities speaking from the sky: 'This is indeed the son of King Śuddhodana, the best of kings, departing from Kapilavastu. Thirsting for a sight of him, she ran out and proclaimed his hundreds of virtues: 'O noble man, how will you fare when separated from your own kinsmen? Surrounded by a host of women, they weep and follow after him who is golden-hued, lamenting piteously as he enters the forest wilderness. Happy are the families of deer in the woods, the forest deities, and the lords of the groves, who behold that hero with the gait of a royal swan as he wanders in the forest. With limbs as delicate as blossoms and feet like precious lotus petals, how will you tread upon the earth, so difficult to traverse and strewn with grass, *kuśa*, and reeds? Risen from the essence of refined food, your body nourished by the finest of various flavors, how will you subsist on roots, fruits, and leaves at the edge of the mountain streams in the forest? Having slept upon a bed covered with choice rugs, set on legs of gold and ivory, and strewn with flowers, how will you sleep upon surfaces spread with grass, *kuśa*, and reeds? O lord of men, having heard the music of drums, lutes, and cymbals within the palace..."
You will hear harsh and terrifying sounds, like the roar of elephants in a state of fury.
May the quarters of the sky be filled with roots, fruits, leaves, and honey for you, along with herds of non-cruel wild animals;
may the sun not scorch your body with its heat upon the rocks while you wander in the forest, hungry and thirsty.
May there be for you, scorched by the summer heat, a grove with its pavilion in the midst of water;
and in the winter, when the clouds have vanished, may the sun shine upon the mountain caves.
Your retinue consists of rākṣasas, yakṣas, and serpents, while you are as delicate as a divine child;
you are the most excellent among the stars and the moon, a body that brings joy to the heart and the eyes.
Like a noble elephant longing for a lotus pond, he enters the penance grove at the foot of the Vindhya mountains; now hear of the various wonders of that excellent forest.

In one place, there were creepers with red shoots and young trees with handfuls of blossoms; in another part of the forest, it was scorched by forest deities, and elsewhere, it was broken by the trumpeting of wandering elephants.
In some places it was adorned with trees that were inaccessible due to their vast, dense foliage and hanging fruits;
in other places, its base was covered by a forest of shrubs and trees, including withered hollow trunks.
In one place there was a beautiful lotus pond; in another, a forest with the splendor of mountain streams;
in yet another, hermitages belonging to families of ascetics, resounded with the songs of cuckoos, parrots, and peacocks.
In some places it was filled with sparse grass and arid wastes; in others, it was crimson with the sprouts of *śara* reeds;
in some places there were *ruru* deer, yak, and buffalo, and here and there were herds of tigers and lions.
In some places, various red-leafed creepers hung from young trees,
like women exhausted from wandering through a garden, now falling asleep.
In some places, the tops of the *kuravaka* trees were in full bloom, their flowers clearly awakened and fully opened,
like women who have just woken from sleep with eyes still heavy from slumber.
In some places, the branches of forests variegated with the blossoms of various trees, stirred by sweet breezes,
lean gracefully against one another like playful women embracing each other.
In some places, the flowering branches of the *kupyaka* forest, bending under their burden and swaying,
appeared like affectionate women embracing their own sisters.
In some places, within the forest groves of flowering *kiṃśuka* trees, or in the great monasteries,
there were women with large eyes, like young ladies wearing red garments as upper cloths.
In one place, a region of the earth was covered with newly blossomed flowers;
it was like a young bride, her garments laden with ornaments, resting gracefully upon her bed.
In some places there were hard thorny creepers, the dwelling-places of the tracks of deer, buffalo, and boars,
drenched with the blood of deer struck by the arrows of the Śabaras.
In some places, heaps of elephant tusks lie upon the ground like white cotton blankets;
in other places, tigers, lions, venomous snakes, and the finest of men, elephants, and boars have been slain.
In some places there are the ravings of *rākṣasas* and the terrifying cries of *piśācas* and *kumbhāṇḍas*;
in other places, the utterances of *guhyakas* circulate through the winds at night.
At times during the nights the clouds thunder, the hosts of serpents respond with joy,
and [beings] terrifying to behold assume many forms.
He dwelt in that forest grove, desiring the welfare of the entire world—
a place made delightful by the loss of pride among the fierce beasts and rākṣasas.
Then the Lord of Beasts, the essence of beings, prayed for the welfare of the entire world—and especially for that of sentient beings—more intensely than for himself; even this is a marvel.

If I must experience suffering for as many incalculable eons as there are sentient beings in order to liberate each and every one of them, I shall deliver all sentient beings; this is my firm resolve.
Having practiced austerities for six years in the forest, Satvasāra attained mindfulness through the exhaustion of karma, realizing: "The path by which I have gone is not the way to liberation."
I remember that in the past, in the Śākya king’s garden of Jambudruma, he attained the first dhyāna; that will become the path to awakening.
And it is not possible for one who is weak, emaciated, and whose blood and flesh are completely withered to attain awakening; therefore, I shall take food once again.
The deities said: "Do not cause yourself distress; let not your fame diminish.
We shall infuse our vital energy into your limbs."
"I am known by everyone as one who is constantly without food;
yet the vital essence provided for me by them is false."
Thus, fearing false speech, he rejected that deity,
saying "Enough," and partook of a soup made of mung beans, kulattha, hareṇu, and phāṇita.
Having gradually restored strength and vigor to his body,
he sought out food and approached Uruvilvā as a virtuous man.

Then Sujātā, of noble family and wise, his nurse from a former birth, stood at the foot of the banyan tree holding honeyed milk-rice. "O practitioner of the holy life, why is your body so emaciated and exhausted? she asked.
Having given the milk-rice, she announced it to the prince.
And for that royal seer there was well-prepared honeyed milk-rice;
the son of the king said to him, "For what purpose do you give this gift?"
She who was the mother of that pure being throughout hundreds of births spoke sweetly: "I pray, may my wish be fulfilled."
At the foot of the Himalayas stands the renowned city called Kapila,
its fame celebrated in every direction, crowded with joyful men and women.
In that city lived the prince, the son of Śuddhodana the Śākya;
having abandoned his kinsmen and renounced his kingdom, he went to the forest.
As he wandered for six years in that fierce forest of asceticism,
through my gift to him, his vow was fulfilled.
"Whatever supreme goal he seeks through that asceticism, may my purpose be fulfilled;
may I too travel by that same path with that great and noble man."
Then a non-human voice emerged from the sky:
"O well-born lady, this is that wise one, born of the Śākya royal lineage."
By him were practiced in the penance grove various forms of austerities— difficult and hair-raising— which dried up both blood and flesh.
Having abandoned those useless things, they proceeded toward the excellent tree;
here, past Buddhas have attained supreme enlightenment.
Then, shedding tears while filled with joy,
she spoke with palms joined in reverence to that tiger among men, trembling as she did so.
O lotus-eyed one, you have been seen arising from fierce austerities in the Bhairava forest;
seeing you, my heart, which was tormented by grief, now experiences joy.
For six years prior to this, I have never before slept on a comfortable bed,
as I contemplated your asceticism with the burning heat of the arrows of grief.
Upon hearing that the end of your asceticism has come, the people, your father, and your affectionate maternal aunt will be filled with joy and gladness regarding that kingdom.
In the city of Kapila, the palaces will resound with the music of hundreds of instruments;
they will be filled with joy and delight, where throngs of men and women are laughing.
Having partaken of honeyed milk-rice as his last meal in a former existence, you became the destroyer of becoming;
at the foot of the king of trees on the earth’s grove, you attained the deathless state, free from sorrow.
The Lamp of Men prophesied: "Five hundred births ago you were my mother;
in a future time, you shall become a Pratyekabuddha named Jinavrata."
Thus ends the Prediction concerning Sujātā from the glorious Mahāvastu.

Then the Bodhisattva, having wandered for alms from Senāpati Village in Uruvilvā, emerged with his bowl filled with various kinds of cakes; and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa emerged with an empty bowl. The Bodhisattva asked him, "Venerable Kāśyapa, was almsfood obtained? Then Kāśyapa addressed the Bodhisattva in verse:
Praskandaka, Balākalpa, Ujjaṅgala, and Jaṅgala—
in these wicked villages, not even a single alms-meal can be obtained.
Then the Bodhisattva replied to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa with a verse:
Praskandaka, Balākalpa, Ujjaṅgala, and Jaṅgala—
from these villages of the Bhadras, behold how the alms-bowl has become full.

When the Bodhisattva departed against the will of his parents, whose throats were choked with tears and whose faces were weeping, King Śuddhodana dispatched men [with the command]: "Bring news of the prince’s daily welfare constantly. Then, when the prince went to Anomiya, to the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha, news arrived from there. When he went from the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha to Vaiśālī, news arrived from there for King Śuddhodana. When he approached Ārāḍa Kālāma at Vaiśālī, news arrived from there as well. When he went from Vaiśālī to Rājagṛha, news arrived from there as well. When he approached Udraka Rāmaputra at Rājagṛha, news arrived from there as well. When he was invited by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra with abundant enjoyments, news arrived from there as well. When he went from Rājagṛha to Mount Gayāśīrṣa, news arrived from there as well. When he went from Mount Gayāśīrṣa to Uruvilvā, to the grove of Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, news arrived from there for King Śuddhodana.

In the grove at Uruvilvā, while he was performing fierce austerities and applying himself to strenuous exertion, news began to spread. When the Bodhisattva practiced the "breath-holding" meditation (*āsphānaka-dhyāna*), due to his asceticism, he blocked the breath through both nostrils and the openings of both ear canals; the inhalations and exhalations were thus obstructed by the Bodhisattva. Those men thought, "The prince has passed away; he neither breathes in nor breathes out. Having gone to Kapilavastu, they reported to King Śuddhodana: "Great King, the prince has passed away. The king did not believe them. He questioned those men: "How do you know that the prince has passed away? They said: "Great King, due to fierce austerity and the consumption of coarse food, he has passed away; he neither breathes in nor breathes out, but sits like a piece of wood. Therefore, we thought that since the prince neither breathes in nor breathes out, and is emaciated with a weak body, the prince has passed away. Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana: "Considering the nature of the prince’s descent into the womb, the worship performed by thousands of gods during his walk in the womb, the manner in which he was born in the Lumbinī grove, how immediately upon birth he took seven steps upon the earth, surveyed the directions, laughed a great laugh, and uttered the words, 'I am the foremost, the eldest, the best, and worthy of worship among gods and humans'—and considering the wonders and marvels that occurred when the prince was born, such as the unconscious earth trembling and the worship performed by thousands of gods, and the perfection of his Great Renunciation—such Great Beings (*mahāpuruṣa*) do not have short lifespans. It must be that the prince, just as before, having not yet renounced the world, sat cross-legged in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered a peaceful meditative absorption (*samādhi*). That is why these men think the prince has passed away. He then said to those men: "Go to the prince. The prince has not passed away; he has entered a peaceful meditative absorption. [This is] the prince's..."

“Bring me news of my son’s daily activities. Then those men went back to Uruvilvā and entered the penance grove; there they saw the prince healthy and well, having emerged from meditative concentration. Those men were amazed, thinking, “King Śuddhodana is wise! When the monks heard this account—that the Blessed One had set in motion the supreme wheel of Dharma—they asked the Blessed One: “How was it, Blessed One, that King Śuddhodana did not believe the report of those messengers when he heard that the prince had passed away? The Blessed One said: “Monks, it is not only now that King Śuddhodana did not believe upon hearing that I had passed away. On another occasion as well, he did not believe when he heard that I had passed away. The monks said: “Was there another occasion, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: “There was another occasion, monks.”

In the past, monks, in times gone by, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was another brahmin. For forty-eight years he had practiced the celibate life of a youth and had studied the Vedas. Having now practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having studied the Vedas, [he thought], "There is no merit in this world for one who is childless," and so he took a wife and fathered children. Then that brahmin thought, "I have enjoyed human pleasures; it is time for me to go forth. So the brahmin addressed his brahmin wife: "Wife, I am addressing you: I shall go forth. She said to him, "Who will provide for the brahmin or for the son? Or who will provide for me? If it is your intention to go forth, I too shall go forth; I too shall practice austerities, I too shall lead the celibate life. Just as you shall practice austerities, so shall I also practice austerities. The brahmin said, "So be it."

"You too should go forth! Then they departed from Vārāṇasī. In the Himalayas there was a hermitage named Sāhañjanī, where a great seer named Gautama dwelt with a retinue of five hundred; he was an attainer of the four dhyānas and possessed the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā). Then that brahmin, together with his brahmin wife, went to that Sāhañjanī hermitage and went forth under the great seer Gautama. His wife also went forth. He then constructed a hermitage not far from that [original] hermitage, making huts of grass and leaves. For that female ascetic Pāragā, a separate hut of grass was made in a secluded spot. While they were dwelling there in that hermitage, applying themselves, striving, and exerting themselves on the external path, they realized the dhyānas and the superknowledges. They became highly fortunate practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārins) who had attained the four dhyānas and the five superknowledges, relying upon fierce austerities. Whatever root-preparation, fruit-preparation, *kodrava* grain, *śyāmāka* millet, *priyaṅgu*, *bhaṅga*, *prāsādika*, leaf-vegetable, or radish the seer brought back, he shared it with Pāragā while she was pregnant. They thought, "What shall this young man's name be? It occurred to them: "This young man is dark-complexioned (*śyāmavarṇaka*); let this young man's name be Śyāmaka. Thus, those parents gave the young man the name Śyāmaka.

In that hermitage, that young man was reared. Thus, in due course, when that young man had grown and was able to walk on his feet, he then played together with the young deer. The sages dwell in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and are highly blessed; the beasts and birds do not fear them. That hermitage was graced by thousands of beasts and birds. Whenever the young deer drank from their mothers’ teats, at that very time Śyāmaka also drank from the teat of a doe along with those young deer. Whichever doe he approached, she would suckle him, just as she would suckle her own fawn.

He suckled him. Thus that young seer Śyāmaka grew up in that hermitage together with those fawns and birds.
