Wherever the fawns and birds wandered, there the young seer Śyāmaka wandered, surrounded by those deer and birds; and those deer and birds took delight in the company of the young seer. Whenever the young seer was lying down in his hut, then many fawns and various kinds of birds would sit at the entrance of the hut until the young seer Śyāmaka emerged from it. Then they would wander about the vicinity of the hermitage. Śyāmaka took delight in the hermitage together with those deer and birds, and the deer and birds also took delight in that hermitage together with Śyāmaka. Even while the young seer was sleeping in the hermitage, the fawns, deer, and birds would remain surrounding him. When the fawns and birds wished to go wandering, they would wake the young seer Śyāmaka by nuzzling him with their snouts. In this way, that young seer grew up in the hermitage together with those deer and birds. When the young seer had reached maturity, he was clothed and covered in the skins of deer. Whatever forest produce there was in that hermitage—whether roots, fruits, *kodrava*, *śyāmaka*, *cinnaka*, *priyaṅgu*, *bhaṅga*, *prāsādika*, vegetables, or radishes—he would bring it and offer it to his parents. He brought water, he brought wood, and he constructed grass huts and leaf huts. He sprinkled and swept that hermitage. With the utmost reverence, he attended upon his parents; first he served his parents, and only afterwards did he take food for himself. From the time the young seer attained the age of discretion, from that point on, he never once...

Having first given food to his parents, Śyāmaka the young seer would then take food for himself; thus he attended upon his parents there in that hermitage. As the young seer attended upon his parents with what was desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing, time passed by. Meanwhile, the parents dwelling there in the hermitage had become aged, frail of body, deprived of sight, dependent on others, and unable to provide their own food, go for water, or enter the grass hut or leaf hut by themselves. Śyāmaka the young seer attended upon those elderly, aged, frail, and sightless parents with every kind of beneficial service. Having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, the young seer lived as one who was gracious, handsome, and beautiful to behold, brought forth by auspicious karma. He was a filial son, a celibate from his youth, devoted to fierce asceticism, and a dweller in remote lodgings. Possessed of great merit, he was beloved by the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, kinnaras, and kinnarīs, as well as by deer, birds, and all living beings. Wherever the young seer went—whether gathering roots, leaves, flowers, or fruits—he went surrounded by deer and birds, gods and nāgas, and kinnaras and kinnarīs.

Now, taking his water-jar and surrounded by deer, birds, gods, nāgas, kinnaras, and kinnarīs, he descended to a mountain river to fetch water and filled his jar from there. Meanwhile, the King of Kāśī named Peliyakṣa—possessing great strength, a vast treasury, and a large retinue—was pursuing a deer on a hunt with a horse as swift as the wind; having left behind his army and vehicles, no one else had reached that region. As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Dharmapada*:
"The forest is the range of deer; the sky is the range of birds."
Dharma is the goal for those who are still subject to differentiation; Nirvana is the goal for Arhats.

That deer vanished right there in the forest thicket. In that forest thicket, the king heard the sound of the ascetic Śyāmaka as he was filling his water-jar from the mountain stream. It occurred to him, "This is the sound of a deer; this forest is not frequented by humans. Then, from the direction where the sound of the ascetic Śyāmaka filling his water-jar came from, he discharged a razor-headed arrow. That poisoned razor-headed arrow struck the heart of the young ascetic. At the sound of that poisoned razor-headed arrow and by the scent of its lethal poison, those deer and birds fled in the ten directions. The ascetic Śyāmaka, having set down his water-jar on the riverbank, lamented piteously: "For the sake of meat, deer and boars are killed; for the sake of skins, lions, tigers, and leopards are killed; for the sake of their tails, yaks are killed; for the sake of their tusks, noble elephants are killed; for the sake of medicine, partridges, *kapila* birds, and water-fowl are killed. But for us, it is not possible to make use of meat, nor of skin, nor of hair, nor of tusks. For what purpose have we—harmless, innocent, and blameless—been slain by a single arrow, three people together? Alas! How the injustice has blazed forth! While the young ascetic Śyāmaka was thus lamenting, the King of Kāśī arrived at that place and saw the young ascetic lamenting, wearing deerskin, matted hair, and bark garments, a man of great fortune shedding tears. Seeing the young ascetic struck by the razor-headed arrow, the king became terrified and alarmed, thinking, "Lest he reduce my city and kingdom to ashes with a curse! He then dismounted from his horse and fell prostrate at the feet of the young ascetic Śyāmaka. "O Blessed One, this arrow was discharged by me under the mistaken impression that it was a deer; I did it unknowingly. I beg the Blessed One’s forgiveness. These drops of tears falling upon the earth—if they were to fall, they would burn the entire continent of Jambudvīpa."

"How much more so, then, for fools like us? The King asked, "Since the Blessed One said that 'with a single arrow they strike down the three,' I do not understand this. The Blessed One is one, not three; how is it that three people have been struck down by a single arrow? The young seer replied, "Great King, my mother and father are aged, elderly, their bodies weak, and sightless. They are celibate, highly fortunate, worthy of offerings from the world including the gods, and dependent on others. I am their attendant. First I provide for their food and drink, and afterwards I attend to myself. Whatever is required for their service, I perform it all; there is no one else who might serve them. Therefore, when I am struck down, they too are struck down; without me being dead, they cannot live. For this reason, I say that 'by a single arrow, three people are killed. King Kāśi said to the young seer Śyāmaśrī, "I have struck you in the heart with an arrow made of sharp poison, unintentionally. I know now that your life is at an end. I grant you one true boon: leaving behind my prosperous and flourishing kingdom, I shall serve your venerable parents. Just as you have served them, so shall I serve them. The young seer said, "Great King, by this, the dart of grief has been removed from my heart. Having heard these words, O protector of the earth, act in such a way toward my elders that you remain true to your promise; great merit will be yours. After performing service and attendance upon those highly fortunate ones, Great King, take this water-pot and go along this path to the hermitage of my parents. In my name, offer greetings and say this: 'Your only son, Śyāmaśrī, asks after your welfare. He says: 'Your only son is dead; you should not grieve, you should not weep. In this world of the living, death is inevitable for one who is born. That state which is unattainable cannot be reached through weeping or grieving. It is not possible for one to [attain] oneself..."

"There is no escaping the consequences of deeds already committed. Nor is it death for me alone; all sentient beings are subject to the law of death. Therefore, do not grieve, do not be distressed. There is separation and parting from all that is dear and pleasing. O Great King, act in such a way that you remain true to your promise toward your teachers. Having understood this, the young seer, his body failing, passed away.

The king, having learned that the young seer had passed away, wept and lamented; wiping away his tears, he took that water-jar and set out along that same path as instructed by Śyāmakaśiri toward the hermitage. As soon as the King of Kāśi had departed from the presence of Śyāmakaśiri, Śyāmakaśiri himself was surrounded by hundreds and thousands of beasts and birds, as well as by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras, kinnarīs, and other beings. Having gathered around the young seer, they raised a great cry of wailing and made a great clamor. "Surely he, a doer of evil deeds, shall go from darkness to darkness; he shall go from one state of misery to another, since he has wronged one who was harmless, innocent, and blameless. The entire forest grove, those mountain caves, and that hermitage were filled with the clamor of beings and resounded with the cries of beasts and birds. Hearing those beings and hearing the cries of the beasts and birds, Śyāmakaśiri’s parents fell into anxiety: "What is this? Never before have we heard such sounds of the clamor of beings, nor have we ever heard such cries of beasts and birds. Could it be that Śyāmakaśiri has been harmed by a lion, a tiger, or some other ferocious beast? "From these omens, from the unrest of our hearts, and from the way my eyes are throbbing, [we know what has happened]. They remained thus restless in body and mind, thinking of Śyāmakaśiri, while the King of Kāśi reached that hermitage and saw hundreds of dead birds there from the hermitage.

The birds cried out and fled; the seers were even more terrified. The King of Kāśi, having tied his horse to a tree trunk at one side and taking that water-jar, approached the parents of Śyāmakaśiri. "I salute you, Blessed One," he said. They greeted him joyfully and asked, "Who are you? The king replied, "Blessed One, I am the King of Kāśi named Peliyakṣa. Is it well with the Blessed One here in this penance grove frequented by wild beasts and devoid of humans? Do roots and fruits appear here? Is *kodrava* and *śyāmāka*, as well as vegetables and roots, obtained with little effort? Is there little illness in your body? Do few stings of gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles fall upon your person? They then said, "Indeed, Great King, we live happily here in this forest hermitage frequented by wild beasts and devoid of humans. Roots, leaves, and fruits, as well as *kodrava*, *śyāmāka*, and radishes, are obtained with little effort. There is little illness in our bodies, and few stings of gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles fall upon us. But is it well with you too, Great King? Is there peace, freedom from calamity, and freedom from distress in your harem, among your princes and ministers, and in your army, mounts, treasury, and granaries? Do the people of the city and the countryside obey you? Do rival kings cause no offense? Does the rain fall in due season? Do the crops flourish? Is your kingdom secure, well-supplied with food, and free from affliction? He then replied, "Indeed, Blessed Ones, there is peace in my harem, among my princes and ministers, and in my army, mounts, treasury, and granaries. The people of the city and the countryside obey me. Rival kings do not offend me. The rain falls in due season. The crops flourish. My kingdom is secure, well-supplied with food, and free from affliction. They then said, "Great King, sit on these seats until Śyāmakaśiri returns. He has gone to fetch water; once he has returned, he will offer you fruit and water. When the king was thus addressed by those seers, he wept. They asked, "Great King, why do you weep? The king said, "Blessed Ones, the one of whom you speak—the one who will come and offer fruit and water—is Śyāmakaśiri."

"He has passed away, and this water-jug was sent into my hands; he greets you and sends this message: 'You must not grieve, you must not weep. There is no purpose served by grieving or weeping. All who are born must inevitably die. Death is not for me alone; all sentient beings are subject to death and subject to passing away. It is impossible to escape from the results of one's own actions. You ask, 'Great King, how did Śyāmaśiri pass away? The king replied, 'While I was hunting, pursuing a deer on a horse as swift as the wind, I reached that region near the water where Śyāmaśiri was filling his jug. In that dense forest, the deer vanished. As he was carrying that water-jug, I heard the sound of him. Then it occurred to me: "That very deer is moving along with the water. As I was hearing the sound of him going, I discharged a poisoned arrow toward that sound. It struck Śyāmaśiri in the heart; this young seer has passed away. Then, having heard this from the king, they wept with choked voices and tearful faces, lamenting: 'Great King, deer and boars are killed for their meat; lions, tigers, and leopards are killed for their skins; elephants are killed for their tusks; partridges and foxes are killed for their medicinal value. But for us, Great King, there is no need for meat, nor for skin, nor hair, nor tusks. For what reason? We are harmless, innocent, and blameless; yet three people have been killed by a single arrow. The King of Kāśī prostrated before the seers and begged for forgiveness: 'Venerable sirs, these tears of yours falling upon the ground could burn even the entire continent of Jambudvīpa, let alone foolish people like us. I shall renounce my kingdom, along with my kinsmen and my children... "

"I shall attend to you here, and I will serve you just as I served Śyāmakaśiri. They then said, "Great King, we are blind and deprived of sight; we are not capable of going to that place without a guide. Therefore, Great King, lead us to that place where Śyāmakaśiri is. By means of a word of truth, we shall restore the young seer, and by means of a word of truth, we shall neutralize that deer-poison. It occurred to the king: "These seers are so highly blessed and capable; they are able to restore him. He said, "I will lead you, venerable sirs, to the place where Śyāmakaśiri is."

Then, placing their hands upon the shoulder of that king, they went to that place. Placing the head of the seer Śyāmaka on her lap, Pāragā, the mother of the illustrious Śyāmaka, wiped his round face with her hand and wept and lamented in many ways: "The hermitage will become empty, bereft of the illustrious Śyāmaka; the forest deities, having lamented piteously, will depart; and even the beasts and birds, not seeing the illustrious Śyāmaka, will depart from the hermitage wailing piteously."

The seer said: "Pāraga, do not weep; do not grieve. What purpose is served by weeping for one who is already mangled? We too have practiced fierce austerities and lived the life of celibates; we are capable of raising him up through the power of truthful speech. Let us make that declaration of truth by which we shall destroy his deer-poison and restore his life. Then, by their truthful speech, that deer-poison was destroyed. [They said: "Just as you, my son, have never conceived an evil thought toward anyone, but have been friendly-minded toward all beings, so let your deer-poison be destroyed. Just as you have never taken food for yourself without first giving to your parents, so let your deer-poison be destroyed. Just as your parents, my son, have always maintained perfectly pure conduct..."

"May that which was killed by you while protecting [us] become like meat. Then, through the power and majesty of his parents, by the force of his word of truth, and by the splendor of his own well-performed conduct, that young seer arose stretching himself, just as a sleeping man would wake.

The Blessed One said: "It may be, monks, that you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the young seer Śyāmaka was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Monks, it was I who at that time, on that occasion, was the young seer named Śyāmaka. That seer who was Śyāmaka’s father was someone else; he was King Śuddhodana at that time, who was the father of Śyāmaka. She who at that time, on that occasion, was the mother of the young seer Śyāmaka, named Pāragā, was someone else; she was Queen Māyā. He who was the Kāśi king named Peliyakṣa was someone else; it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Monks, it was the Elder Ānanda who at that time, on that occasion, was the Kāśi king named Peliyakṣa. Even then, monks, when this King Śuddhodana heard that I had passed away, he did not believe it, saying: 'That great king has not passed away; Śyāmakaśiri has been deluded by deer-poison. Do not go to that place of ours; we shall destroy that deer-poison with a word of truth and we shall raise up that Śyāmakaśiri. Now too, when this King Śuddhodana hears that I have passed away for his sake, he does not believe it."
The narrative of the Śyāmaka-jātaka is completed.
I shall proclaim the former conduct of the Blessed One, the virtuous one, the world-transcendent Lord of the World whose fame in the world is immeasurable.
For the conduct of a bodhisattva cannot be surpassed by anyone in the world of gods, gandharvas, and humans; therefore, the One Possessing Ten Powers is unconquerable.
Whatever power of mindfulness the Tathāgatas possess regarding their various births,
as they compassionately regard the world with loving-kindness and pity—
that well-practiced conduct belongs to the Blessed One, who has accumulated merit for hundreds of thousands of eons.
I shall proclaim it; listen with respect and give your full attention.
At that time, the Blessed One was reborn as a being endowed with wisdom in a family of forest-dwelling ascetics, which was utterly pure.
His parents had become old and were deprived of their sight;
for their benefit, may a supramundane one arise. . . .
With all his limbs faultless, possessing supernormal powers, gentle, and large-eyed,
he was known by that very name, Śyāma, at that time.
It is a marvel that whether a human or a god, whoever beholds the young seer who has reached the perfection of beauty and virtue, is never satiated while gazing upon him.
The Bodhisattva himself, seeking what is wholesome, undertakes it;
having undertaken that pure, wholesome dharma, he abides by it.
The hero, having established unbroken, stainless, and completely pure service toward his parents, who are prone to evil deeds and laziness, attends upon them with intense devotion;
as a practitioner of the holy life, he himself observes the vow of celibacy.
This was his vow regarding his beloved parents and dear ones:
"I must certainly not engage in conceptual proliferation toward those who are blind and led by others."
Gathering roots and fruits, I shall serve with love and reverence those who are sick, aged, and advanced in years, honoring my teachers as I attend to them.
Having served one's mother and father with food and drink, by providing medicine for the sick, and with clothing, bedding, and seats.
Moreover, in this matter, the Bodhisattva said to his parents: "Do not be distressed;
you need not grieve, for I myself shall be your attendant."
Śyāmasundarī said to him: "Do not wear rags; let no evil come upon you, and may the spirits not terrify you as you have gone astray from the path."
Let even those who seek flesh and blood—the mighty lion kings and the exceedingly powerful elephants—depart from the path; and let no beings cause you fear.
He dwells together with young deer in delightful hermitages.
Like a deer among deer, the young seer dwells in the forest.
While he was dwelling there in that hermitage, practicing patience, self-control,
and renunciation, he showed compassion for the world through loving-kindness and pity.
Then the King of Kāśi appeared, a monarch of great power and high renown;
he terrified both the deer and the birds in that hermitage.
Within the forest, the king beheld herds of deer;
having seen them, he very hurriedly fixed sharp arrows to his drawn bow.
This horseman has dispatched the best of all steeds, possessing the speed of the wind, with its mane disheveled and moving swiftly toward the deer.
And now the young seer, taking his water-pot, has set out;
let him descend into the Girinadī river while the deer and birds are still unalarmed.
Then that king, provoked to the highest anger,
pursuing deer with a drawn bow, did not see the young seer in his wrath.
He fixed an arrow to his bow, with which he struck Śyāma;
pierced by that poison-smeared shaft, the even-natured one fell down.
Being struck, he said: "By whom am I, who am innocent, being killed? Father, mother, and one arrow—three have been slain; once again, unrighteousness has flared up."
For the sake of their tusks, elephants are killed; for the sake of their meat, deer;
for the sake of their hair, the yak; and for the sake of their skins, the leopard.
But for me, there are no teeth, nor skin, nor hair, nor even flesh.
For what purpose indeed would we, who are harmless, be killed?
Having heard those words, the king approached that young seer;
he consoled him and asked for forgiveness, saying, "The Blessed One was struck by me unknowingly."
This was not an intentional arrow; you were struck by me unknowingly.
Whatever wound has been caused by me through ignorance, let that indeed be forgiven.
And as for what you said while lamenting—"Three were struck by a single arrow"—explain this, O practitioner of the holy life; declare the meaning of this to me.
Addressing his beloved parents, the Bodhisattva,
having brought forth a specific reason, uttered these words:
They have long been my practitioners of the holy life—my mother and father, aged and decrepit;
for them, being sightless, I alone am their refuge and their protector.
Their death without a protector has arrived; because of that, O King, I grieve. They, who have not been cared for by me, will die a death without a protector.
For this reason I say: "Though struck by a single arrow, three [vital organs] are hit;
yet while being nourished by you, I shall not be killed."
The Lord of Kāśī, who possessed sharp intelligence, also understood his purpose;
bowing his head at the feet of that young seer, he spoke to him.
"I shall fall into hell for having killed this innocent son of a seer;
for those who have committed such acts cannot be released from the hells."
Even those drops of tears that fall from you, whose being is utterly pure, could burn the entire world; how much more so fools such as us?
I speak the truth: if by my death your life were to be saved, I would even sacrifice my own life; yet such a possibility does not exist.
O son of a seer, you have been struck in the heart with a sharp poison;
I know that your life is at an end, yet it causes me no grief.
And thus, O you of great renown, I shall grant you my promise; have confidence in me.
For truth is established in the world of the living; this is the ultimate reality.
Having abandoned my flourishing kingdom and having renounced women and sensual pleasures,
I shall serve your parents, gathering roots and fruits for them.
The Bodhisattva said to him: "O elephant among kings, by uttering these words, you are removing this harsh burning of the arrow of my grief."
"Taking this very water-pot,
go along these footpaths to our hermitage and speak these words on my behalf."
Again and again you spoke salutations to your mother and father;
"Your son has passed away, and he sends this greeting to you."
One should not grieve in any way, nor is there any purpose in grieving like a wretch;
everyone born into this world of living beings must inevitably die.
This, indeed, is the natural order: the life of humans is not very long;
death is the ultimate end for both the wealthy and the destitute.
Nor is it possible to escape from the fruit of actions performed by oneself;
for upon the turning of the wheel, both happiness and suffering fall.
Nor have I heard from those endowed with wisdom, nor do I myself know,
the instability of that which is momentary, weak, and subject to conditioned formations.
Nor is there death, nor indeed is such suffering mine alone;
this matter has been experienced by me—there is nothing in the world that has not been encountered.
"This is my dart of grief: that they will become overwhelmed with sorrow upon hearing the news that you have grown old and are deprived of sight."
If it be so, O Kāśivardhana, look now; may you be one whose promise is true.
That shall serve as my service toward my teachers, O lord of men.
The wise praise that service of great benefit toward those who are aged and weak;
for, O lord of men, it possesses three constituent qualities.
There will indeed be merit, fame, renown, and roots of goodness;
ask, O King of Kāśi, and attend upon his words.
Having heard "So be it," the King of Kāśī, dejected and wiping away his tears,
departed, realizing that Śyāma was dead.
And now the King of Kāśi has departed, along with many hundreds of deer;
flocks of birds and even deities have surrounded Śyāma.
Seeing him fallen there, lying on the bank of that river and unconscious,
even the deities and many hundreds of beasts and birds wept.
Truly, that evil-doer goes from darkness to darkness,
from one miserable state to another miserable state, who thinks of evil against you, whose nature is free from evil.
There was the clamor of beings in the sky and a roar upon the earth;
winds blew violently, and the seer thought, "Alas, what misery!"
Surely the young seer has been harmed, judging by what is seen:
these many fierce and piteous sounds of "ruta-ruta."
The winds blow distressingly, and birds utter harsh cries; my heart is unsettled, and my entire body is restless.
These mental discursive thoughts were occurring, and he was named Peliyaśa;
as he proceeded toward the hermitage, the flocks of deer and birds were terrified.
Terrified and afflicted by fear, even the deities fled in all directions; perceiving this, they became even more despondent as they watched, their hopes destroyed.
Neither a human nor even a non-human has ever come from anywhere to this region;
nor, having seen the young seer, do the many hosts of beasts and birds depart.
Without doubt, there will be a great and hair-raising being,
at the sight of whom the herds of deer and the flocks of birds will be terrified.
Having approached his parents who were already aware of what had happened,
he greeted them with sweet words, even though they were terrified that their life was at stake because of his failure to return.
He said to them, "Welcome to you! From where have you come? Whose messenger are you?
We are blind and sightless; Śyāma has gone to fetch water."
The king said: "I went out from the city of Kāśī for a hunt with my army;
by the name of Peliyakṣa, I am searching for deer."
O elephant among kings, does the rain fall for you and do the seeds sprout?
Is my inner court free from illness, as are the princes and the foremost of the army?
In my cities and provinces there is security, and the people are devoted to me;
my enemies do not increase, and my entire treasury grows.
There is righteous protection for the ascetics and brahmins within the provinces;
[the population] increases and does not decline, yet I do not give gifts with due honor.
Even in the forest frequented by thieves, tigers, and many beasts of prey,
no beings whatsoever do you harm, just as if they were those who have gone astray.
Abundant flowers and fruits, śyāmāka grain, and plentiful vegetables and roots are obtained with little effort; thus, there is little illness in the body.
Before long, the prince arrived; sit down upon these leaf-litters, worthy, righteous, and exceedingly pleasing to the mind.
Then the king, shedding tears, uttered words that were poison-like, undesirable, and life-destroying for that community of ascetics.
"He whom you call the son of a seer, a practitioner of the holy life, a follower of the Dharma, and one who lives in equanimity—he has just now passed away; he sends his salutation to you."
One should not grieve in any way, nor is there any purpose in lamenting for the body;
everyone born into this world of the living must inevitably die.
Having heard those words—which were undesirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable—they thought: "By speaking thus, you are indeed cutting short my life."
He said: "This matter arose through my own conduct when I committed evil while ignorant;
may the gods thus forgive me."
I too have come here for this purpose, O young seer;
you shall carry that burden, and I shall carry it as well, and I, O gods, shall attend upon you.
His mother laments for him, whose complexion was as beautiful as a well-bloomed blue lotus,
as she reflects upon the former smiles and speech of her beloved son.
Alas, beloved Syāmasundara! In the past, the occurrence of separation from you will burn my heart, just as fire consumes dry grass and wood.
This hermitage appears empty, terrifying, and unpleasant,
for it is bereft of that noble, virtuous, and eminent seer.
"Suppose he were to grant us all our desires and bring about peace through them;
that would be better for me than such suffering ever occurring."
I believe that various and manifold ascetic practices inferior to ours have been performed;
this is their ripened fruit, that we are now deprived of our beloved son.
Greatly afflicted and exhausted by the weeping of Ruṇḍa,
she remembered the hundreds of virtues of the noble and righteous one.
They said to the King of Kāśi: "Thus have we been entreated; take us there. We are blind and sightless; we are not capable of going there."
He said: "I shall surely go to that place where the young seer dwells;
perhaps that youth may yet live, though he has been struck down by the poisons of the deer."
That king of Kāśi, proceeding by the path he had come,
before long reached that region where the young seer was.
Seeing him fallen and lying there on the riverbank, unconscious,
his mother, weeping, wipes the jewel from his mouth with her hand.
Alas, beloved only son! You are the kinsman of us who are destitute, poor, and friendless; how have you been harmed, my child?
Even the forest deities have no concern for those who are not human;
yet they see that this dark youth has not turned back his calf, however small it may be.
The food for the journey is difficult to endure... [as are] the many hundreds of leagues, since he who was worthy, righteous, and dear as a son has departed.
Surely those deer and birds in the hermitage grove,
not seeing the glory of Śyāmaka, cry out piteously, finding no delight.
Do not grieve, Pāraga; there is no purpose whatsoever in grieving for Ruṇḍa.
Everyone born in this world of the living must inevitably die.
We too are celibate, having long abstained from sexual unions;
we shall utter a word of truth, and by that we will destroy his poison.
Just as your mind, O dark and beautiful one, never clings to evil, so too has the deer-poison been destroyed; arise by the power of this word of truth!
Just as your parents maintain a morality that is eternally pure, so too has your deer-poison been destroyed; arise at the word of Satu!
Just as in you there is no conceit regarding existence, nor pride, nor hypocrisy,
so may the poison of the deer be removed from you by the power of this word of truth.
Then, as the deer-poison had departed, he arose while yawning,
through the power of his parents, the power of his own well-practiced conduct, and his own inherent strength.
Seeing him thus arisen by that word of truth, the king,
with his hair standing on end from joy, fell at his feet and asked for forgiveness.
The Bodhisattva said to him: "O Great King, together with your yoked draft animals, your queens, and your cities, towns, and provinces, may you be happy."
Behold, O Kāśivardhana, the result of reverence for one's mother and father,
just as the poison of the deer was completely eradicated by the power of good conduct and well-spoken words.
O Kāśīvardhana, those who desire to go to heaven must perform service, join their palms in reverence, and offer prostrations to their mother and father.
Having brought all the jewels from this Jambudvīpa, honor your mother and father; one should not fail to repay one's parents.
Thus, O Great King, I say that it is not easy to repay one's mother and father;
have compassion for them, as well as for the teachers of old and for the world.
One should bow down to those human deities as if they were gods;
those whose parents receive honor from them are not to be pitied.
She who was his mother at that time was Māyā then;
King Śuddhodana was the father of the Blessed One at that time.
By that word of truth which gave rise to such great majesty,
he was the Blessed One Bodhisattva Śyāma at that time.
He who was the king at that time was Ānanda;
for many thousands of births, he was a kinsman and a servant of the Blessed One.
This was not something he fully awakened to anywhere, nor was it a knot he untied by himself;
for it was indeed the perfection of the Dharma through the Blessed One’s past conduct.
The Śyāmaka-jātaka is completed.

The Bodhisattva practiced austerities in the penance grove at Uruvilvā. For eighteen months, he subsisted on a single jujube fruit per day, remaining committed to a diet of jujubes. For eighteen months, he subsisted on a single sesame seed per day, remaining committed to a diet of sesame seeds. For eighteen months, he subsisted on a single grain of rice per day, remaining committed to a diet of rice. For eighteen months, he remained committed to taking no food at all.
His food was a single jujube fruit, a single sesame seed, or a grain of rice;
yet, in some instances, the wisdom of the Perfectly Awakened One did not abide within those who lacked diligence.
His entire body was as cold as a black stone;
his limbs became like the footprint of a camel, and his jaw then became like that.
Just as the interior of a dilapidated cow-pen has crumbled away at its sides,
so too was the body of the Great Seer completely withered by his asceticism.
Just as a long braid of hair is high and low when wound around,
so too did his back and neck become high and low.
His eyes shine like stars in a water cistern;
his deep breath is like the bellows of smiths.
Just as an autumnal lotus-stalk withers when cut green,
so too did the head of the great seer wither through his ascetic heat.
With body stilled, the Great Hero, having heard nothing from his own mind,
practices fierce austerity for the sake of all sentient beings.
It is impossible to fully describe, even with all speech at one's disposal,
the hardships that the Hero undergoes upon seeing sentient beings suffering.
Just as a bird does not find a limit in the sky,
and just as the water in the great ocean is immeasurable;
Thus, it is not possible for all speech to express the limit of the qualities of the Buddhas, the lamps of the world, who are kinsmen of the sun.
His skin was unstained, yet his back was smeared;
all his limbs had fallen away, yet he did not lose his vigor.
He grasped the sage’s front body while holding onto his back;
when he rose up with force, the sage fell out through his mouth.
Seeing the body of the Hero so weak, the four deities said:
"The Sage has passed away; he does not endure through his vigor."
While the Supreme Person was practicing such fierce asceticism,
the world— including its gods, asuras, and humans— was struck with wonder.

Having heard from the messengers who had been questioned that the prince was performing such fierce asceticism, King Śuddhodana, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, Yaśodharā, and the entire Śākya kingdom were filled with anxiety. They thought, "May the prince indeed emerge safely from this severe austerity. It occurred to Yaśodharā as well: "It would not be good for me, nor would it be fitting, if while my noble husband is suffering, practicing difficult austerities, and lying on a bed of grass with coarse food, I here in the royal palace should eat foods fit for kings, drink drinks fit for kings, wear clothes fit for kings, and use beds and seats fit for kings. What if I too were to take coarse food, wear common clothes, and prepare my bed even upon a layer of grass? She then took coarse food, wore common clothes, and prepared her bed upon a layer of grass.

And when the Blessed One, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dharma, was dwelling at Rājagṛha surrounded by a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks, then King Śuddhodana dispatched Chandaka and Kālodāyin as messengers to the Blessed One at Rājagṛha, saying: "The Blessed One has shown compassion toward gods and humans; may the Blessed One also show compassion toward his kinsmen. Whatever the Blessed One says, you must do. They too arrived from Kapilavastu at Rājagṛha and approached the Blessed One. They reported to the Blessed One the entire message of King Śuddhodana and all the members of the kinship circle. The Blessed One, knowing the right time, the right hour, and the right occasion, waited for the proper time, hour, and occasion to go to his birthplace. The Blessed One addressed Chandaka and Kālodāyin: "Chandaka and Kālodāyin, will you go forth [into the religious life]? They replied: "We have been commanded by King Śuddhodana: 'Whatever the Blessed One tells you, you must do. Yet they see neither a barber here nor any saffron robes."

Those with whom they were clothed, following the Blessed One, said: "We shall go forth, O Blessed One. Then they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monks; Chandaka and Kālodāyin, lead the holy life under the Tathāgata. Now, as soon as they had been addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a householder, banners of a householder, protections of a householder, or ornaments of a householder they possessed all vanished completely; three robes appeared, a bowl was provided, their hair remained in its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years. Such was the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monkhood for these venerable ones, Chandaka and Kālodāyin.

The Venerable Udāyin said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, Yaśodharā followed the Blessed One’s vows. While the Blessed One was practicing austerities in the forest of penance, Yaśodharā also took coarse food, wore common clothes, and—having renounced beds and seats worthy of a king—made her bed upon a layer of grass. The monks asked the Blessed One: “How is it, Blessed One, that Yaśodharā follows the Blessed One’s vows? The Blessed One said: “Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā has followed my vows; at another time as well, Yaśodharā followed my vows. The monks said: “Was there another time, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: “Indeed, monks, there was another time.”

Long ago, monks, in the distant past, there lived in a certain forest retreat a deer named Śiriprabha. He was graceful, beautiful to behold, and possessed a well-proportioned body; his hooves were red, his feet were red, and his eyes were as if anointed with pigment. He led a herd of five hundred deer. Now, that king of deer had a chief queen who was devoted to him through his power and faithful to him; she was never separated from that deer for even a moment. There was another hunter named Nīlaka, who [lived] there in that forest retreat among the deer.

The snares were set. Śrīprabha, surrounded by that great herd of deer, was caught while roaming there in the forest wilderness. When all the male and female deer saw the king of deer bound, they fled; however, one female deer who was devoted and faithful to that king of deer remained and did not flee. And that female deer addressed Śrīprabha with a verse:
Exert yourself, Śiriprabha; exert yourself, O lord of beasts!
Before that hunter arrives by whom this snare was set, break the wheel-like snare. I shall find no pleasure without you.
Then, monks, the deer king Śrīprabha addressed that doe with a verse:
I take my strides, yet I am unable; I fall to the ground with great force.
Firm is the leather thong of the snare; it cuts into my foot.
The forests, mountains, and groves are delightful;
you shall enjoy them, O blessed lady, together with another husband.
Then, monks, that doe replied to the king of deer in verse:
Delightful are the forests, mountains, and groves;
even in other births, I shall take my pleasure together with you.
And having heard them lamenting and crying out in distress,
that hunter, a man of most cruel and evil deeds, went there.
Then the king of deer saw that hunter approaching from afar, dark-skinned with white [marks].
Having seen him with fangs, red eyes, resembling a man-eater, and wearing blue garments, he addressed that doe again in verse:
This is that hunter who comes, dark and clad in blue garments—
he who, having cut my skin and flesh, will kill me.
Not far from him, that doe went out to meet the hunter where he was and addressed him with a verse:
Gather the palāśa leaves and draw out your sword, hunter;
having first struck me down, you may then kill the great deer.

Then, monks, this thought occurred to that hunter: "Even from afar, deer see me and flee, disappearing from sight; yet this doe, being utterly unafraid, comes forward even at the risk of her own life—she neither deceives nor flees. Then the hunter, seeing the discipline of that doe, was struck with wonder and filled with amazement: "Such as this doe is! We do not possess those virtues which they have. They are no mere animals who possess such greatness of virtue, such firmness of mind, such gratitude, and such devotion. We are the ones who are truly animals, seeking food only with our snouts, we who would even inflict harm upon such a noble-minded deer as this. I shall not carry off this deer from the snare! Then the hunter addressed that doe in verse:
I have neither heard nor seen that a doe speaks human speech;
therefore, O blessed lady, may you be happy, for I release this great deer to you.

Then that hunter released the king of deer, Śiriprabha, who had been bound by the snare. Seeing that the king of deer was freed, the doe was uplifted, joyful, filled with gladness and serenity, and she addressed the hunter in verse:
In this way, hunter, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen,
just as I rejoice today having seen the great deer released.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One, the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
The Blessed One explained this matter with reference to the self: those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases.
In the beginningless and endless cycle of existence where I formerly dwelt,
I was Śrīprabha and Yaśodharā was a doe.
Ānanda was the hunter; thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Thus this ancient cycle, encompassed by much suffering and characterized by high and low conduct, has been traversed; now, free from fever, free from fear, and without sorrow—
He recited his own birth story in the midst of the community of monks.
The Jātaka of the Lion King Śrīprabha is completed.

Then, while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities at Uruvilvā in the forest of penance on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, Māra the Evil One approached him and said: "What will you achieve through this striving? Dwell in the midst of a household; you shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin). Perform great sacrifices—the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the Soma-drinking, the Nirargada, the Padma, and the Puṇḍarīka. Having performed these sacrifices, after death you will rejoice in the heavens and produce abundant merit. Striving is difficult, hard to undertake, and..."
“O Evil One, there is no loss of merit for one who dwells in the holy life. The Bodhisattva said: “I have no need for merits, O Evil One.
Having beheld the delightful wildernesses and forest thickets, I have applied myself to exertion in the vicinity of Uruvilvā.”
Having approached him as he was exerting himself to attain the supreme goal,
Namuci came there, speaking words of compassion.
"You are emaciated and ill-colored; death is near for you. Abandon your great exertion, for life is as uncertain as hope."
Life is better for you, most excellent; living, you shall perform meritorious deeds.
Perform those meritorious deeds by which you will not grieve after passing away.
"By practicing the holy life and offering the fire sacrifice, infinite merit is produced; what will you achieve by abandoning them?"
"Renunciation is far off; it is difficult and hard to accomplish"—this was the speech that Māra spoke in the presence of the Bodhisattva.
To that Māra, the Bodhisattva then spoke thus:
"O Evil One, kinsman of darkness, I have not come here seeking merit."
O Māra, I have no need for even atom-sized merits;
but as for those who do have need of merits, why do you not speak to them, O Māra?
I do not think that I am immortal, for life indeed ends in death;
I shall go forth irreversibly, devoted to the holy life.
This wind might even dry up the currents of rivers;
why then would it not dry up the blood of me, who have set my soul upon liberation?
The body is withering away; now let the bile, the phlegm, that born of wind, the flesh, and the blood alike be consumed.
As the [defilements of] fleshly desires wane, the mind becomes even more serene;
mindfulness, energy, and concentration become further established.
And for him who dwells thus, having attained the supreme state, look at the purity of this being; here, the body is not seen as subject to decay.
This life-destroying [creature] is ready; fie upon our vulgar life!
Therefore, being mindful, alert, and free from acquisitions... [the wise one attains final liberation].
Having cultivated both this mind and the supreme mind in battle,
and having broken through the forest by means of strength, I have accomplished what was to be accomplished.
While still beneath the Bodhi tree, before I had attained the state of immortality,
I beheld the army of Namuci, armored and with banners raised high.
I shall go forth to battle; I did not sit here for the sake of remaining stationary.
I will bring back that army of yours in due order.
Sensual desires are your first army; the second is called discontent. The third is hunger and thirst, and the fourth is called craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor; the sixth, O timid one, is said to be fear. The seventh is doubt for you, and the eighth is the pursuit of pride.
Greed, worldly renown, honor, and whatever fame is acquired through wrong means—these are the [remaining] fetters.
This is the army of Namuci, armored and with banners raised;
here some ascetics and brahmins are seen to be deeply immersed in it.
The coward does not conquer it, or having conquered it, he grieves;
through wisdom, I shall shatter that [craving] for you, like an unbaked clay vessel with water.
Having brought that thorn under control and established well-founded mindfulness,
dwelling with energy aroused, I shall indeed discipline my disciples as well.
Foolish people of weak intellect are devoted to negligence;
I shall tell you where suffering ceases for one who is free from desire.
While he was overwhelmed with grief, his prosperity went to ruin;
and then the dejected yakṣa vanished right there.

Just as the Bodhisattva, being afraid of intentional lying and loathing intentional lying, rejected that deity, saying "Enough," and then consumed substantial food for the sake of comfort; thereafter, the group of five auspicious companions, becoming disillusioned, withdrew [from him], thinking: "The ascetic Gautama has fallen away from concentration; he has become lax and has again consumed substantial food."

Māra the Evil One also followed closely behind the Bodhisattva for six years while he was practicing austerities, seeking an opportunity and looking for a flaw. Having followed the Bodhisattva for six years without finding an opportunity, without finding a foothold, and without finding a point of attachment, he became despondent and withdrew.
Wherever Māra cannot prevail, nor the wind the Himalayas,
there the world together with its gods honors the one who dispels the King of Death.

The monks said to the Blessed One, “With the intention of liberation, the Blessed One performed difficult austerities. The Blessed One said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have performed difficult austerities with the intention of liberation. The monks asked, “Was there another time too, Blessed One? The Blessed One said, “There was another time too, monks.”

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a fowler who would capture birds in forest regions, confining them with nets, snares, and cages. Having nourished them repeatedly with fodder and water, he made them grow large and sold them for a desired price. In that place, another bird was caught and confined in a cage. Now, that bird was wise by nature; he observed those birds previously cast into the cage, fattened on fodder, and grown large, being bought by people and then dragged out from their cages. Seeing this, that wise bird reflected: "This fowler does not give us fodder or water out of a desire for our welfare; he gives us fodder or water for the sake of profit. When we have become fat and large, he will sell us for a desired price."

"I shall act in such a way that no one will buy me; even if they do not obtain my official license, no one will take me. I shall consume only such food that I neither grow fat nor die. He then consumes only such food and drinks only such water that he neither grows fat nor dies. A man who buys birds arrives. Then that bird stands right in front of the door of its cage. That man, the bird-buyer, puts his hand into the cage and feels the bird; yet the meat does not come into his hand—it is light, and he does not find it heavy. Then, having set it aside from the cage, he takes other fatter, heavier birds back to their dwelling. Thinking that this is a dry bird or one that is ill, no one takes it. The fowler also observes this: "This bird must be ill. When it has recovered from its illness, it will eat more fodder and drink more water. Once it has grown fat, it will be sold. Lest it make the other birds ill through contagion, let it be driven out of the cage and kept outside. It will receive its own fodder and its own drink separately. When it has become fat, then it will be sold."

That wise bird also became distrustful of that fowler. Whenever the fowler opened the door of the cage for the sake of the birds—for the sake of fodder, or for the sake of water—that bird would enter the cage unawares; but whenever he was out of sight, [the bird would fly away].

Then he would enter that cage of his own accord; and when he desired to emerge from the cage, he would likewise run out by himself. No one would stop him, thinking, "He is ill. Now, that bird was so weak in body that he could enter and exit that cage even through the top opening. And because they thought the bird was ill, they neglected him. Then, at the time when he knew, "These fowlers have become trusting toward me," he ate more fodder and drank more water than usual, until he was able to escape by flying far away. When he became emboldened and thought, "This is my time to flee," he stood above that cage and at that moment spoke this verse in front of those birds:
A person who does not reflect does not attain distinction;
behold, through the power of reflection, I am liberated from my own bondage.
Having spoken this verse, that bird flew up from the fowler’s house and returned once more to the forest.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the wise bird was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way. And why is that? Monks, at that time, on that occasion, I myself was that wise bird. It might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the fowler was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way. And why is that? Monks, Māra the Evil One was the fowler at that time, on that occasion. Even then, with the intention of liberating this Māra the fowler from his cage, I performed difficult austerities."
The Śakuntaka-jātaka is completed.

The monks said to the Blessed One: "By means of his extraordinary intelligence, the Blessed One was released from being in the hands of Māra, under his control, and confined in a cage while he was in the form of a bird. The Blessed One said: "On another occasion as well, by means of his extraordinary intelligence, I was released from being in the hands of this Māra, under his control, and placed in a basket. The monks said: "Was there yet another occasion, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: "There was another occasion as well, monks."

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a river named Paripātrikā. On its bank was a forest-grove belonging to another florist. Now, at that time, this florist, having gone to the forest-grove for the sake of garlands, gathered flowers, took his flower-basket, and set out from the florist’s workshop toward the village. Then, a tortoise emerged from the river and was eating cow dung not far from that florist. He was seen by the florist, and it occurred to him: "This tortoise will make an excellent ornament for me today. So he set down his flower-basket to one side, caught the tortoise, and placed it inside the basket. And that tortoise spoke to him in human speech: "I am smeared with mud; therefore, these flowers of mine will be ruined by the mud. Wash me here in the water and then place me in the basket; then these flowers will not be ruined. Then the florist thought: "This tortoise is indeed beautiful. I shall go and wash him here in the water; then these flowers will not be ruined by the mud. Stretching out his five limbs—his tail being the fifth—he slipped from the florist’s hand. There, the water was deep; emerging onto the bank not far from that river, the tortoise addressed the florist in verse: [The tortoise speaks: "O florist, you have been deceived by me, For I have escaped from your grasp. Go home and look at your basket; You will see the flowers ruined by mud. The florist went home and looked at his basket; he saw the flowers ruined by mud. He thought: "Alas, I have been deceived by this tortoise! He then went back to the riverbank and searched for the tortoise, but he did not find him. He returned home and told his wife: "Wife, I have been deceived by a tortoise. She asked: "How so? He replied: "While I was gathering flowers, a tortoise came out from the river and was eating cow dung not far from me. I caught him and put him in my flower-basket, but he spoke to me in human speech, saying: 'I am smeared with mud; wash me in the water and then put me in the basket. I thought, 'This tortoise is beautiful; I will wash him in the water so the flowers will not be ruined,' and he slipped from my hand. I went to the riverbank and searched for him, but I did not find him. She said: "Husband, do not be angry. This tortoise is a wise being. Go to the riverbank and search again. He went to the riverbank and searched, but still did not find him. He returned home and told her: "Wife, I have searched again but have not found the tortoise. She said: "Husband, do not be angry.
