Like a thousand moons in the sky.
Then, having risen from one another, they were cast down upon that earth with even greater force,
like painted cloths tossed from the sky.
In that very way, she then became like a mother to Māra.
Free from fear and incomparable field of merit,
having formerly practiced the most excellent supreme Dharma,
you shine upon the world like the king of rays.
This is suffering, and this is its origin;
likewise its cessation and the supreme path.
When this exists, that comes to be.
When this is destroyed, that comes to an end.
Ignorance is the cause of the conditioned formations of existence; it becomes the condition for knowledge.
With consciousness as the cause, there is name-and-form in existence.
And it becomes the condition for the six sense faculties.
The six sense faculties arise, and from them contact is born;
contact is the cause of feelings.
Experiencing these, one becomes possessed by craving.
With craving as condition, clinging comes to be.
They recollect existence as the cause of clinging;
likewise, there are birth, old age, death, and disease,
as well as sorrow and lamentations.
Exertions result in suffering and mental distress.
The Bodhisattva, having investigated the phenomenon of dependent origination,
perceives their cessation within unimpeded omniscience;
thus beholding their very nature, he sees them in this way.
He has attained the incomparable, supreme, and excellent awakening.
And when the Jina has attained the supreme enlightenment, the immeasurable and pure vision,
his wisdom having proceeded throughout all directions, he is free from attachment.
The sound traveled through the three worlds by way of successive transmission.
The immeasurable drum was struck, and then an immeasurable sound arose;
the multitudes of men and women attained freedom from sorrow.
The gods, nāgas, humans, and mahoragas.
Infinite thousands of millions and billions of sons of gods, pure in their dwellings, have arrived;
they, having raised their hands with ten fingers joined in *añjali*, [stand before him].
I praise the One of Ten Powers who has reached the further shore.
Like the king of mountains in the midst of the ocean,
like Vaijayanta upon the summit of Sumeru,
or like a thousand suns in the sky.
Thus did the Jina shine at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
For whose sake generosity was given in previous existences, and for whose sake stainless morality was observed in the past;
and for whose sake supreme wisdom was cultivated—
O best of kings, you have attained awakening.
The one with vision, the destroyer of cataracts,
the essence of beings who has reached the end of the nature of destruction;
the self-become, the caravan leader among the best of men.
There is no one at all equal to you in the entire world.
All world-systems have been illuminated by you with a dense radiance, as if by the moon;
likewise, the divine splendor of the deities blazes forth.
And of the nāgas, asuras, and mahoragas.
It might be possible to weigh Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains,
by reducing it to dust; one could even divide it into as many equal portions as there are mustard seeds.
It is impossible to exhaust the praise of the Buddhas, the Victors.
Just as the drops in the great ocean filled with water can be grasped by the hand and counted— billions, trillions, and hundreds of millions— so too [can those beings be counted].
It is impossible to describe the qualities of the Victors.
It might be possible to know everything here within this trichiliocosm up to the peak of existence— the trees, winds, and fires of all lands,
as well as the number of grasses, creepers, and medicinal herbs— along with their potencies.
The praise of the Buddha cannot be fully exhausted.
Even if one were to divide the sky into hundreds or thousands of parts,
it might be possible to count the expanse of the heavens;
yet the number of the four directions is as vast as that.
The praise of the Buddha cannot be fully exhausted.
Even if one were able to count all the realms of sentient beings, and even all the body hairs and the hair on their heads,
the bodies of those who have passed away in the past would likewise be beyond counting.
It is not possible to exhaust the praise of the Victors.
Those beings who, having heard such qualities as these,
with serene minds call to mind the Lord of the World,
for them there is a great gain, as they shall abandon the miserable states of existence.
And their awakening is considered to be not far off.

Furthermore, monks, after the Tathāgata had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he spent seven full days in a single cross-legged posture. Then indeed, the gods who range over the earth, the gods who range through the atmosphere, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, Mahābrahmā, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapāriṣadya gods, the Ābhā gods, the Parīttābhā gods, the Apramāṇābhā gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, and the Śubha gods...

And the gods of the Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens, for a full seven days honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the Tathāgata who had reached the supreme seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). And the entire trichiliocosm became adorned with a single ornament for a full seven days. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Having awakened to supreme enlightenment, the Perfectly Awakened One, the shrine of the entire world, did not rise from his seat for seven full days.
Thousands of millions of deities assembled in the sky and rained down a shower of flowers for no less than seven nights.
There the gods will rain down beautiful blue lotuses, red lotuses, campaka flowers, and white lotuses, lovely with their thousand petals.
And Māra was dejected; he scratched the earth with his arrow:
"I am conquered by the God of Gods, the Śākya Lion, the Fierce One."
The Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and those who are Nirmāṇarati, as well as the Paranirmita gods— all those established in the realm of desire.
Divine red sandalwood, aloeswood, and campaka flowers,
as well as divine rains of blossoms, were scattered from the sky;
this Buddha-field was showered with streams as thick as axle-trees.
Thousands of millions of Brahmās have gathered in the sky;
they rain down a fine powder of divine red sandalwood.
Beginning with the gods of the earth and extending to the Śuddhāvāsa deities who are self-luminous,
the entire realm was thus completely filled by gods, one surpassing the other.
With parasols, banners, and flags, they completely fill the sky,
performing the most excellent worship of the glorious, perfectly awakened Buddha.
A vast radiance was released, completely illuminating the Buddha-field;
even the world-systems up to the peak of existence became the same color as fire.
The hells became completely pacified throughout this buddha-field;
the embers were turned to coolness, and sentient beings became happy.
For those beings whose hellish suffering has been completely exhausted,
they pass from the hells and will be reborn among the gods.
In the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Tapana, Pratāpana,
and Raurava hells, the fire was extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
Then, in the Avīci hell, in Saṃghāta, and in the individual hells,
the fire was completely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
In as many world-systems as there were individual hells,
the fire was completely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
And those who belong to the animal realm and feed on flesh and blood,
being suffused with loving-kindness by the Buddha, do not harm one another.
The Bodhi tree was adorned with parasols, banners, and flags;
it was covered with gabled pavilions fashioned by the sons of the gods.
Stumps, thorny thickets, gravel, and even sand were established all around the seat of awakening, down to the ground beneath it.
The seat of enlightenment was completely covered by ground made of jewels,
which had been fashioned here in this buddha-field by the sons of gods.
Thousands of sons of gods stood upon the earth;
taking up incense burners, they worshipped the Leader of the World.
And below, all the dhāraṇīs were completely covered with lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, which had arisen through the majestic power of the Buddha.
And those beings who were diseased, suffering, and without refuge,
became healthy and happy, suffused by the rays of the Buddha.
Those born blind shall see forms once they have obtained clear vision;
and they shall speak to one another when the Protector has attained enlightenment.
At the time when the Great Seer, the Lion of the Śākyas, attained enlightenment, the stains of passion, hatred, and delusion were removed from his body.
The palaces, along with the celestial mansions and delightful gabled chambers,
were all turned toward the Bodhisattva, the Protector.
As many men, women, and kinnaras as there were within the Buddha-field,
they all turned their faces toward the Bodhisattva, the Protector.
The deities, the sons of gods, and the beautiful daughters of gods—
all turned their faces toward where the Great Seer’s enlightenment was located.
The nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas—
all turned their faces toward where the Great Seer had attained enlightenment.
The girls and boys likewise lay down upon their beds and seats; they remained with their faces turned toward where the Great Seer’s seat of awakening was located.
And whatever divine ornaments there were, distinguished and made of jewels,
which had been fastened upon the gods, all turned toward him.
Then, all the ornaments of the nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, and rākṣasas went toward the place of awakening.
Then the celestial palaces of the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas,
and the rākṣasas turned their faces toward where the Great Seer’s seat of awakening was located.
Ankle-bells, bracelets, or even armlets—
by means of these, the garment of the Buddha who has attained enlightenment becomes suspended.
Necklaces for people and beautiful golden coins were worn by men, by whom awakening was rendered unshakable.
He has fastened liberation-pearl necklaces, variegated jeweled earrings,
bracelets, and rings, by which unshakable awakening was attained.
However many inconceivable realms of sentient beings there may be within a buddha-field,
whether they know it or do not know it, by that [wisdom] awakening is rendered immovable.
And cool winds, fragrant and delightful,
will blow throughout the entire buddha-field of that Protector who has attained awakening.
As many as there are gods, nāgas, and humans, asuras, kinnaras, and yakṣas within the buddha-field, they all behold the Leader.
Having taken up incense burners, they all remained in comfort and worshipped the Light of the World, who was established at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
They paid homage with joined palms and praised him with verses;
established at the seat of awakening, they made offerings to the Buddha.
All see the Lord of the World, the light-maker, as being near;
no one perceives him as distant, for he stands as if at a distance of only one fathom.
No one in the world-system sees the Buddha from behind;
for in every direction, he is seen face-to-face by the vision of all.
From the left and right sides, no one perceives the Leader of the World, the Great Hero; yet all behold the Leader. Immediately thereafter, incense was burned throughout the Buddha-field.
Tens of millions of Buddha-fields in every direction were filled with fragrance.
It is not possible to calculate how many millions of beings,
having beheld the glory of the Buddha, have set out toward supreme enlightenment.
The grasses, the wood, the herbs, and the forest trees—
all of them were turned toward that direction where the Great Seer’s seat of awakening was located.
Who, having heard such dharmas as these shown by the Lord of the World, would not be satisfied, except for one belonging to the faction of Māra?
It is not possible to fully describe with speech, even by one speaking with supernatural power,
all the glory that belonged to the Buddha, the Protector, when he had attained enlightenment.
Those wise ones who have seen the Perfectly Awakened One established at the seat of enlightenment,
and who have honored the Great Hero, are filled with joy upon hearing this.
And those monks who are well-established in the aggregate of ethical discipline that is without flaw,
having heard this sutra, will experience auspicious joy.
Endowed with patience and gentleness, with bodies and minds undaunted,
and seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, they shall find satisfaction.
Those beings who have been comforted by these [teachings] shall be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven; having awakened to supreme enlightenment, they will experience great joy.
Those best of the twice-born who have honored previous Buddhas,
upon hearing this sutra, will become joyful, O Great Seer.
If those miserable beings have been satisfied with food and drink,
they will, upon hearing this sutra, show reverence toward the Buddha.
Those beings who, though poor, are covered by wealth—
having heard this sutra, they will show reverence toward the Buddha.
And those who have previously constructed beautiful reliquaries for the Buddhas,
having awakened to excellent faith, will indeed become joyful.
Those who in former times upheld the true Dharma of the Lord of the World,
having renounced gain and honor, will indeed be filled with joy.
Those who possess unconditioned life and are free from punitive actions— they,
as the heart-sons of the Lord of the World, shall indeed perform worship.
Those who, having seen the perfectly awakened Maitreya, the supreme among bipeds,
shall perform extensive worship, will experience great joy.
Those who, having seen you— the lion, the great elephant, the shrine of the world—
shall perform extensive worship, for them there will be joy.
For those who, desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, shall perform worship to Ketu, the Lord of the World, they will experience great joy.
And those who shall perform worship for the Buddha Pradyota,
desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, will experience great joy.
And those who, having seen the Buddha Aparājita, shall behold Jyotindhara and offer him great worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who, having seen Sunetra, the Illuminator of the World, shall honor him,
will experience joy through their immeasurable worship.
There will be two Buddhas named Kusuma, Tathāgatas who are protectors of the world;
those who see them and honor them will experience great joy.
Those who, having seen Maru, the best of bipeds, the perfectly awakened one, the foremost of speakers, shall honor him, will experience great joy.
And having seen the supreme Buddha, the best of bipeds,
those who shall offer him the highest worship will experience great joy.
Those who are greedy for gain and honor, relying on crooked wisdom— having heard about that state of having few desires, they will be filled with terror.
And those who delight in company and are established in living in a group—
upon hearing of the Buddha’s solitude, they feel no distress.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the Buddha, those of immoral conduct will bow down before the Lamp of the World and show intense reverence.
Those future bodhisattvas who have been prophesied by the Buddha—
those who are well-disposed and pleasant to dwell with— they shall experience joy.
Those for whom there is no turning back from the Buddha-knowledge in any respect—
those people, having heard this sutra, will become happy.
Those former Buddhas, the essence of beings, the lords of men, who were honored, revered, and worshipped—
before them, with a humble mind, he was instructed in the wisdom of the Buddha.
Having heard [this], O one of the finest color among men, they become joyful.
And those who are unimpaired, pure in every way, endowed with hundreds of millions of excellent qualities,
and who uphold the Dharma while it is decaying—
With a joyful mind, [he dwells] within the teaching of the Sugata.
And those who were not fickle, who were steadfast, not loquacious, nor were they of scattered speech;
they were not possessed by pride.
Having heard the excellent color of the Conqueror, they become joyful.
Those who have not abandoned the wisdom of the Buddha,
whose stainless and incomparable awakening is thus infinite,
and who practice their vows with vigilance—
Having heard the excellent praise of the Jinas, they become joyful.

"Monks, endowed with four qualities, the Tathāgata, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, attained preeminence over the entire world. What are these four? [They are: an unbroken aggregate of ethical discipline;

a mind intent on the welfare of all beings; and a mind that bears the burden of all beings. Monks, endowed with these four qualities, the Tathāgata, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, attained such omniscience as this."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
In the teaching of the Lord of the World, the aggregate of ethical discipline is the supreme wealth;
neither gold nor silver is described as the wealth of a monk.
One who is well-established in the Teacher’s dispensation should honor ethical discipline;
one who is immoral and trembling is far from being a disciple of the Buddha.
Having guarded their morality without flaw, the supreme among bipeds— the Lords of the World, the great heroes endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks— behold them.
One who is intent on the aggregate of virtue through loving-kindness, eager for dwelling in the forest,
gentle, and pleasant to live with— this is the wealth of a recluse.
Having little desire, being easily contented, gentle, well-composed, and endowed with moral shame and dread of blame— this is the wealth of the ascetic life.
Indeed, monks of virtuous conduct, having cut through the ensnaring net of craving, cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment; this is the wealth of the ascetic life.
The Sage meditates on emptiness and peace, and has turned away from existence;
this wealth of the ascetic life is free from much suffering and devoid of essence.
He becomes truly wealthy who practices in this way;
indeed, that monk who is perfected in practice is truly wealthy.
The monk who is perfected in virtue is called "wealthy";
for a monk does not become possessed of great riches merely through pearls and coral.
A virtuous monk who practices non-violence is pleasant to dwell with;
for it is not by the acquisition of robes that a monk goes to the heavenly realm.
Having practiced pure morality, one avoids all unfavorable rebirths;
the Teacher does not praise a monk who seeks gain from his kinsmen.
Having applied effort toward virtuous conduct, heaven is not difficult to attain;
wherever one is reborn, one becomes beloved and pleasing to all.
A wise person, desiring the three kinds of happiness—
praise, the acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death— should guard their virtue.
Virtue is the most excellent cloak; it is a radiant ornament.
A monk adorned with virtue does not suffer when giving.
Through completely pure ethical discipline, the body becomes radiant;
and no burning fever arises for him when death is present.
When morality is completely pure, the attainment of its fruit is not difficult;
how much more so, then, that one attains a heavenly rebirth and beholds the Lord of the World!
A monk adorned with pure and gentle morality is truly distinguished;
it is not by loud speech that a monk becomes praised.
Possessing virtue and being fearless, he never fears at any time;
he never goes to an evil rebirth among living beings for his transgressions.
Possessing virtue, he has few concerns and little business, delighting in spiritual qualities;
he quickly attains concentration and also gains serene confidence.
With the aggregate of ethical discipline well-guarded, a monk becomes confident;
his vision is never lost when he beholds the disciples of the Jina.
And having purified his virtue, O monk, he remembers his former dwelling for thousands of millions of eons, being fully conscious and mindful.
And this is the natural outflow of his virtue:
that the Great Hero, the shrine for all the world, gazes upon the Brahma-world as he goes.
Through perfectly pure ethical discipline, the divine eye becomes purified;
for such a person, there is no further coming at all to any of the Buddha-fields.
Through the perfect fulfillment of ethical discipline, the immeasurable Tathāgata,
the Leader, knows the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings.
One who possesses virtue, wandering through the world, heedful and striving with diligence—
for such a person, the delightful voice of the Buddha is not difficult to obtain.
One who possesses virtue becomes dear to all beings and is honored everywhere;
being respected and esteemed as well, such a one has a pure mind and is free from blemish.
By means of perfectly pure ethical conduct, a person sees one who is passing away.
A beautiful and excellent celestial chariot, frequented by hosts of apsarases.
By means of perfectly pure morality, a person sees one passing away and being reborn on the beautiful summit of Mount Sumeru, in the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Through perfectly pure morality, he beholds the Yāma deities and that very celestial city, filled with apsarases.
Through perfectly pure ethical conduct, one beholds the Tuṣita deities;
one beholds their celestial palaces, variegated and composed of jewels.
Through perfectly pure ethical discipline, one beholds the Nirmāṇarati gods and sees the Sunirmita sons of the gods, beautifully adorned.
Through perfectly pure ethical conduct, one beholds the beautiful gods established in their celestial palaces as masters over the creations of others.
Through perfectly pure ethical conduct, one beholds Māra’s abode,
covered with canopies of jewels and frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
Having applied effort toward moral conduct, one beholds Brahmās and deities,
as well as Jāmbūnada palaces adorned with jewels.
The virtuous monk beholds the gods of the Brahma-realm and the gods who are the Ministers of Brahmā,
established within their celestial palaces.
A virtuous monk beholds the gods of the Retinue of Brahmā and the deity Mahābrahmā established within their celestial palaces.
Endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline, one beholds the radiance of the deities;
one beholds their distinguished celestial mansions made of jewels.
The virtuous monk sees the auspicious gods of great psychic power;
he sees the Śubhakṛtsna gods and also sees the Apramāṇābha gods.
Having guarded pure ethical discipline, one beholds the Parīttaśubha deities and thousands of sons of gods established in the realm of form.
Through completely pure ethical conduct, one sees the Bṛhatphala [heaven]; likewise, through completely pure ethical conduct, one sees the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana [heavens],
and one also sees the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens].
Those who attain final nirvana there, like a fire extinguished by water,
they too behold those monks because they have guarded their excellent moral conduct.
In former lives, he was always unblemished in virtue, distinguished by his excellent marks;
for that reason, he approaches the Teacher, the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
His body shines with the primary marks.
In morality and always in concentration, the Jina practiced with heedfulness throughout infinite past eons;
by that, he became the Lord of the World's Dharma.
Just as the sun, the king of rays, situated in the sky.
Having thus practiced such perfectly pure ethical conduct for immeasurable and likewise infinite eons,
the Sugata, adorned with the marks, shines with splendor.
From his mouth wafts the fragrance of sandalwood.
Constantly perceiving these virtues and maintaining the ethical discipline praised by the best of Victors,
dwell in the forest with uplifted minds.
Those which are honored by the best of sages are called "exquisite."
I have seen former Buddhas, the caravan leaders, who had destroyed all passion and were honored and worshipped as self-arisen ones; thus,
the aspiration for supreme enlightenment has been born within me.
Having heard these qualities, the bodhisattvas become uplifted.

Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata is pure in morality, pure in concentration, pure in wisdom, pure in liberation, and pure in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Monks, the Tathāgata is pure in patience; monks, the Tathāgata is pure in gentleness; monks, the Tathāgata is pure in loving-kindness; and monks, the Tathāgata is also pure in compassion and sympathetic joy. Monks, for one who would pay honor to such a perfectly pure Tathāgata with flowers, garlands, perfumes, banners, flags, music, ointments, and unguents—it is not possible to reach the limit of that merit. Nor can that mass of merit ever be exhausted, except by means of one of the three vehicles until final *parinirvāṇa*; even then, its limit remains beyond reach. Why is that? Because, monks, just as the Tathāgata is immeasurable in all his qualities, even so, monks, the offering established in the Tathāgata is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, limitless, and ineffable. Moreover, monks, if someone were to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgata while he is currently living and maintaining himself, with flowers, perfumes, garlands, parasols, banners, flags, music, incense, ointments, food, drink, vehicles, and clothing—and if another were to honor even a relic the size of a mustard seed after he has passed into *parinirvāṇa*—these two are exactly equal.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Having directed the mind toward awakening for the benefit of all living beings,
whoever performs a circumambulation of the stūpa of the Lord of the World,
Possessing mindfulness, possessing intelligence, and possessing merit,
one becomes confident in all births while practicing the conduct of awakening.
Having performed a circumambulation of a stūpa, one becomes honored everywhere among all births by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
One should avoid the eight unfavorable conditions that have been taught by me,
and instead cultivate even a single favorable condition— the most auspicious appearance of a Buddha.
Endowed with excellence of complexion and form, adorned with the [major] marks,
possessed of a sublime appearance, and with a mind free from dejection.
One becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and merit, and free from envy;
having seen the Light of the World, one honors him again and again.
Having seen selflessness and emptiness in all phenomena, he is not deluded regarding those phenomena;
he quickly attains serene confidence and becomes skilled in the Dharma.
He is reborn into wealthy and prosperous merchant families;
he is a preeminent master of generosity, heroic, liberated in renunciation, and free from envy.
Whatever distinguished and noble families there may be in Jambudvīpa, there that hero is born; he avoids those that are low.
A wealthy householder, empowered by the splendor of Śiri,
becomes honored everywhere by having performed a circumambulation of a stūpa.
A great brahmin householder is wise and learned;
a great kṣatriya householder is wealthy and possesses great riches.
The king too becomes righteous, a lord over Jambudvīpa;
he rules this entire earth, which is girt by mountains.
A universal monarch of great supernatural power, lord of the seven jewels,
established in his kingdom, repeatedly honors the Buddha.
Having passed away, one who has faith in the Buddha's teaching goes to heaven;
one even becomes Śakra, the lord of the gods, a sovereign upon the summit of Mount Meru.
One becomes Suyāma, the lord of gods, and also Santuṣita;
one becomes Nirmita, the lord of gods, and the sovereign Vaśavartin.
Even in the Brahma-world, he becomes a wise lord, a Brahmā,
honored by tens of millions of gods, having circumambulated a stūpa.
It would be impossible to exhaustively describe, even in hundreds of millions of eons,
those who perform circumambulations of the stupa of the Lord of the World.
Having directed the mind toward awakening, whoever pays homage to the shrine of the Teacher shall never become blind or one-eyed for tens of millions of eons.
By performing a circumambulation of the shrine of the Lord of the World, one obtains eyes that are pure, large, and beautiful with their dark blue hue.
Endowed with strength and vigor, he does not fall into indolence;
he remains ever vigilant after having performed a circumambulation of the stupa.
Possessing firm vigor, firm strength, being a leader, and possessing firm prowess,
one quickly attains skillfulness by performing circumambulation of a stūpa.
The wise person never meets death by fire, poison, or weapons;
he meets his end only when his full lifespan has been exhausted.
He was renowned throughout the royal capitals, kingdoms,
and market towns for his beauty, wealth, and enjoyments, having performed circumambulations of the stupa.
With pure body and pure garments, established in the white dharmas,
he does not indulge in sensual desires while practicing the conduct of awakening.
Having fashioned a garland of flowers and offered it at a stūpa,
having directed the mind toward awakening, one shall never suffer defeat.
Having passed away from here and died, he indeed goes to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
he quickly obtains a celestial palace made of various jewels.
Having offered garlands upon a stūpa, one enjoys celestial palaces and gabled mansions frequented by hosts of apsarases among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
May I obtain a divine lotus pond, complete with the excellence of its eight qualities, strewn with golden sand, and covered with lapis lazuli and crystal.
Having enjoyed divine riches and having fulfilled his goals, the wise man,
passing away from the world of the gods, becomes a human being possessed of wealth.
And by that root of merit, the heedful and discerning one propitiates the Tathāgata and honors the Best of Bipeds.
Having honored the Supreme among Bipeds, he is not conquered by passion, nor is he humiliated by hatred; he never becomes deluded.
Having honored the Leader of the World, one becomes free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion, with sense faculties restrained in all births.
For hundreds, thousands, and millions of billions of births,
one will be honored everywhere after having offered a garland at a stūpa.
Having offered a garland at a stūpa, one becomes even a universal monarch, or Śakra the lord, or even Brahmā in the Brahma-world.
Having offered a silk ribbon at the stūpa of the Lord of the World,
all one's aims are fulfilled— both those that are divine and those that are human.
He avoids low-born families and is not reborn there;
rather, he becomes wealthy, possessed of riches, and a lord in Jambudvīpa.
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata, one becomes distinguished everywhere in terms of physical form, enjoyments, complexion, and supernatural power.
He becomes one who remembers his past lives and is not led astray by passion;
knowing the fault of sensual desires, he undertakes the holy life.
Unconquered by forms, sounds, and tastes,
he commits no evil deed after having honored the Supreme among Bipeds.
Having honored the Leader, he is never overcome by fragrances or tactile sensations; he remains mindful and clearly comprehending.
Neither thieves nor kings can seize his mass of wealth,
nor does fire consume it, for he has rendered worship to the Tathāgata.
Having offered a silk ribbon and flowers to the Leader of the World, he never again falls into sorrow or the weariness of grief.
In all his births he shall be free from sorrow and unharmed;
having worshipped the Lamp of the World, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch of great supernatural power.
Having worshipped the Leader of the World, one’s hands and feet become well-knit, one attains the beauty of the limbs, and becomes endowed with excellent complexion and form.
Avoiding evil karma while practicing the conduct of awakening,
one beholds those supreme among bipeds who are so difficult to find in the world.
Having enjoyed happiness for hundreds, thousands, and nayutas of millions of eons, that wise one awakens to supreme enlightenment.
Having constructed a flower-garland monastery for the relics of the Lord of the World,
the king becomes one of great supernatural power, surrounded by an unbreakable retinue.
One avoids those unwholesome states that have been shunned by the Noble Ones,
and one practices those wholesome states that have been praised by the Buddhas.
He becomes beloved and dear, honored and praised by the gods,
the nāgas, and those who are wise in the world.
Accompanied by a magnificent and vast retinue, he of great strength worships the Unconquered One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Best of Bipeds.
In whatever household he is born, enflamed by the power of his merit,
that family becomes honored by the kingdom and the town.
Having constructed a monastery, one should direct the mind toward awakening;
this is the perfection for him that has been praised by the Buddhas.
Neither hunchbacked nor lame, nor stumbling or limping,
he is adorned with the marks wherever he is reborn.
Seeing poor beings, he covers them with wealth;
yet, while practicing the conduct of awakening, he remains unshakeable.
Having renounced this entire earth, the one of great intelligence becomes undaunted in mind; he never desponds.
Having cast aside sons and daughters, as well as a wife who is auspicious and blessed,
he who has set out for awakening goes forth.
He becomes one who initiates conversation first, pleasant-faced and easy to look upon;
he is never overcome by envy nor ever by pride.
Thus, free from envy and gentle, having reached the perfection of patience,
seeking the welfare of others and endowed with virtues, he has set out for awakening.
A jewel in all the world, his arising is difficult to find:
he who is irreproachable, worthy of offerings, and has set out for enlightenment.
A child might be able to count the stars in the sky in a single blink of an eye,
but it is impossible to describe the limit of his virtues with words.
It is possible to know the minds of all sentient beings throughout the three times;
yet it is not possible to describe the limit of his virtues with words.
The four great oceans, the sands [of the Ganges],
and thousands of millions of nāgas— even these cannot describe his virtues.

Even if one were able to count, in a single blink of an eye, all the hairs on the bodies of all sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence in the world, it would still not be possible to describe his virtues.
Wherein this entire earth is established upon the mass of water—
no fool is able to create such a thing, nor can his qualities be fully described.
Those trees that stand here between the temple and those that have not yet grown in the ground, as well as those whose lives will endure for an eon.
It is possible for one who possesses knowledge to count the flowers and fruits,
but it is not possible to describe the limit of the virtues of that son of the Buddha.
They might speak a delightful garland of praises for that hero,
yet it is not possible to describe the limit of the virtues of a son of the Buddha.
He who would do what is unpleasant for hundreds of thousands of births—
having avoided gods and humans, hell is his domain.
He becomes blind and sightless, miserable and without refuge—
whosoever, being ignorant, inflicts suffering upon the Bodhisattvas.
Having passed away, he would go to Avīci, which is terrible and fearsome;
with a massive body, he experiences agonizing sensations.
With a body one *yojana* in height, he is born there,
surrounded by a complete mandala and scorched on all sides.
Five thousand heads are established upon his body,
and on each single head there are no fewer than five hundred tongues.
A hundred hells are manifested upon a single tip of the tongue;
he who cooks there experiences that most terrible fruit of his minor karmic actions.
Having passed away from Avīci, as well as from Tapana and Pratāpana,
the person of dull wit experiences there the ancient evil deeds he committed.
The ignorant person who causes oppression to the sons of the Buddha will never again easily obtain a human birth.
For hundreds of thousands of births, for hundreds and for nayutas,
one experiences painful sensations and is tormented because of that cause.
The devourer of marrow becomes a poison; he is a terrifying oppressor who inflicts suffering upon the sons of the Buddha, the protectors.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, this is the fruit of evil karma;
even when obtaining food, he never eats to his satisfaction.
Having passed away from there, he is devoured in great cauldrons in the world of Yama;
he never finds protection, having caused oppression to monks.
Having passed away and died from that state, he comes to the human world.
He becomes blind from birth, dull-witted, evil-minded, and unrestrained.
Speech that is ill-spoken becomes untrue and harsh in sound;
having passed away from among humans, one quickly goes to a state of misery.
He who, being unrestrained, causes oppression to the sons of the Buddha, shall never see a Buddha for thousands of millions of eons.
O sons of the Buddha, by providing righteous protection for things,
one avoids all miserable destinies and quickly goes to a heavenly rebirth.
He becomes wealthy and possesses great riches; he is powerful and confident.
Endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, he is happy and free from affliction.
And when the illuminators of the world have passed into parinirvāṇa,
having seen the stūpas of the Buddhas, they pay them honor again and again.
Who, having heard such teachings spoken by the Buddha,
would not repeatedly develop serene confidence in the sons of the Buddha?
And whoever should honor hundreds, thousands, and nayutas of Buddhas— as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges— for so many eons;
And whoever should uphold for even a single night and day the True Dharma shown by the Lord of the World as it is perishing, their merit will be superior.
I am honored when established in the wisdom of a Buddha;

He who protects the Teacher’s instruction while the True Dharma is perishing shall never suffer harm for thousands of millions of eons.

he is never overwhelmed by thousands of unpleasant things.
One who is perfected in patience, gentle, amiable, and mild,

Happy and joyful,

Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was decaying.

Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was decaying.

Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.

Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was decaying.

From the depths below up to the peak of existence,
this entire Buddha-field, made of Jāmbūnada gold— such glory as this could be exhausted.

Not equal to one who offers even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
It would be possible to exhaust such glory as this by filling the world-system from the bottom up to the peak of existence with kārṣāpaṇa coins.
Not equal to one who offers even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.

Having inspired faith in the Supreme among Men, they gave a parasol to the Blessed One, the supreme Buddha, the bull among men, as he was walking along.

Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Jina.

his body becomes fragrant and his complexion is distinguished;
he never suffers any decline.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
He becomes a hero of firm vows and heedfulness, who finds no delight in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
through renunciation, his mind becomes undaunted.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
Having avoided the unfavorable conditions,
he attains distinguished favorable conditions;
he performs incomparable worship of the Buddhas.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
He never abandons the thought of awakening,
nor does he become one of broken morality or unrestrained conduct;
he attains the pure Dharma of dispassion.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
He abandons all unattractiveness at all times and relinquishes ignorance entirely;
having attained distinction, he wanders through the entire world.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
He obtains pure food and acquires distinguished garments, variegated with gold,
endowed with dyes, most beautiful and lovely to behold.
Having offered a net to the shrines of the Victorious One.
Having removed the withered flowers from the shrines of the Jinas, he was satisfied, joyful, and filled with fervor;
loathing harsh and painful speech.
May he please the Caravan Leader endowed with the ten powers.
He becomes gracious, with a purified body, worthy of being looked upon, and honored by many people;
even a king will not harbor a malicious mind toward him.
And whoever removes withered flowers from a shrine.
The evil paths are closed off for that bodhisattva who stands firm in the aggregate of ethical discipline and would raise up [offerings] at the shrines of the Jinas.
One should discard a flower that has previously withered.
He abandons sorrow and fault at all times,
and he abandons every trace of passion within the body without exception; having attained consolation, he shall remain for infinite eons.
And whoever removes withered flowers from a shrine.
He becomes a Buddha, a caravan leader together with his retinue, honored by the gods with infinite splendor;
he is adorned, his body perfectly pure.
And whoever removes withered flowers from a shrine.

One should offer five auspicious divine flowers— either *māndārava* or *pāṭala* blossoms— or even those that have been previously offered; likewise, one who removes withered flowers from the *caityas*.
That person becomes radiant as a result of that maturation.
Neither poison nor weapon, nor the blazing mass of fire, nor the consuming flame, shall take effect upon his body;
even wicked thieves cannot prevail against him.
He who removes withered flowers from the shrines.
It is not easy to proclaim the merit of one who has taken up such vast merit by offering even a single withered flower at the shrines of the Jinas.
Having heard it, he was satisfied and filled with the force of great joy.
One whose body is uplifted becomes noble, always practicing the most excellent pure karma;
for such a person, supreme and foremost enlightenment is not far off.
Having removed the faded floral offerings from the stūpa of the Jina.
Whoever, having generated the aspiration for supreme enlightenment, should scatter sandalwood upon the Leader,
becomes forever worthy of worship in the world.
Gracious, well-disposed, and full of splendor.
All the world—
gods, nāgas, humans, and mahoragas—
bows down before that very king throughout the entire thousandfold world-system in full bloom.
Then you were a hero in sovereignty.
Those who dwell in his realm are established in the world in excellent wisdom and knowledge;
having transcended all evils, they abide there.
They practice the Dharma among gods and humans.
His retinue becomes indivisible;
he is possessed of merit, mindfulness, and wisdom.
Having attained consolation, he wanders through the entire world.
It generates joy in them according to their inclinations.
His introductory speech is pure and possesses the qualities of tone;
with words that are exceedingly friendly and gentle, he makes beings understand.
No one among people perceives anything as belonging to a lord in him.
He becomes one who is worthy of being looked up to by many people.
Pleasant speech, generosity, beneficial conduct, and consistency between words and deeds toward the many people— he, even when reviled, does not give rise to anger.
Whoever bows with their fingers toward the Buddha’s alms-bowl.
He shall not fall again into an evil state; he avoids low families in the world of mortals,
and he becomes wealthy with abundant treasuries.
Whoever pays homage with joined palms to a stupa of the Buddha.
Even when he becomes a human being, he is born as a king;
there is never any decline for him who bows with palms joined to a stupa of the Buddha.
He never speaks improper words;
he always speaks well-spoken speech. Sentient beings are never sated by his words.
Whatever excellent word he might utter but once.
As he was passing away, he beheld the Conqueror;
with a charming voice, he entered the royal capital.
Standing at the threshold of Indra’s gate, he [beheld] the Lord of the World.
Having seized the flowers, he scattered them with impetuous haste.
Having invited the Jina to his own home and having him eat the meal while preaching the Dharma, he,
filled with serene faith, honored the Jina.
Having taken the vessel, [he went] to the leader of Vraja.
The Jina, having understood his mind and his noble conduct, accepted [the gift] from him;
his fame shall spread throughout the world of the gods.
He is distinguished in the world, peerless, and worthy of offerings.
Knowing that the Sugata had accepted the bowl,
he was filled with impetuous joy and a satisfied heart; he then looked up toward the world of the gods.
I would conceive such a desire as this.
May I liberate beings who have encountered manifold sufferings;
may I become the eye for the blind throughout all worlds,
having attained illumination and destroying the darkness of ignorance.
May I also ferry across those beings who have not yet crossed over.
May I liberate those not yet liberated from the unconditioned;
having touched the peaceful, supreme, and foremost enlightenment,
may I travel through the ten directions unshakable.
Having attained wisdom, he liberates those who suffer.
Having understood his such-like vow,
just as Citta [is resolved] upon the Buddha-knowledge,
the Jina smiles and grants him a prophecy.
"You shall become a Buddha, a protector of the world."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; and the monk Viśuddhamati, with a joyful mind, along with the world of gods, humans, and asuras, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Sūtra named Avalokita, which is an appendix to the Mahāvastu, is completed.

On the bank of the Nairañjanā, you who move with unhurried gait, free from affliction, a lion among men, whose face resembles a flame fed by clarified butter— O Naga, I pay homage to you, the Blessed One, at the time of your passing.
Then, being uplifted and filled with the bliss of joy,
he paid homage to the Bodhisattva and spoke this verse:
Just as those world-protectors of great renown were seen by me in the past, you too are their equal; of this I have no doubt.
Having crossed over the state of existence, look all around.
Beholding that peerless Supreme Person, the Great Naga saw him like a blazing mass of fire or a flash of lightning amidst the clouds.

On the bank of the Nairañjanā, you who move with unhurried gait, free from affliction, a lion among men, whose face resembles a flame fed by clarified butter— O Nāga, I pay homage to you, the Blessed One, at the time of your passing.
Then, being uplifted and filled with the bliss of joy, he—
Paying homage to the Bodhisattva, he spoke this verse:
Just as those world-protectors of great renown were seen by me in the past, you too are their equal; of this I have no doubt.
Just as you lift your right foot while surveying the directions, O Supreme among Men, today you shall become a Buddha.
Since this earth resounds like a struck bronze vessel,
O Great Hero, there is no doubt that today you will become a Buddha.
And just as my dwelling was filled with pitch-black darkness, today it is all suffused with light; you shall become a Buddha.
Just as this celestial palace stands resplendent with brilliance on all sides,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
And since my Leader’s eyes are stainless and pure,
O Great Hero, there is no doubt that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as you cast off your garments of bark and as you bathe in the cool waters of the Nairañjanā, today you shall become a Buddha.
Just as the delightful Nairañjanā River is strewn with flowers,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as the gods rain down flowers and scatter garments,
and all the trees bow down, today you shall become a Buddha.
And having bathed in pure, flowing water, the son of the best of kings,
rising up, performed the consecration.
When he approached the seat where former Buddhas had sat.
Having cast aside the entire earth, with its four continents and mountains, like a globule of spittle without regard for it,
the Lion among Men requested grass from Svastika.
Seated there, he attained supreme enlightenment.
To him, who resembled a golden image and was marked with the svastika, Svastika then offered a handful of grass as soft as fine cotton.
And having grasped it with hands whose fingers were as soft as cotton, he—

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva strode with the stride of a lion for the sake of bringing forth the unsurpassed nectar; he strode with the stride of an elephant; he strode with the stride of a bull; he strode with the stride of a swan; he strode with the stride of a crane; he strode with the stride of one who is invincible; he strode with the stride of the foremost arising; he strode with the stride of the most excellent arising; he strode with the stride of the first arising; he strode with the stride of the timely arising; he strode with the stride of the arising preceded by a vow; he strode with the stride of the crusher of enemies; he strode with the stride of the unconquered; he strode with the stride of a Great Man; he strode with the stride of the undaunted; he strode with the stride of the fearless; he strode with the stride of the non-deficient; he strode with the stride of the unafraid; he strode with the great stride of one seeking welfare for the sake of making [the world] free from darkness; he strode with the stride for victory in the great battle and for the sake of bringing forth the unsurpassed nectar.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva strode with the stride of a lion; he strode with the stride of an elephant; he strode with the stride of a bull; he strode with the stride of a swan; he strode with the stride of a crane; he strode with the stride of one invincible; he strode with the stride of the foremost arising; he strode with the stride of the most excellent arising; he strode with the stride of the primordial arising; he strode with the stride of the arising of a pair; he strode with the stride of the arising preceded by aspiration; he strode with the stride that crushes enemies; he strode with the stride of the unconquered; [he strode] with the great—

He strode with the stride of a man; he strode with an undaunted stride; he strode with a fearless stride; he strode with a stride of one who is not terrified. Seeking the welfare of others, he strode with a great stride for the sake of creating light where there was no darkness. He strode with a great stride for the sake of victory in the great battle and for the bringing forth of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality. Five hundred arrows circumambulated and revolved around the Bodhisattva. Five hundred swans circumambulated and revolved around the Bodhisattva. Five hundred cranes circumambulated and revolved around the Bodhisattva. Five hundred peacocks circumambulated and revolved around the Bodhisattva. Five hundred jīvaṃjīvaka birds circumambulated and revolved around the Bodhisattva. Five hundred maidens circumambulated and followed after the Bodhisattva.

The Naga king named Kāla saw [the Bodhisattva], and having seen him, he spoke thus to the Bodhisattva: "Come, Great Śramaṇa! Come, Great Śramaṇa! O Great Śramaṇa, by whichever path you come, the Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Krakucchanda, also came by this path; he attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and you too, Great Śramaṇa, come by this path today; today you too shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. O Great Śramaṇa, by whichever path you come, the Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Konākamuni, also came by this path; he attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and you too, Great Śramaṇa, come by this path today; today you too shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. O Great Śramaṇa, by whichever path you come, the Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Kāśyapa, also came by this path and attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; you too, Great Śramaṇa, come by this path today; today you too shall attain perfect enlightenment."
Then indeed, the Naga king Kāla praised him as he was proceeding to the seat of enlightenment with verses.
Then, having seen that supreme Śākya walking away after having practiced for thousands of eons under thousands of millions of self-mastered ones, Kāla spoke to him.
O Best of Bipeds, by which path you go unhurriedly and without fear,
today you awaken to the conduct of all sentient beings for the sake of the Jina’s perfection.
By that same gentle path upon which those former Buddhas set out,
you, O Hero, bowing down today, shall become a Buddha.
The Blessed One Krakucchanda was a Buddha, as was the Sage named Konāka;
the Blessed One Kāśyapa was a Buddha, and you, sir, have likewise set out upon this same path.
"By the path by which Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and Kāśyapa went, by that same path go now, O Hero; today you shall become a Buddha."
Just as you grasp the grass, just as you ask Svastika,
and just as you have stepped upon the circle of the earth— today you shall become a Buddha.
Just as these Śuddhāvāsa deities, having attained mastery, pay homage with palms joined, so too, O Son of the Śākyas, is your honor equal to theirs.
Just as the celestial mansion was entirely filled with splendor by those previous ones,
O Great Hero, there is no doubt that today you will become a Buddha.
And just as my dwelling, which was shrouded in blinding darkness,
is now entirely suffused with light, so shall you become a Buddha today.
And since my eyes are stainless and purified, O Leader,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
And since the earth resounds like a struck bronze vessel,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as the winds blow, just as the trees are stirred,
and just as the birds warble, today you shall become a Buddha.
Just as the earth is adorned when it is covered with flowers,
so too does it become thus embellished only upon the arising of Buddhas.
Just as five hundred arrows circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as these fifty birds perform a circumambulation of you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred swans are circling you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred cranes are circumambulating you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred peacocks circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha;
just as five hundred pheasants circumambulate you to the right.
Without doubt, O Great Hero, today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred full jars circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred maidens circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
And when he approached the perfection of the Victor in person, at the time of the Svastika, that Lamp of the World sat upon the seat of the former Buddhas.
He sat down near the top of a great tree.
Then indeed, Kāla, the Naga king, praised the Bodhisattva as he sat upon the lion throne.
Just as you have spread this mat with soft grasses and sit upon it cross-legged,
today you shall become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred arrows circumambulate you to the right near the king of trees, today you shall become a Buddha.
O hero among men, you too today practice the conduct formerly followed by [the Buddhas];
you shall consume the host of the wicked, together with its horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry.
Just as you possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man upon your body,
you shine forth, having undoubtedly shattered the army of Māra.
Today, having uprooted the mind with its outflows and its afflictions and intoxications by means of wisdom, you shall attain enlightenment and awaken.
"Today there shall be no one to answer you in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus spoke Kāla, the great nāga, the most excellent among serpents;
joyful and with palms joined in reverence, he said: "Today you will become a Buddha."
The Bodhisattva addressed Kāla, the Naga king: "It is so, O Mahākāla; it is even so, O Great Naga. Today I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
And at that time, the Lord of Men, his body suffused with joy and rapture,
said: "Today, O Kāla, your word has become true."
Today you shall touch unsurpassed enlightenment.
Even if the great mountains, the best of peaks, were no more, and even if the moon were to fall from the sky,
I would still not fail to go there.
O Lord of Serpents, be joyful in mind!
The wind might shatter the peak of Mount Meru,
and the earth and sky might come together;
but one like me would never [leave] this most excellent lion throne.
Having approached it, they would not touch the nectar.
Seated there near the excellent tree, he released his voice:
"Today, the entire root of all existence shall be destroyed without remainder."
I infer this at the time of the end of the night.
Having praised the Fully Awakened One, who possesses the thirty-two excellent marks,
and having performed a circumambulation, he vanished right there.

Once seated, the Bodhisattva attains five perceptions: namely, the perception of the past, the perception of security, the perception of bliss, the perception of the impossible, and furthermore, he attains this perception of others: "Today I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. [The four policies are as follows: conciliation, force, sowing dissension, and bribery.]

Then indeed, Māra the Evil One approached the foot of the Bodhi tree and stood in the sky, in mid-air, with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Bodhisattva. Then the Bodhisattva addressed Māra the Evil One with this verse:
You stand in the sky, in the intermediate space, like a deer-herd intoxicated with speed;
bowing with palms joined, you pay homage.
You pay homage here to that one who is worthy of veneration.
"I am your lord and king, wise among all living beings; I am one who knows happiness and suffering, and who understands the cycles of the world."
O hero of great renown, as long as you possess youth and health,
enjoy human pleasures and dwell in your father’s house.
Dwell upon this delightful earth, flourishing and encircled by the ocean;
performing great sacrifices, O Gautama, rule over the kingdom.
Having performed the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the lotus sacrifice, and the unobstructed sacrifice—
having offered these sacrifices, you shall become an immortal god.
Having performed this sacrifice, the Trāyastriṃśa gods together with Indra enjoy their desires at will.
Thus, O worthy one, act and carry out my word;
do not let yourself be frustrated in the future by abandoning the fruit visible in this very life.
Māra recited this verse in the presence of the Bodhisattva,
and the Bodhisattva addressed Māra as he was speaking thus.
O evil one of deluded intellect, for whose sake have you come here?
You are certainly not a sovereign king, nor Brahmā, nor Prajāpati.
Even if you were the lord of this [world] and did not beg from me with palms joined,
I would still not welcome any birth— whether highly prosperous, low, or middling— for I am indeed indifferent even to you.
Even those sensual pleasures that are perfectly abundant— whether inferior, superior, or middling—
I do not delight in them, for I am indeed indifferent toward them.
Even these five strands of sensual pleasure which are considered happiness by the world,
I do not delight in them, for I am indeed indifferent toward them as well.
Just as an elephant, having broken through the snare and torn apart its bonds,
goes wherever it desires, so too,
having severed the bonds of the household, I shall go to the excellent city.
"Oh! They proclaimed the Dharma in the sky, thrilled and overjoyed."
Again, Māra approached the foot of the Bodhi tree and stood in the air above in the sky; the Bodhisattva said to him, "Who are you? Māra replied:
I am the lord who brings intoxication to gods and men; the best of the Suras and Asuras dwell within my sphere of influence.
Those trapped in the cage of saṃsāra are overcome by passion.
Those afflicted by desire are released from the noose of death.
Standing upon the circle of the earth, the Great Seer, who perceives the ultimate truth, spoke to Māra with sweet words:
"Though you have been endowed with a flood of merit for ten million eons..."
The speech of the bull among men, the roar of the preeminent man.
If you are a hero of the mind, you possess mastery; if you are a lord of desire, you are clearly not a master [of yourself].
For women, O Womb of the Lord of Men, are indeed afflicted by passion.
Those whose crests are adorned with hanging jewels and gems fall into the mire.
Upon the backs of those lords of the earth who have fallen in such a manner, playful women descend;
filled with the impetuous force of lust and passion, they laugh.
At that moment, those women became servants of Yama.
Having fallen into servitude to women, you speak of sovereignty; behold how deluded you are!
For one who is afflicted by passion possesses no mastery.
"It did not exist, nor will it ever exist"—this is my certainty.
Therefore, having defeated you along with your army in battle today,
I shall become a Buddha when the dawn breaks;
for no one, O Kṛṣṇa, has ever ascended the lion-throne.
The Buddha has arisen as one who has reached his final birth.
Māra said:
Why do you roar while sitting comfortably upon this excellent tree?
For you do not yet see here the thousandfold host of warriors—
the army consisting of hosts of piśācas, rākṣasas, and yakṣas.
The fourfold army, joyful and equipped with many mantras and yantras.
The Bodhisattva said:
If tens of millions of billions of Māras were to assemble against that bull among men, who has accumulated a flood of merit,
they could not move even a single hair; how much less you, O kinsman of darkness?
Go back; why do you lament so fruitlessly?

Māra, having been repulsed by the Bodhisattva, went to his own abode and informed his retinue: "Friends, this Bodhisattva has sat at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi). He must be displaced from that place; lest he lead a great multitude of people beyond my domain. Then his son, named Janīsuta, said: "Father, do not create an obstacle for him! Let him awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. Just as I have experienced his descent into the womb, his birth, and his Great Departure, and how he has now approached and sat at the seat of awakening—this very day he will awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. There is no being, nor any host of beings, capable of creating an obstacle for the Bodhisattva regarding his unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
Like a lion seated at the foot of a tree, difficult to assail, illuminating the directions—
this is never to our liking.
That you have thus assailed such a seer.
Endowed with morality, patience, and austerity, he has reached the supreme goal;
such as he is, his banner is raised high.
Just as an elephant will break its own bonds.
Behold him, the best among all bipeds,
who shines like the full moon on the fifteenth day,
even though he has received such an injury.
One might fall into a pit of glowing coals, or one might not touch a venomous snake with the hand;
yet one born blind is terrified by dogs on his back.
Thus, being sightless, he would fall into a blind well.
Thus these ones become small-minded,
and for such as them there is no mantra,
even though they [claim] to have such a perfectly pure range of conduct.
Those lacking faith and devoid of vision fall away.
If you do not accept these words while standing on the path, you will remember them when you have gone astray,
fleeing in all four directions.
Just like a jackal that has fallen from its place.
The minister Kāla recited this verse:
When this entire subtle meaning has been fully established,
one who is near to delusion possesses a mind devoid of right perception;
O King, it is just as this [person] is unconvinced.
The son of Janī produces an improper intellect.

Then Māra, having donned his great armor, approached the Bodhisattva. He was repelled by the sound of the Bodhisattva’s cough. Again, Māra donned his great armor and went to the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) near the Bodhisattva, accompanied by a vast fourfold army consisting of kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas. Spreading out for thirty yojanas on all sides, he mounted a vehicle yoked to a thousand horses; bearing a variegated bow, clad in armor, with banners and flags raised high, he was surrounded by a terrifying and deformed host of spirits (bhūtagaṇa) who let forth the clamor of many bherīs, mṛdaṅgas, marujas, paṭahas, paṇavas, and conchs, along with shouts of "kilikila" and "prakṣveḍita. For example: some had the faces of horses, others the faces of camels, others the faces of donkeys, others the faces of goats, others the faces of rams, others the faces of deer, others the faces of lions, others the faces of tigers, others the faces of leopards, others the faces of bears, others the faces of dogs, others the faces of boars, others the faces of cats, others the faces of crows, others the faces of cocks, others the faces of vultures, others the faces of ospreys; some were headless trunks (kabandhas), some had only one head, some had many heads, some had two heads; some were eyeless, some had only one eye, some were handless, some were footless, some were armless, some had ten arms; some bore swords, some bore spears, some bore javelins, some bore slings, some bore pikes, some bore tridents, some bore plows, some bore wheels, some bore clubs, some bore mallets, some bore axes, some bore scimitars, and some bore *karaṅkas*. Some vomited fire from their mouths, others vomited snakes, and others whirled razor-edged wheels in the air. Others, seizing an elephant with their feet, [attacked] the Bodhisattva—

They rush forward: some seizing camels, others seizing horses, others seizing donkeys, others seizing headless trunks, others seizing skeletons, others seizing venomous serpents, others seizing lions, others seizing tigers, others seizing leopards, others seizing bears, others seizing gayals, others seizing buffaloes, others seizing skulls, others seizing mountain peaks, and others seizing trees with their roots. Some cause a rain of embers to fall from the sky; others cause rains of venomous serpents to fall; others cause rains of stones to fall. Some are mounted upon elephants, others upon horses, others upon camels, others upon buffaloes, others upon donkeys, others upon gayals, others upon deer, and others upon...
Mounted upon boars, they rushed toward the Bodhisattva; yet not even a single hair of the Bodhisattva’s body quivered, nor did his mind undergo any change.
Then, having conjured an army in the sky consisting of chariots with oxen and horses, and joined by many steeds and elephants,
he advanced toward the supreme seat of the Bodhisattva.
Mounting a vehicle yoked with a thousand horses and wielding a variegated bow, he uttered these fierce words: "Slay! Slay! Seize him quickly!"
With faces like elephants, donkeys, horses, and camels, these fierce hosts of Rākṣasas, maces in hand,
roam about in terror wherever that slayer of enemies is found.
Other headless trunks, like venomous serpents, rise from the earth;
"Kill this one! Seize this one! they cry out with a terrible sound of distress.
Others vomit serpents, fire, and poison from their mouths;
hosts of piśācas seize lordly elephants with their feet and charge forward.
Others, vomiting forth mountain peaks, rush toward the sage;
other hosts of piśācas rain down showers of glowing coals from the sky.
Others whirl wheels with razor-sharp edges through the atmosphere;
they crackle in the sky and produce terrible sounds like thunderclaps.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva, having stroked his head three times and having stroked his cross-legged posture three times, struck the earth with his right hand-jewel—marked with beautiful lines, the color of a coating of liquid lac, soft like the touch of cotton, with copper-colored nails, and endowed with the roots of merit from many millions of eons. It resounded deeply, vibrated subtly, and reverberated. Just as a Magadhan bronze vessel, when struck against a mountain peak, reverberates and resonates with a deep sound, even so was the earth struck by the Bodhisattva with his right hand-jewel—with its copper-colored nails, beautiful lines, the color of a coating of liquid lac, soft like the touch of cotton, and endowed with the roots of merit from many millions of eons—and by that sound of the earth, they were shattered, broken, utterly destroyed, and transformed. The elephants sank down; the horses sank down; the chariots sank down; their feet sank down; their hands sank down; and their weapons fell away. The quarters of the world became obscured for them, and they fell into the Nairañjanā River where there was no ford. Some fell on their left side, others on their right side, others face upwards, others on their feet, others on their knees, others head-first, and others belly-downwards—frightened, terrified, and crying out to one another.
Then that Lord of Men struck the earth with his trunk, which was like soft cotton;
the earth, together with its oceans and mountains, trembled.
By him, the army of Namuci was broken.
And then, moving about by the splendor of the Bodhisattva, he abandoned that vicinity of the Bodhi tree along with many horses, elephants, and warriors.
They plunged into the sacred ford named Nairañjanā.
With their horses, chariots, and weapons fallen and crushed,
Māra and his hosts of rākṣasas fled in all directions,
not even knowing the name of the Nairañjanā.
He has crossed over; he is free from the scriptures; he is the ford.
The army of Rākṣasas, terrified by the power of his supernatural faculties, fled for a distance of a thousand yojanas;
yet even so, they did not tremble out of fearlessness.
"By good fortune you live; we have been released from danger."
Other hosts of yakṣas, embracing his neck,
wept aloud; and the gods rained down mandārava and karkārava flowers.
With joyful minds, they uttered these words.
Upon the victory of the King, there was the sound of drums in the sky and a roar of joyful cries;
the Teacher’s victory made the heavens stainless.
The son of a god, having gone to the world of the gods, said:
That state of the Supreme Being,
who has arrived at the bank of the Nairañjanā,
cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
I shall proclaim a mere portion [of it].
I saw him, shining like Jāmbūnada gold, with the radiance of the sky and limbs adorned with the marks;
he set out, traveling alone.
From the Nairañjanā River as far as the seat of enlightenment.
As he placed his steps, which shone like lotus petals,
upon this earth,
so did that delightful land tremble.
The earth delights in manifold sounds.
I have seen Māra’s assembled army,
thousands of koṭis of yakṣas gathered on all sides;
they cause terror and my heart trembles.
They do not cause the Essence of Beings to waver.
And his existence was not perceived on earth by the thousands of millions of gods all around;
they raised their voices, crying out: "A Jina shall arise!"
Greatly rejoicing, they waved their garments.
Five hundred jīvajīvaka birds, peacocks, swans, kalaviṅkas, and cuckoos were seen by me;
as I set out, they became a single sound.
From the Nairañjanā River as far as the seat of enlightenment.
I have seen the path fashioned by the immortals,
from the Nairañjanā river as far as the seat of awakening,
[provided] with incense, flowers, and garlands.
Abounding in various flowers and possessing most delightful fragrance.
When Māra was utterly broken and his splendor destroyed,
he purified his vision during the first watch; and in the middle watch, he was the destroyer of Māra.
You remember your past lives and former deeds.
And when the dawn had risen, you attained the supreme awakening—
whatever has been awakened by previous Buddhas—
and you achieved mastery over the qualities of a Buddha.
The Lord of the World, who has destroyed the passion for existence.

In the last watch of the night, at the time when the dawn is breaking, during the Nandīmukhā portion of the night, whatever [is to be accomplished] by a man who is a true man, a great man, a bull among men, a substance among men, a hero among men, an elephant among men, a lion among men, a king among men, a lotus among men, a kumuda-lily among men, a white lotus among men, a bull among men, a thoroughbred among men, a leader among men, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, one who is valiant and courageous, alone and peerless—

Dwelling intoxicated with ardor, withdrawn, with a resolute self, possessed of movement, mindfulness, steadfastness, intelligence, and wisdom, being purposeful and desirous, he—by means of a wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind regarding everything that is to be known, understood, and fully awakened to in every way and everywhere—fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The sons of the gods stood holding perfumes and garlands, wondering: "Is the Blessed One’s mind truly liberated? The Blessed One, knowing the minds of those deities with his own mind, at that time spoke this inspired utterance (*udāna*) to cut through their doubt: "Having severed craving, I have abandoned passion; the dried-up outflows do not flow. The path is cut off and does not proceed. This indeed is the end of suffering."
Then, multicolored masses of flowers,
most wonderful and fragrant, fell,
released from the palms of the hands of the sons of gods.
They circumambulated the king of the gods.
He whose vigor is incomparable, like the essence of a mountain,
and who is always like a crest of fire to his noble lineage—
pay homage with palms joined to that peerless one!
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When one understands phenomena together with their causes.
This is dependent origination in its forward order.
When these qualities appear for a brahmin who is ardent and meditative,
then all his doubts vanish away.
He understands the exhaustion of conditions.
This is dependent origination in reverse order.
Māra the Evil One created insects that were tearing at the Blessed One’s cross-legged posture; as the sun was rising, they all melted away.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
When these phenomena appear to the Brahmin who meditates with ardent exertion,
the army of Māra stands defeated.
The atmosphere was illuminated by the sun itself.
Then, indeed, at that time when he had first attained awakening, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
The ripening of meritorious deeds is pleasant, one's intentions are fulfilled,
and one swiftly attains supreme peace and liberation.
Whatever obstacles there may be before them, even deities belonging to the host of Māra,
they truly cannot create any hindrance for one who has performed meritorious deeds.
The conflicts that arise for one of little merit do not become powerful;
for those who possess the equipment and are endowed with merit, their meditative concentration becomes powerful.
Whether one is in the world of the gods or among the Vasavartin [devas], or even as a human—
if one seeks after anything that ought not to be done, it will not succeed for them in any way whatsoever.
Or again, if one aspires for the deathless state of Nirvana, which is free from sorrow,
one will attain the path that pacifies suffering with little difficulty.

Then the Blessed One said: "He enters the concentration called 'Victory over the World. This world is born of anguish; it experiences passion for itself, ceasing from contact. For by whatever means people become intoxicated, they do not see things otherwise. This world is attached to existence (*bhava*), stained by existence, and delights in existence. Where there is existence, there is suffering. Indeed, monks, the holy life is lived by the Tathāgata for the sake of abandoning [existence]. Whosoever say that there is an escape from existence through existence, I declare them all to be those for whom existence is not an escape. And whosoever, monks, say that there is liberation from existence through existence, I declare them all to be those who are not liberated from existence. Dependent upon acquisitions (*upadhi*), there is the arising of suffering; through the destruction of all acquisitions, monks, there is no arising of suffering. Behold this wide world, enveloped in ignorance, beings arisen from beings, not yet liberated. Whatever existences there may be, they all lead to every state of becoming. All those existences are impermanent, subject to suffering, and subject to change. Thus one sees this as it truly is with right wisdom. The thirst for existence is exhausted; one does not delight in existence at all. The total exhaustion of thirst is Nirvana. For him who has attained Nirvana, monks, there is no further becoming. Māra is overcome, the battle is won, the enemies are conquered, and all existence is abandoned."

The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having realized the purpose for which he had come, shattered Māra the Evil One—along with his army and his mounts—at the foot of the Bodhi tree by the sound of his coughing. He [attained] unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Having attained full awakening, he set in motion the sublime wheel of Dharma and, having gathered a great assembly, the Teacher dwelt at Rājagṛha—honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by gods and humans; one who had attained the preeminence of gain and fame, and was a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick. There, unsullied like a lotus by water, establishing beings destined for merit in meritorious deeds, establishing beings destined for the fruits [of the path] in those fruits, and establishing beings destined for latent impressions in those impressions, he distributed the nectar of immortality to gods and humans in no small measure. Leading hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings to the attainment of the deathless, he rescued them from the vast wilderness of the beginningless cycle of birth, old age, and death, and from the great precipices of the miserable states such as hell, and established them in the patient, auspicious, level ground of fearlessness: Nirvāṇa—having thus won them over.
