In Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Ceti, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Aśvaka, Avantī, and Daśārṇa—having personally realized his prowess through knowledge, the Self-Existent One dwells in divine abidings, dwells in brahminic abidings, dwells in imperturbable abidings, dwells in noble abidings, dwells in continuous abidings; as a Buddha, he dwells in the abidings of a Buddha; as a Conqueror, he dwells in the abidings of a Conqueror; as a Knower, he dwells in the abidings of a Knower; as the All-Knowing One, he dwells in the abidings of the All-Knowing One. Having attained mastery over the mind, the Buddha, the Blessed One, dwells in whichever abidings he desires.

The monks heard this account that at the foot of the Bodhi tree, by the sound of the Blessed One’s coughing, Māra the Evil One, together with his army and his mounts, was defeated. Those monks said to the Blessed One: "Behold, Blessed One, the marvel of the Lion among Men, the subduer of pride and anger! How is it that by the Blessed One’s mere coughing, Māra, along with the foremost of his forces, was utterly conquered? By that single, peerless, wise one, through a mind of loving-kindness, many millions of yakṣas and the vanguard of his army were defeated by a mere cough; even lions, tigers, hyenas, leopards, wild boars, and elephants were [subdued] by that single moon-faced one."

"The Evil One, along with his wicked methods and his exertion in evil conduct, was conquered at the very moment of a sneeze. How was the Blessed One, together with the vanguard of his army, defeated? The Blessed One said: "O monks, what is the wonder here? When the Tathāgata had attained supreme enlightenment, Māra the Evil One, together with his army and mounts, was shattered by the sound of a sneeze at the foot of the Bodhi tree. On another occasion as well, when I was still a youth, this Evil One, along with the vanguard of his army, was conquered by the sound of a sneeze. The monks said: "Was there yet another time, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: "There was another time, monks."

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king named Subandhu. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, was of great renown, possessed great power, and had a vast treasury. He ruled over a kingdom of sixty thousand cities that was prosperous, flourishing, with subdued punishment, legal proceedings, and thieves; it was secure, well-supplied with food, free from plagues and calamities, and teeming with people. Now, King Subandhu possessed sixty thousand elephants equipped with ivory tusks, covered with golden nets, adorned with gold ornaments, with beautiful hooves and coral-like trappings, and accompanied by their riders, who held arrows and spears in their hands. He had sixty thousand horses from Sindh, swift runners, adorned with every ornament. He had sixty thousand chariots covered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins, resounding with joyful shouts, bearing victory banners, with beautiful hooves and coral-like trappings, and with flags and pennants raised high. He had sixty thousand milch cows, all of which yielded milk according to one's desire. He had sixty thousand women wearing jeweled earrings and adorned with every ornament. He had sixty thousand couches made of gold, silver, and ivory. He had sixty thousand golden vessels, sixty thousand vessels made of precious gems, and sixty thousand treasuries. There were twenty thousand brahmans who received daily meals. His storehouses of wealth and grain were abundant, as were his female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; his ministers, officials, and military forces were numerous, as were his war machines.

[The Story of the Sugarcane] In the bedchamber of King Subandhu, a great clump of sugarcane suddenly appeared. In the midst of that sugarcane clump, one stalk of sugarcane emerged that was most beautiful of all; it surpassed all the other stalks of sugarcane in strength, color, luster, and foliage. When King Subandhu saw the sugarcane clump, he was struck with wonder and entered into an ocean of anxiety: "Whose omen is this? Is it auspicious or evil? Then King Subandhu summoned the brahmins, the royal chaplains, and the royal preceptors, and addressed them: "Sirs, a great clump of sugarcane has appeared in my bedchamber. In the middle of that sugarcane clump, one stalk has emerged that is most beautiful of all, surpassing all the others in color, luster, and foliage. Examine it, sirs, and find out whose omen this is—whether it is a blessing or an evil portent. Whatever must be done, do it. Then those brahmins, royal chaplains, and royal preceptors examined the sugarcane clump. They saw it as a marvel, pleasing, beautiful to behold, and delightful to the eye. Having seen it, they offered congratulations for victory to King Subandhu and said this: "By good fortune, O Great King, there is prosperity! An auspicious omen has appeared in the inner apartments. From this sugarcane clump of yours, O Great King, a prince will be born—one who has performed meritorious deeds, of great renown, of great majesty, difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, difficult to withstand, pleasing, and beautiful to both gods and men. May he be dear to Your Majesty! Then those brahmins, having been satisfied and regaled by King Subandhu with excellent solid and soft foods, were presented with laps full of silver and gold and then dismissed.

Then that stalk of sugarcane, having grown over days and nights, in the course of time became a great stalk of sugarcane; even that middle stalk of sugarcane grew into a large sugarcane the size of a bamboo pole—tender, beautiful, and thick—which surpassed all other stalks of sugarcane. Now, for that King Subandhu...

The chief queen was named Surucirā; she was gracious, beautiful to behold, noble in appearance, and endowed with the highest excellence of radiant complexion. Then King Subandhu lay upon a royal bed together with the chief queen Surucirā—a bed draped with bundles of silk ribbons and cords, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and surrounded by golden and silver lamp-stands, while hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, eunuchs, and chamberlains remained awake.

Then, indeed, during the last watch of the night at the time of dawn, a prince emerged from the base of that sugar-cane stalk—gracious, beautiful to behold, with a noble presence, and endowed with the highest excellence of golden hue. Thereupon, that prince was received by Queen Surucirā. Now King Subandhu, seeing the prince born from the sugar-cane stalk, was struck with wonder: "How marvelous! What kind of being will this one be who has emerged from a sugar-cane? Then King Subandhu performed delightful birth-rites for the prince for seven nights. For seven days he distributed food, drink, hard and soft delicacies, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and garments among ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, and the great multitude of people. Streams of oil flowed, streams of ghee flowed, and various kinds of beverage-streams were poured out. A vast circle of kinsmen assembled; many hundreds of kings gathered, and many thousands of brahmins assembled. Great rejoicing took place in the house of Subandhu; hundreds of musical instruments resounded and hundreds of songs were sung. For seven days the entire city was honored. After performing the birth-rites for seven days, when that period had passed, King Subandhu addressed the brahmin household priests and royal preceptors: "Sirs, give the prince a name worthy of him. Then they thought: "This prince was born from a sugar-cane; let his name be Ikṣvāku. Those brahmins then informed the king accordingly.

"Great King, this prince was born from a sugar-cane; let the name of this prince be Ikṣvāku. Then King Subandhu, having heard the name of the prince from the presence of the brahmins, became joyful; a fitting name had been established for the prince. Others too, having heard the name of the prince, became joyful. Then King Subandhu, having given those brahmins abundant hard food and soft food, dismissed them after giving them much gold and bullion.

Then King Subandhu appointed four suitable nurses with their attendants for the prince: one to rub him down and put him to sleep, another to suckle him, another to remove his excrement and urine, and another to hold him in her lap. Thus, being properly attended to and cared for by the four nurses, that prince of the Ikṣvākus grew like a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white water lily, or a great white lotus on the banks. As it was said by the Blessed One:
For one who has performed merit thrives like a banyan tree in fertile soil;
but one with little merit, though born like a tree by the roadside, withers away.

Thus, as the prince was being raised, when he reached the age of seven or eight years, he then trained in writing, scripts, arithmetic, calculation, sealing, and memorization; in elephant-riding, horsemanship, archery, and the use of the bamboo staff; in running, jumping, sprinting, and leaping; in the science of weaponry, combat, cutting, piercing, and the front of battle; and in all royal arts. He became one whose qualities were firmly established in every respect: respectful toward his mother, devoted to ascetics and brahmins, habituated to saluting, greeting, and rising for others, endowed with winning charm, endowed with gentleness, not harsh, not abrasive, calm, pleasant to live with, the first to speak, speaking kindly, and beloved by the king.

He was beloved by the queen, the harem, the ministers, the entire army, the domestic chaplain, the guild-leaders, the merchants, and the people of the countryside; he was beloved, dear, and pleasing to rival kings. He was free from illness and possessed a digestive system that was well-balanced, capable of proper digestion, and able to assimilate food—neither too cold nor too hot—even amidst changes in the seasons. He was long-lived, his lifespan measuring eighty-four thousand years, as stated by the Blessed One.
All sentient beings will die, for life ends in death;
they shall go according to their karma, reaping the fruits of merit and evil.
Those of evil deeds go to hell, those who have performed merit go to a good rebirth, and others, having cultivated the path, attain final Nirvana, free from outflows.

Now, King Subandhu, having ruled his kingdom righteously for a long time and a great duration, passed away according to the law of time after eighty-four years had elapsed. Prince Ikṣvāku obtained the kingdom. Then the king ruled from Vārāṇasī over his father’s sixty thousand cities; he had laid aside the rod of punishment, subdued his adversaries and enemies, and was free from thorns. His people were devoted to him, and he possessed great power, a vast treasury, and many vehicles. His harem was extensive, consisting of many thousands of women, all of whom were without offspring; not one of them had a son or a daughter. In the course of time, King Ikṣvāku, while ruling the kingdom, entered into an ocean of anxiety: "My kingdom is vast and my harem is vast, yet I have no son. Lest I should pass away childless, and then this realm of mine be seized by adversaries. Then King Ikṣvāku consulted with his domestic priest: "How might I have a son? The priest said to him: "Great King, this female apartment must be cleared three times a fortnight—on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth day. Then [your desire] will be fulfilled for you..."

"A prince shall be born, and the Ikṣvāku lineage shall become extensive. Now, King Ikṣvāku, having heard these words from the presence of his domestic priest, established Queen Alindā as the chief consort in the royal palace and dismissed those other many thousands of women three times during the fortnight, saying: "Go! Let each woman go with whomsoever she desires and enjoy herself with him. Thus, many thousands [of women] rushed out from the royal palace with joyful minds, adorned with all their ornaments. Like terrified does, they approached door after door—some speaking seductively, others laughing, others running and chasing after one another. All stumbled; all fainted. In the city of King Ikṣvāku, the people were overwhelmed and fell into a swoon along with those royal wives.

Now there was another man, born into the family of Subandhu and connected by kinship, who, being a human being, was endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind. Having lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, he passed away from among humans and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa host of gods as the divine king named Śakra. He then reflected: "Where is King Subandhu now? Is he still existing in this body, or is he dead? He then saw that King Subandhu had passed away, and his son named Ikṣvāku had obtained the kingdom. An improper, unfit, and unsuitable course of action had been given to King Ikṣvāku by his domestic priest: "For the sake of the progeny, the harem must be abandoned three times over for the faction of Subandhu's family. Then Śakra, lord of the gods, manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin—an old man, aged, advanced in years, one who had reached the end of his journey, his body covered in wrinkles, his head grey, and his limbs marked with spots. He went to the gate of King Ikṣvāku and said, "I wish to see Ikṣvāku. The doorkeeper entered the royal palace and informed King Ikṣvāku.

"A great king, a brahmin, stands at the gate wishing to see the king. King Ikṣvāku said, "Welcome to the brahmin; let him enter. Then, by that doorkeeper, the brahmin was ushered into the royal palace. Seeing the aged brahmin, the king rose from his seat and said, "Welcome to you, brahmin; please sit here on this seat. The brahmin then sat down after offering greetings of victory. The king asked him, "Brahmin, from which direction have you come? What do you seek? What is it that pleases you? What shall I give to you? The brahmin said, "Great King, I have come from a distant region having heard of your noble fame, renown, and verses of praise: 'Ikṣvāku thrice a fortnight releases his harem for the sake of the people. Therefore, O King, I have come from a far-off land seeking a woman; grant me a share of your women. Then the king, hearing the brahmin's words, became joyful and satisfied. He addressed his chamberlain: "Ho there, my good chamberlain! Quickly show this brahmin my harem. Whichever woman he likes, give her to him. The chamberlain then led the brahmin into the inner apartments in the midst of many thousands of women. [The chamberlain said: "Brahmin, this is the harem of King Ikṣvāku. Take whichever woman you desire and depart. Then the brahmin chose Queen Alindā, the chief consort of King Ikṣvāku, who never stepped out from the royal palace. "Let her be mine," he said. The queen then wept, thinking, "This brahmin is either my grandfather, my great-grandfather, or perhaps even my superior. May King Ikṣvāku, firm in his vows and commitments, not release me to serve and attend upon this brahmin!"
Now, at that time, a hunchbacked female garland-maker was weaving a garland for Alindā. Then that hunchback—

He spoke to that brahmin: "Brahmin, you are old, aged, and decrepit, yet you desire a young woman! Never shall a young woman touch you with her hand or her foot. Go away! What do you want with Queen Alindā, who has not been abandoned by King Ikṣvāku? Then that brahmin said to the hunchbacked woman: "Have little concern, hunchback; weave your garland. I am as dear to Queen Alindā as no one else is to you. Now, Queen Alindā had another maidservant who ground cosmetics. She spoke to that brahmin: "Brahmin, you are old, aged, and decrepit, smelling of bedding and clothes and reeking of foul odor. The queen would not even wish to look at you, much less speak to you. Go away! What do you want with Queen Alindā, who has not been abandoned by King Ikṣvāku? Then that brahmin said to the maidservant: "Have little concern, maidservant; grind the cosmetic. I am as dear to Queen Alindā as no one else is to you. Then Queen Alindā said: "By no means whatsoever will this brahmin be sent away. Then the queen wept aloud; as the queen was weeping, her retinue also began to weep. A great sound of lamentation arose there in the inner apartments. King Ikṣvāku, staying in his excellent upper palace, heard the loud and great noise from the inner apartments. The king then asked the eunuchs and chamberlains: "Ho, sirs, what is this sound of women’s lamentation that is being heard? The eunuchs and chamberlains replied: "Your Majesty, Queen Alindā has been seized by that brahmin. I was offered a choice by King Ikṣvāku: 'Whichever woman pleases you, take her. Therefore, let this one be mine. Then Queen Alindā wept, and as the queen was weeping, her retinue also raised a cry of lamentation. Having heard them, the king entered his own inner apartments and spoke to that brahmin: "Brahmin, you are old, aged, and decrepit. If you wish to eat daily meals in the royal household, I shall give that to you. What do you want with Queen Alindā? Take another! He then said: "Great King..."

“I am old, aged, and afflicted with a cough; from moment to moment I faint. I am unable to rise by myself; I wet my own bed. Therefore, give her to me; she will help me up and she will attend to me. Do not, O Ikṣvāku, offer your wife to me and later regret it. Now, I say this because you, O Ikṣvāku, are making a false request; I shall depart. The King said: “I do not, O Brahmin, make a false request, nor do I regret having given. However, you are old, aged, and infirm, while this queen is young and delicate; she does not desire you. Furthermore, your harem is vast, consisting of many thousands of women. Take whichever woman pleases you and enjoy yourself with her; she will wait upon you. The Brahmin said: “Enough, Great King! Let her alone be mine—she who stands there proud, faultless-limbed, looking down modestly. Let her alone be mine—she who stands there proud, faultless-limbed, looking with the gaze of a doe. Let her be mine—she who stands there proud, faultless-limbed, bathing her face in tears. Enough for me, Great King, of the women of the harem! Let this queen alone be mine; she will help me up, she will wait upon me, and she will serve me. Do not, O Ikṣvāku, offer your wife to me and later regret it. Now, I shall depart. King Ikṣvāku said: “...However, you are old, aged, and infirm, and this queen is young and delicate; she does not desire you. Here is a low-caste hunchback, a slave-girl seeking sexual pleasure. Let her be yours; take her wherever you wish. She will wait upon you. The hunchback said: “Great King, this Brahmin is foul-smelling, wrinkled, with a grey-haired face, as ill-odored as a jujube flower, like a goat that has smelled its own excrement. O Lord, if you give him to me, I shall die after consuming poison. Or, when we are in private, I shall kill this decrepit old man with broken limbs. Then the Brahmin said:
I have enmity toward all the hunchbacks who dwell upon this earth,
wherever these low-caste women wish to suckle my child.

"Enough, Great King! Let this hunchbacked woman suffice for me; let this queen alone be mine. She shall attend to me and she shall serve me. Do not, after having offered me your wife, feel regret. I bid you farewell and depart, lest you make a false request. The king said: "O Brahmin, I do not make a false request, nor do I regret having given. However, you are old, aged, and decrepit, while this queen is young and delicate; therefore, she does not desire you. Had you been young, this queen might have yearned for you. But I do not make a false request. Go, take Queen Alindā and lead her wherever you wish. Then that Brahmin, having received the word from King Ikṣvāku, became thrilled, satisfied, and joyful. Embracing Queen Alindā, as he was entering the palace gate, he fell right upon her. A loud burst of laughter was let out by the thousands of women: "A noble and worthy man has been found for the queen! Queen Alindā, however, with a throat choked with tears and a weeping face, cried out in distress. Seized by the hand by the Brahmin, she was dragged and pulled; she clung here and there. Sighing and gasping, with tears streaming down, her voice failing, and urinating in every place as she was being firmly gripped, she was dragged out from Rājagṛha without support, utterly broken and distraught.

That brahmin, having constructed a crooked and dilapidated hut in a poor village along the city wall, spread out grass and leaves upon a broken-down couch and set down a cracked water-pot. There, Queen Aliṃdā was ushered in, her garments completely worn out and her ornaments shattered and ruined, with nothing remaining but the barest fragments. Never—

Having touched the ground with his feet, his sandals having fallen off, with his bare feet wounded and bruised, that brahmin sat down there in the middle of the dilapidated shed and said: "O blessed lady, having dressed yourself well, wash my feet and wash your own feet; then delight me, O excellent one! I am delighted; delight me thoroughly, O blessed lady! Delight me properly, O blessed lady! By my word, O blessed lady, delight me! With charm, O blessed lady, delight me! Thus, throughout the entire night, she said to the goddess: "Delight me thus, delight me thus! Make me rise up, make me lie down; let me lie down. When the night had passed and at the time of the rising of the dawn, Śakra stood there in his own form, wearing armlets and earrings, possessing a divine body, illuminating everything with his noble complexion, and bearing excellent, stainless earrings. Having become the King of the Gods, he emitted his own radiance, and by his splendor, the entire shed was illuminated on all sides. Then Queen Alindā, seeing Śakra, the Lord of the Gods, in his true form, was overwhelmed with passion, thinking: "What have I done, that I have not taken delight with him? Śakra, the Lord of the Gods, invited Queen Alindā to choose a boon.
I am Śakra, the Indra of the gods, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa;
choose a boon from me, O blessed lady, whatever you desire in your heart.

Then Queen Alindā, having joined her palms in reverence toward Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this: "Śakra is withholding a boon from me; I say this because my boon is for a son. Then Indra gave her a medicinal pill, saying: "Dissolve this pill in water and drink it; from that, you will have a son who is like a lion, powerful, and a crusher of enemy armies. In energy, there will be no one equal to him in the world. However, he will be ugly in complexion and form, because I did not attend upon you when you were joyful. Thus spoke Indra.
Having now granted a boon to Queen Alindā, and having caused the dilapidated hall to disappear, he reappeared in the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Then Queen Alindā, having tied that medicinal pill to the corner of her silken garment, entered the royal palace with a face the color of a lotus and with perfectly pure faculties, thinking: "In such a vast inner apartment, a son shall be born to me. Now Queen Alindā was seen by King Ikṣvāku from afar as she was entering the gate-hall, with a face the color of a lotus and with perfectly pure faculties. The king then asked the queen: "Your face is the color of a lotus and your faculties are perfectly pure; did you sleep comfortably? Did you experience pleasure and delight? Have you obtained anything noble and auspicious? The queen then said: "Great King, how could there be comfort for me in sleep, or have I experienced pleasure and delight? Śakra, the lord of the gods, having assumed the guise of a brahmin, came here. He kept me awake the whole night, making me rise and lie down. When the night had passed and at the time of dawn, he made that brahmin’s guise disappear and stood in his own form, illuminating all directions with his radiance. He offered me a boon, saying: 'Choose a boon, O blessed lady.'"
I am Śakra, the Indra of the gods, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa;
choose a boon from me, O blessed lady, whatever you desire in your heart.

In that regard, O Great King, I requested the Bestower of Sons, saying, "Grant me the boon of a son. Śakra gave me this medicinal pill and said, "Mix this pill with water and drink it; from that a son will be born who shall sit upon the lion-throne, be powerful, and crush the armies of his enemies. In terms of energy, he will have no equal in the world; however, as for his complexion and form, he will be ugly, which is why I did not attend upon you with joy and satisfaction. Then that king—

Having heard this, the king became angry with the queen: "Since you were authorized by me, why did you not attend upon him with joy and satisfaction? Then, out of anger, the king snatched away the medicinal pill from the queen. The king then ground the medicinal pill on a stone, mixed it with water, and gave it to five hundred noble ladies, each of whom was like a young girl, for them to drink from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. Queen Aliṃdā, however, did not receive any of that medicinal pill to drink, thinking, "Lest the queen give birth to an evil son. Then Queen Aliṃdā asked her maidservants, "Where has that medicinal pill been taken? The maidservants said, "Your Majesty, the king took that medicinal pill of yours, ground it on a stone slab, and gave it to five hundred noble ladies, each like a young girl, for them to drink. The queen asked, "On which stone slab was that medicinal pill ground? The maidservant replied, "Your Majesty, that medicinal pill was ground on this very stone slab. Then Queen Aliṃdā made a drop of water on the stone slab, touched the tip of her tongue with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, and swallowed it. That queen also conceived in her womb. In this way, all five hundred queens became pregnant.

Then those five hundred queens gave birth after the lapse of nine or ten months. Four hundred and ninety-nine princes were born, handsome, beautiful to behold, of noble presence, endowed with supreme excellence of complexion. But to Queen Aliṃdā also a son was born who was ill-favored and unsightly, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, a large belly, and black as a heap of soot. Then the eunuchs and chamberlains informed the king: "Your Majesty, four hundred and ninety-nine queens have given birth; four hundred and ninety-nine princes have been born, handsome and beautiful to behold. To Queen Aliṃdā a son has been born who is ill-favored and unsightly, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, a large belly, and black as a heap of soot."

Upon hearing this, King Ikṣvāku became angry and fell into a state of dejection, thinking: "Since I did not give the medicinal pill to the queen to drink—thinking that she would not give birth to a son—how is it that such a son has been born to her? The eunuchs and chamberlains said: "Great King, at the very spot where the Lord ground that medicinal pill for Niṣadha, the queen took a drop of water from that grinding stone with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass and placed it on the tip of her tongue; thus was a son born to the queen. The king said: "May a son of mine never stand before the queen! I do not wish to see such a thing. Then King Ikṣvāku, having heard the description of the beauty and form of those four hundred and ninety-nine princes, was filled with joy and satisfaction. Setting aside the son of Queen Alindā among those handsome princes, for seven days delightful birth-rites were performed. Food, drink, hard food, soft food, clothing, perfumes, garlands, and ointments were distributed to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, and other people. Channels of oil and channels of ghee were set flowing, as were various kinds of beverage-channels. For each individual prince, four nurses were appointed. One nursed him, another bathed him, another removed his excrement and urine, another gave him the breast, and another held him in her lap. Nurses were assigned to the son of Queen Alindā, and then personal attendants were assigned to Queen Alindā herself. In this way, the princes were raised and brought up. Then King Ikṣvāku gave names mixed with the word *kuśa* to all those five hundred princes. Some were named Indrakuśa, some Brahmakuśa, some Devakuśa, some Ṛṣikuśa, some Kusumakuśa, some Drumakuśa, some Ratnakuśa, some Mahākuśa, some Haṃsakuśa, some Kroñcakuśa, some Mayūrakuśa, and so forth; names mixed with *kuśa* were given to them all. To Queen Alindā’s son, the pure name Kuśa was given.

Now King Ikṣvāku gave various kinds of children’s toys to all four hundred and ninety-nine princes, but he did not give a toy to Prince Kuśa, the son of the queen. Then Prince Kuśa would take whichever toy his brothers desired, and after playing with it and enjoying himself, he would give it back to them. In this way, King Ikṣvāku gave those princes various kinds of vehicles for play—elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and chariot-vehicles, various noble and royal-worthy conveyances—but he did not give a vehicle to Prince Kuśa. Prince Kuśa, however, would take whichever vehicle he desired—an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, a chariot, a palanquin, a litter, a gallī, an ardhagallī, a leaf-carriage, or a sky-chariot—from his brothers, and after driving it, he would give it back, saying, "What is the use of keeping these? In this manner, as those princes grew up and reached the age of discretion, at seven or eight years old, they were then instructed in writing, scripts, arithmetic, calculation, sealing, memorization, and in the management of elephants, horses, chariots, bows, and bamboo-poles; in running, racing, jumping, and in the science of archery, in combat, wrestling, cutting, piercing, striking, and at the head of battle, and in the conduct of royal policy—they became certain and proficient in everything. No one taught Prince Kuśa any craft; yet by his own intelligence, his own wisdom, and his own vigor, he was better trained than all his brothers and the rest of the great multitude of people. He was highly skilled in the science of archery and excelled all others among the princes in all the various fields of craft and art.
Then it occurred to King Ikṣvāku: "What if I were now to test these five hundred princes to see which among them shall become king after my passing? Thereupon, by that King Ikṣvāku—

Five hundred sweetmeats were prepared, and one large sweetmeat was placed in their midst and covered with the other sweetmeats. [The king thought: "Whoever shall take this large sweetmeat, I shall know that he will become king after my passing. Then King Ikṣvāku, having made that heap of sweetmeats ready, summoned the five hundred princes and addressed them: "Quickly, with three claps of the hand, each of you take one sweetmeat from the heap! Now all those princes ran out first, and then the prince [Kuśa] ran out. That prince, having reached out with his left and right hands past all his brothers, took hold of that large sweetmeat. It occurred to King Ikṣvāku: "This Prince Kuśa will become king after my passing. However, he is ill-favored, unsightly, thick-lipped, thick-headed, thick-footed, pot-bellied, black as a heap of soot, unpleasant and repulsive to behold. Who will accept him as king? What if I were to test these princes a second time? At the time and place for food, I shall have the princes served face-to-face. Whosoever among them receives the food first, I shall know that he will become king after my passing. Then King Ikṣvāku, at the time and place for food, summoned those five hundred princes and had them sit down before him; he then presented the meal. Those princes waited for the food. Prince Kuśa received that food on the ground; with as much food as he desired, he made a heap of boiled rice on the ground. Right there, he received the side dishes and ate while resting upon the earth. It occurred to King Ikṣvāku: "This Prince Kuśa will become king after my passing; he is a lord of the earth who eats while resting upon the earth. Then, at another time, King Ikṣvāku asked his domestic priest: "Preceptor, which of these princes will become king after my passing? The priest said: "Great King, it is indeed this Prince Kuśa who will become king after Your Majesty's passing. He possesses the marks of a king. Then King Ikṣvāku... [text continues].

Having heard the words of the domestic priest, the king became sorrowful and thought: "What means might there be so that this Prince Kuśa shall not become king after my passing? What if I were now to bury great treasures in secret places throughout various regions of the royal palace, unseen by anyone? Whoever, after my passing, should know of these treasures, discover them, and dig them up, let him become king; perhaps in this way another prince might indeed become king. Thereupon, King Ikṣvāku buried great treasures in secret places throughout various regions of the royal palace, unseen by anyone. After the lapse of a long time, when the end of his life had come, King Ikṣvāku instructed his ministers at the time of his death: "O ministers, listen! Whoever among these five hundred princes, after my passing, should know of these treasures, discover them, and dig them up—him you must consecrate with the kingdom. There is a treasure at the edge, a treasure outside, and a treasure neither at the edge nor outside. There are four treasures beneath the four royal *śāla* trees; a treasure in the ocean, a treasure in the sea, a treasure at the *yojana* [mile], a treasure at the release, a treasure at the tip of a tree, and a treasure on the mountain. There is a treasure where Vairocana rises, and a treasure where the light-making sun sets. There is also a treasure deposited where the gods are honored. O ministers, whichever prince knows of these treasures and has them dug up without being told—him you must consecrate with the kingdom; he alone shall be the king. Then King Ikṣvāku, having thus instructed his ministers, was joined with the law of time and passed away.

Now, when their father had passed away, those five hundred princes, for the sake of the kingdom, quarreled with one another, saying, "I am king! I am king! Yet, because they were righteous, they did not harm one another. Then the ministers said to the princes: "O princes, do not quarrel; this is the command of your King Ikṣvāku."

"What is it? [They asked. "At the time of my father’s death, a message was given: 'He who shall know the message left by my father shall become king. The princes said, 'O ministers, tell us exactly what this message given by our father was. Then those ministers proclaimed that message of King Ikṣvāku before the five hundred princes: 'There is a treasure at the end; a treasure outside; a treasure neither at the end nor outside. Beneath the four royal *śāla* trees are four treasures. There is a treasure in the ocean; a treasure in the sea; a treasure at the *yojana*; a treasure at the release. There is a treasure at the tip of a tree; a treasure at the peak of a mountain; and there is a treasure where Vairocana rises. Where the light-making sun sets, there is a treasure. Where the gods are honored, there too a treasure is placed. 'O princes, this is the message given to you by your father Ikṣvāku: 'Whosoever among you shall know these deposited treasures and shall dig them up, he shall be your king. The four hundred and ninety-nine princes did not know or understand the treasures as they were being proclaimed. But Kuśa, possessed of great intelligence and great discernment, grasped the entire meaning; he was pure and clear-sighted. He then said: 'I shall report this word of my father there, O sirs. All those treasures proclaimed by you, I shall have dug up. Regarding what my father said, 'A treasure at the end'—that treasure was placed inside, beneath the threshold at the gate of the royal palace. That place was caused to be dug up by the ministers, and a great treasure was found. Regarding what my father said, 'A treasure outside'—that treasure was placed outside that very same threshold. That great treasure also was caused to be dug up by the prince. Regarding what my father said, 'Neither at the end nor outside'—that treasure was placed beneath the threshold at the middle gate. That great treasure also [was found] by the prince."

"Underneath the four royal *śāla* trees," said my father, "there are four treasures where King Ikṣvāku’s couch—made of *śāla* wood and overlaid with golden feet—is laid out; beneath the legs of those couches, there are four treasures. Those great treasures were also caused to be excavated by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'In the ocean there is a treasure,' there was a pleasure-pool in the royal Aśoka grove; there too a treasure was deposited. That too was drawn out from the pleasure-pool by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'The treasure of the ocean,' there was a well in the King Ikṣvāku’s bathing hall; there too a treasure was deposited. That great treasure was caused to be excavated from the well by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'A treasure at the league-mark (*yojana*),' in whatever place the King Ikṣvāku’s vehicle was yoked—whether an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, or a carriage—that too, as a great treasure, was caused to be excavated by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'A treasure at the unyoking-place,' in whatever place the King Ikṣvāku’s vehicle was unyoked—whether an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, or a carriage—a treasure was deposited there. That great treasure was caused to be excavated by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'A treasure at the top of a tree,' in the King Ikṣvāku’s viewing-hall there was a great tree; where its shadow fell first when the sun rose, and where the final shadow fell when the sun set, there too a treasure was deposited. Those two great treasures were also caused to be excavated by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'A treasure on the mountain,' on that stone slab where the King Ikṣvāku’s head-bath, ointments, and perfumes were ground, there a treasure was deposited beneath it. That great treasure was also caused to be excavated by the prince. "When it was said by my father, 'A treasure where Vairocana rises,' there too, where my father Ikṣvāku was born from a sugar-cane stalk, a treasure was deposited."

"Treasure! That great treasure too was caused to be excavated by the prince. As for what my father said—that where the sun Prabhāṅkara sets, there a treasure is hidden—and where King Ikṣvāku passed away, there too a treasure was hidden—that great treasure too was caused to be excavated by the prince. As for what my father said—that where the gods are honored, there too a treasure is hidden—and where King Ikṣvāku had five hundred princes served a meal, there too a treasure was hidden—that great treasure too was caused to be excavated by the prince. Thus, as those treasures were being excavated by Prince Kuśa, the ministers, the princes, the domestic priests, the brahmin royal preceptors, the army commanders, and the people of the towns and countryside—all were filled with wonder at those treasures being excavated by Prince Kuśa: 'Oh, how great is the intelligence and the great discernment of Prince Kuśa! For he has discovered every single great treasure that was hidden here and there in the royal palace of King Ikṣvāku, and he has excavated them all. He shall be the king.'"

Then it occurred to those ministers: "Lest Prince Kuśa should hear this from others, let us test him again and again under some other pretext. So the ministers spoke to the princes: "O princes, whoever among you shall first bow to all the gods and sit upon the lion-throne, he shall become king. Then those four hundred and ninety-nine princes mounted various kinds of vehicles and, hurrying with great speed, ran toward the temple to pay homage to the gods. Prince Kuśa also approached the all-golden consecration lion-throne; having extended his joined palms in reverence toward the gods in the four directions and having circumambulated that throne out of respect for former kings, he sat down. Indeed, [he was surrounded] by the princes, the ministers, and the army commanders.

And because he was regarded as wise by the merchants and the people of the countryside, he was consecrated in the kingdom; he was honored by all the sixty thousand cities, towns, and districts, as well as by the royal ministers and princes, [with the thought]: "This one is the king. Thus, Prince Kuśa now attained the kingship.

Now, King Kuśa, having obtained the kingdom, paid homage to his mother, Queen Alindā; he honored her, revered her, respected her, and worshipped her. Having thus ruled the kingdom righteously for a long time, at another time King Kuśa made this request to his mother, Queen Alindā: "Mother, bring me a wife, a chief queen, who is gracious and beautiful, such that no other woman would be her equal. Queen Alindā said: "Son, who will give a gracious and beautiful wife to you, whose form is so wretched? I shall bring you only a wretched wife in form, one who will not cause you delight. King Kuśa said: "Mother, if you bring me a wretched wife, I shall not touch that wretched wife with my foot or my hand. Bring me a wife who is gracious and beautiful. Mother, I have neither heard nor seen it said that a king is wretched, nor that a king delights in a wretched woman. Bring me a beautiful wife, Mother. Queen Alindā said: "Son, husbands and wives live happily when they possess similar characteristics and do not despise one another. A wife of beautiful form may despise a husband of wretched form; a husband of beautiful form may despise a wife of wretched form. Son, I shall bring you a wife of such a kind as is suitable for you—one who is wretched in form, yet one who will not despise you, son. King Kuśa said: "Mother, I have no need for a wretched wife. Bring me a wife who is dissimilar to me in form. Queen Alindā said: "Son, who will give a beautiful wife to you, whose form is so wretched? King Kuśa said: "Mother, even from afar, spend wealth, silver, and gold on the task of bringing me a beautiful wife."

Then Queen Aliṃdā, having summoned her ministers and domestic priests, addressed them: "Sirs, seek out a wife for King Kuśa as his chief queen—one who might be the foremost and eldest among the many thousands of women in the royal household. The ministers and domestic priests, having assented to the queen, dispatched Brahmins and messengers throughout the cities and provinces of the realm, saying: "Go, sirs, and seek out such a maiden as would be suitable for King Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku. Those Brahmins and messengers, searching through the sixteen provinces, arrived at a city named Kasmakubja in the Śūrasena country. There, a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka was ruling. He had a daughter named Sudarśanā, who was gracious and beautiful; in all of Jambudvīpa, there was no other maiden equal to her in beauty. Now, that princess, mounted upon a chariot drawn by four horses, accompanied by her friends and maidservants, and surrounded by great royal splendor, majesty, and a vast retinue, was driving out to the pleasure gardens. She was seen by those Brahmins and messengers, and they thought: "This princess is truly gracious and beautiful; she is fit to be the chief queen of King Kuśa. On the following day, those Brahmins and messengers, having dressed and clad themselves early in the morning, stood at the gate of the royal palace. When King Mahendraka was seated in the audience hall, the Brahmins and messengers saluted the king and stood before him. The Brahmin, having greeted King Mahendraka with cries of victory, said this: "Great King, in Vārāṇasī there is a king named Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku; he requests your daughter Sudarśanā as a wife for himself. That King Kuśa is distinguished, for he rules over the sovereignty of sixty thousand cities. King Mahendraka thought: "A connection with such a man is indeed fitting. Then King Mahendraka spoke to that Brahmin and the messengers.

"Friends, King Kuśa is my ally; I shall give him my daughter to be his wife. Then that brahmin, having bought sweetmeats and summoned the other brahmins, offered them to them, saying: "Gentlemen, this Mahendraka, king of the Madrakas, offers his daughter Sudarśanā to be the consort of King Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku. Therefore, gentlemen, offer the water of alliance! Then those brahmins and messengers, acting upon the word of the brahmin, took leave of King Mahendraka and set out. In due course, they arrived at Vārāṇasī.

Then those brahmins and messengers reported to the ministers and domestic priests: "A maiden such as this has been found, to whom no other maiden in all of Jambudvīpa is equal in beauty. In the province named Śūrasena there is a city called Kanyakubja; there resides a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka. His daughter is named Sudarśanā, who is gracious and beautiful. Having heard this, the ministers and domestic priests then informed Queen Alindā: "A maiden such as this has been found, to whom no other maiden in all of Jambudvīpa is equal in beauty. In the province named Śūrasena there is a city called Kanyakubja; there resides a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka. His daughter is named Sudarśanā, who is gracious and beautiful. Upon hearing this, Queen Alindā became joyful and delighted, thinking, "I have obtained a peerless wife for my son. Then Queen Alindā expressed her approval to her son Kuśa: "Son, a maiden such as this has been found, to whom no other maiden in all of Jambudvīpa is equal in beauty. In the province named Śūrasena there is a city called Kanyakubja; there resides a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka. His daughter is named Sudarśanā, who is gracious and beautiful. When King Kuśa heard his mother’s words, he became joyful and delighted. He addressed the ministers, courtiers, brahmin priests, and royal preceptors: "Sirs..."

"In the country named Śūrasena there is a city named Kanyakubja; there dwells a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka, and he has a daughter named Sudarśanā. Go and bring her here for my sake. Then those ministers, courtiers, brahmin priests, and royal preceptors, having assented to King Kuśa, equipped a fourfold army and set out with great prosperity and great splendor. Now, as they were departing, it occurred to Queen Aliṃdā: "What means might there be so that the princess Sudarśanā does not know what King Kuśa is like in appearance and form? Then it occurred to Queen Aliṃdā: "Suppose I have a private chamber built where King Kuśa may sport, enjoy himself, and take his pleasure with his wife, and yet she does not know what King Kuśa is like. Queen Aliṃdā then had such a private chamber constructed—plastered and well-smeared, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, and strewn with loose flowers—wherein King Kuśa would sport, enjoy himself, and take his pleasure.

Then those ministers, courtiers, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors, traveling by stages, arrived at the city named Kanyakubja in the Śūrasena country. They approached King Mahendraka of Madra, greeted the king with cries of victory, and standing before him, spoke as follows: "Great King, King Kuśa, your son-in-law, inquires after your welfare along with that of your retinue. He requests that you grant his daughter Sudarśanā, whom you promised, to him as a wife. Then King Mahendraka, having welcomed and exchanged greetings with those ministers, courtiers, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors, gave them garments, ornaments, and articles of enjoyment befitting kings. Having stayed there for some days, those ministers and courtiers addressed King Mahendraka: "Great King, we have been gone for a long time; let the marriage be performed, and we shall depart. Then King Mahendraka, with great royal splendor...

With great royal majesty, amidst the shouts of "Hakkāra" and "Hikkāra" from a vast multitude of people, and to the sounding of kettledrums, clay drums, war-drums, and conchs, the marriage ceremony was performed and the daughter Sudarśanā was given as a wife to King Kuśa. Then the ministers and priests, having completed the marriage rites and taken leave of King Mahendraka, set out. In due course, they arrived at a grove on the outskirts of Vārāṇasī. Thus, with great honor and a grand procession, the princess Sudarśanā was led into the city of Vārāṇasī. She was then ushered into the royal palace; approaching her mother-in-law, Queen Aliṃdā, she bowed her head at her mother-in-law’s feet and stood before her. Upon seeing her daughter-in-law, Queen Aliṃdā became overjoyed, filled with gladness and a sense of well-being.

Now King Kuśa was dwelling there in that inner chamber, which was without light, sporting, delighting, and enjoying himself with the princess Sudarśanā amidst costly articles of luxury and enjoyment. While the princess Sudarśanā was thus sporting, delighting, and enjoying herself with King Kuśa in that inner chamber without light, this thought occurred to her: "This royal lineage of King Kuśa, of the Ikṣvāku clan, is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and an inexhaustible mine of jewels; yet this bedchamber of ours is without light, and even the lamps do not burn. Indeed, we cannot see one another’s eyes; I do not know what King Kuśa is like in complexion and form, nor does King Kuśa know what I, Queen Sudarśanā, am like in complexion and form. I do not understand this matter: for what reason do the lamps not burn in our bedchamber neither by night nor by day? Then Queen Sudarśanā questioned King Kuśa when he was in private: "Great King, this royal family is prosperous, flourishing, and an inexhaustible mine of jewels; yet in this bedchamber of ours, the lamps do not burn either by night or by day. We live together as if in darkness; we cannot see one another’s eyes. I do not know what my husband is like, nor does the Great King know what I, Queen Sudarśanā, am like. I do not understand the cause of this."

"For what reason do lamps not burn in our bedchamber? King Kuśa said, "Queen, I too do not know for what reason lamps do not burn in our bedchamber. My mother will know; ask her. Then, when the night had turned to dawn and King Kuśa had departed, Queen Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, dressed herself in garments, put on her ornaments, and approached the chief queen, Aliṃdā, to pay homage at her feet. Having bowed at her mother-in-law's feet, Sudarśanā said, "Lady, this royal family is prosperous, flourishing, and a mine of endless jewels. Yet in our bedchamber, lamps do not burn by day or by night. We live together as if in darkness; we cannot see one another with our eyes. What is the cause that lamps do not burn in our house? The chief queen Aliṃdā said, "Daughter Sudarśanā, both you and your husband are of such noble form that I see no one else who is their equal in beauty. I feared that upon seeing each other’s noble forms, you might fall into madness. Furthermore, I have made this vow to the gods for a long time: 'When my daughter-in-law Sudarśanā bears a son or a daughter, then in the twelfth year you shall see one another. This is our family custom. Then the royal daughter Sudarśanā said, "Indeed, it is a misfortune that the gods have been entreated by my lady that for a long time we must not see one another. The chief queen Aliṃdā said, "Daughter, what can I do? I have made this vow to the gods, and I protect it so that you two, upon seeing each other’s noble complexion and form, might not fall into madness. Thus was the royal daughter Sudarśanā consoled by her mother-in-law, the chief queen Aliṃdā.
Then, after a long time, that princess Sudarśanā prostrated herself before her mother-in-law and made this request:

"Madam, I wish to see my husband. Queen Aliṃdā said, "Be patient, daughter; you shall see him in due time. Then Sudarśanā requested her mother-in-law again and again, "Madam, I wish to see him just once. Then it occurred to Queen Aliṃdā: "This Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, desires to see Kuśa. If I do not satisfy her curiosity, it will become a great source of distress for her. Queen Aliṃdā said, "Daughter Sudarśanā, tomorrow I will show King Kuśa to you in the audience hall, and he will be presented to the public. Then Queen Aliṃdā summoned King Kuśa and said, "Son, this Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, wishes to see you. Since you are ill-favored in appearance, let it be so that Sudarśanā does not have her heart set on you upon seeing such a form. Rather, let him who is the most handsome and most pleasing among all those five hundred princes sit upon the royal throne as the king, and then let him be shown to Sudarśanā, saying, 'This is King Kuśa. Then Sudarśanā will know that King Kuśa is like this, and her heart will not turn away from him. King Kuśa said, "Mother, let it be done accordingly. Now, among those princes, Prince Kuśadruma was handsome and pleasing to behold. So, having adorned Kuśadruma with garments and ornaments fit for a king, making him appear as if he were the king himself, he was seated upon the lion-throne in the audience hall as the sovereign. All those other princes were likewise adorned and well-ornamented, and they were seated upon their respective thrones. The ministers, priests, the army commanders, the guild-leaders, merchants, village heads, and country folk—all the assembly together with the king—shone like a divine assembly. Then King Kuśa, taking the parasol, held it over his brother Prince Kuśadruma, who was seated upon the royal throne, shading him from the left side. Then Queen Aliṃdā, accompanied by her daughter-in-law Sudarśanā and surrounded by many hundreds of other queens, emerged from the palace and stood within the lion-window. Then indeed, Queen Aliṃdā...

She presented Prince Kuśadruma, who was seated upon the royal throne, saying: "Daughter Sudarśanā, this is your husband; look at him! Then Sudarśanā, seeing Prince Kuśadruma seated on the royal throne, was delighted in heart and thought: "I have gained a great fortune, for my husband is so handsome, pleasing, and beautiful that he outshines the entire royal assembly with his form. Then Princess Sudarśanā surveyed the assembly until she saw the king’s umbrella-bearer among the thousand women. Upon seeing that royal umbrella-bearer, Sudarśanā’s mind was struck; she became filled with pain and dejection, and spoke to her mother-in-law, Queen Mahādevī Alindā: "Madam, King Kuśa is radiant, and the princes are meritorious and handsome. The entire royal assembly shines like an assembly of gods. Yet this umbrella-bearer is unsightly and unfit for a king such as he, who is like a son of the gods. This umbrella-bearer is deformed—stout-lipped, stout-headed, stout-footed, pot-bellied, black, and the color of a heap of soot. Because of this umbrella-bearer, the splendor of the entire royal assembly is marred. In such a vast kingdom, there is no other man who could hold the king’s umbrella. If my husband wishes to do what is pleasing to me, then let this umbrella-bearer not remain in the king’s presence; let another man be made to hold the umbrella. Queen Alindā said: "Daughter Sudarśanā, do not speak thus. It is not by outward appearance that one is fit for this task. Although this umbrella-bearer is poor in form, he is great-souled in his virtues: he is virtuous, truthful, righteous, meritorious, powerful, and a crusher of enemy kingdoms. By his power, no adversary has caused harm to our sixty thousand cities, including the towns and provinces. By his power, we all live in happiness. Thus did Sudarśanā speak to Queen Alindā.

She was thus consoled. Then Sudarśanā, having gone into private with King Kuśa, spoke: "Great King, in your vast kingdom there is no other man who could serve as your umbrella-bearer. This umbrella-bearer of yours is unsightly. If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, then release this umbrella-bearer and appoint another man as the umbrella-bearer. The king said: "Do not revile this umbrella-bearer. What is the use of physical beauty? What will beauty avail one who is endowed with virtue? This umbrella-bearer is a great soul, excellent in virtue and possessed of great strength; by his power, not a single adversary can cause harm to these sixty thousand cities. Thus was Queen Sudarśanā consoled by King Kuśa.

Now King Kuśa, desiring to see Queen Sudarśanā, made a request to his mother, Queen Aliṃdā: "Mother, it is my wish that I might see Queen Sudarśanā. Queen Aliṃdā said: "My son, you are ugly in appearance. If Sudarśanā were to know that King Kuśa is such as this in color and form, it is possible that she would take her own life by some means. King Kuśa said: "Mother, what can be done? A stratagem must be devised so that I may see Sudarśanā, yet she does not know who this person is. Queen Aliṃdā said: "My son, there is this stratagem: when Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, goes out to the park grounds with the other queens and all the women of the harem to see the blooming blue and red lotuses, then you should go to the park in your natural state, descend into the lotus pond up to your neck, and sit there covering your head with a lotus leaf. We shall act in such a way that Sudarśanā will descend into the lotus pond herself by the very same steps where you are standing in the pond for the sake of the lotuses. For Sudarśanā is exceedingly fond of flowers and leaves; therefore, you will see her according to your desire."

Now, at that time, various kinds of flowers—blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*paduma*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), and fragrant lilies (*saugandhika*)—as well as various types of garlands, were being brought into the royal palace by the florists. When Sudarśanā saw those blooming blue and red lotuses, she made a request to her mother-in-law, Queen Aliṃdā: "Madam, I wish to see the ponds filled with blooming blue, red, white, and fragrant lilies. Queen Aliṃdā said: "Daughter, look well; we shall all go out to see the ponds. Then Queen Aliṃdā informed King Kuśa: "My son, you should know that Princess Sudarśanā wishes to go out with the women of the inner court to see the ponds. If you desire to see her, then go to the park grounds beforehand and stay in such a place that Sudarśanā will not recognize you as King Kuśa."

Then King Kuśa, having promised his mother, went at daybreak in his ordinary attire to the park grounds as usual and sat waiting for the women of the harem. King Kuśa then descended by that staircase where there were many lotuses and white lotuses; he sat there, concealing himself with a lotus leaf. All the women of the harem rushed out. Just as the Nandana grove shines when filled with throngs of *apsarases*, so did that park shine with the king and his harem. Then Queen Sudarśanā, seeing the lovely blue, red, white, and white-lotus flowers in full bloom in those ponds, said to the other queens: "O queens, come! We shall gather lotuses from the ponds. Those queens said: "Very well, O Queen."

“We shall take the lotuses. Then Queen Sudarśanā, together with the other queens, went down by the same staircase where King Kuśa was standing; having placed Sudarśanā at their head, they descended. Now, for the sake of taking a lotus, Sudarśanā stretched out her hand, thinking, “I will take a lotus. Thereupon, King Kuśa suddenly embraced her. At that moment, it occurred to Queen Sudarśanā: “I have been seized by a water-demon (udakarākṣasa)! I am being devoured by a water-demon! I am being devoured by a water-demon! She cried out, “Help! Help! I am being devoured by a water-demon! Then all those women of the harem stood aside. King Kuśa was about to sport with the queen, and Sudarśanā was crying out, “Help! Help! I am being devoured by a water-demon! When the women of the harem realized that King Kuśa had acted according to his desire, they performed a propitiatory rite (balikarma) for Queen Sudarśanā’s retinue. They held up a flaming ladle and said, “May your evil be pacified and extinguished! By good fortune you have been released from the water-demon! Then Queen Sudarśanā, having spent that day playing, sporting, and enjoying herself in the lotus pond with the other queens, entered the royal palace late in the evening. Queen Sudarśanā entered King Kuśa’s bedchamber. The king said, “My queen, you went to see the lotus pond, yet you did not bring me any lotuses. Am I not dear to you, my beloved? The queen replied, “Great King, how could I have lotuses? I went down to the pond thinking, ‘I will take some lotuses,’ and there I was embraced by a water-demon. I thought I was being devoured by the water-demon, until I was rescued by the women of the harem. Great King, I think that water-demon in the lotus pond was just like your own umbrella-bearer; I believe they were born of the same mother. Then King Kuśa said:
"O Queen, do not go out again to look for the lotus pond; for I too was there at that pool, and I have indeed been devoured by a water-demon."

At that time, during the mango season, various kinds of mangoes were brought into the royal palace by the king’s mango-keepers. When Queen Sudarśanā saw those various kinds of mangoes, she requested her mother-in-law, the chief queen Mahādevī Āliṃdā: “Madam, I wish to see the mango groves. Mahādevī Āliṃdā said, “Daughter, look well; tomorrow I shall have the mango groves cleared out. Then Mahādevī Āliṃdā summoned the mango-keepers and gave them this command: “Tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out with the women of the inner court to see the mango groves. Therefore, sprinkle and sweep the mango grove. Wrap the mango trunks in variegated spring-colored cloths, hang clusters of silk ribbons and garlands, burn incense, and decorate the mango grove by scattering loose flowers. Then, at the mere word of Mahādevī Āliṃdā, those park-keepers decorated that garden, the mango grove. Queen Āliṃdā then informed King Kuśa: “Son, as you commanded, tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out with the women of the inner court to see the royal mango grove. If you wish to see the princess Sudarśanā, then go there in ordinary dress and stand in that place so that Sudarśanā does not know, ‘This is King Kuśa. Having assented to his mother’s words, he went to the mango grove in ordinary attire and stood beneath the most beautiful mango tree in the entire park. Then Queen Sudarśanā, surrounded by the women of the inner court and with great royal splendor and majesty, mounted various highly decorated royal chariots and set out for the mango grove. When Queen Sudarśanā alighted from her carriage, surrounded by many hundreds of queens, she entered the mango grove—just like the Miśrakāvana garden of the gods with its wonderful chariots.

Just as the *yātraka* and *kovidāra* trees of the Trāyastriṃśa gods shine when surrounded by deities, even so did that royal mango grove shine when surrounded by the king’s women of the inner apartments. Then Queen Sudarśanā, together with others, while walking about and wandering through that mango grove, plucking choice mangoes and eating mango fruits, and gathering various kinds of flowers, eventually reached the middle of the mango grove where King Kuśa was sitting. Then King Kuśa rose from the foot of a mango tree and embraced Queen Sudarśanā from behind. Terrified and trembling, Sudarśanā thought, "I have been seized by a forest-demon (*vanapiśāca*). She cried out, "Help! Help! I am being devoured by a forest-demon! I am being devoured by a forest-demon! The women of the inner apartments fled here and there. King Kuśa played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with Sudarśanā in the mango grove; and Sudarśanā would cry out, "Help! Help! Run, women of the inner apartments! I am being devoured by a forest-demon! When the women of the inner apartments realized that King Kuśa had been playing, dallying, and enjoying himself with Sudarśanā according to his desire, they took various kinds of flowers in their laps and went to that place. Then those many hundreds of queens showered King Kuśa with handfuls of flowers and raised a clamor, crying, "Shame on the demon! Shame on the demon! Then King Kuśa, having released Queen Sudarśanā, entered the royal palace. The ritual for averting evil (*balikarma*) performed by Queen Sudarśanā’s retinue was joined to him; the ladle was heated until glowing, and they cried, "Peace! Peace! The evil is stilled! By good fortune you have been released alive by the forest-demon. Then Queen Sudarśanā, together with other queens, having played, dalled, and enjoyed herself in that mango grove for the rest of the day as she pleased, entered the royal palace at the wrong hour. She then entered King Kuśa’s bedchamber. The king—

She said: "The Queen ran out to look for mangoes; neither were those mangoes brought back, nor am I dear to her. The Queen said: "Great King, where are my mangoes? I ran out to look for mangoes, and there I was embraced by a forest-demon (*vanapiśāca*). I was nearly devoured by the forest-demon, but then I was rescued from the hands of the forest-demon by the women of the inner apartments. Great King, such as your umbrella-bearer is, and such as that water-demon (*udakarākṣasa*) in the lotus pond is, such too is the forest-demon in the mango grove. I think all three persons were born of one mother; they are all exactly alike. King Kuśa said: "Queen, do not go again to look at the mango grove. I too was nearly devoured by the forest-demon in that mango grove."

Then, at another time, Queen Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā: "I wish to see King Kuśa’s elephant corps. I have heard that King Kuśa has a vast elephant corps consisting of sixty thousand elephants. The chief queen Alindā said, "My daughter, tomorrow you shall go out to see the royal elephant corps. Then the chief queen Alindā summoned the chief elephant-keeper and gave him this command: "Tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out with the women of the inner apartments to see the royal elephant stables. Therefore, decorate the elephants and the stables. Having heard the chief queen Alindā’s command, the elephant-keeper decorated the entire elephant corps—the sixty thousand elephants—with every ornament: they were covered with golden nets, adorned with ivory ornaments and trunk-ornaments, and their hooves were like coral. He had the elephant stables sprinkled and swept, strewn with loose flowers, draped with bundles of silk ribbons, and perfumed with incense. Then the chief queen Alindā addressed King Kuśa.

"My son, you must know that tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out with the ladies of the harem to visit the royal elephant stable. Therefore, go to the elephant stable beforehand and stay in such a place there that Sudarśanā will not recognize you as King Kuśa. Then King Kuśa, having promised his mother, went to the elephant stable at dawn, disguised as an elephant-keeper. He remained at the foot of the elephants, waiting for Sudarśanā. Meanwhile, Princess Sudarśanā, accompanied by her mother-in-law, Queen Alindā, and surrounded by all the women of the harem, mounted royal horse-chariots and entered the elephant stable. She then dismounted from her chariot and, surrounded by hundreds of maidservants, entered the elephant stable. King Kuśa, acting as an elephant-keeper at the foot of the elephants, sat there gazing intently at Sudarśanā. When it was time for Queen Sudarśanā to turn back and return to the palace, she was struck from behind by King Kuśa with fresh, steaming elephant dung. Her royal garments were defiled by the elephant dung. Then the princess Sudarśanā addressed her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā: "Madam, this royal elephant-keeper must be punished! How could he strike the chief consort of King Kuśa with elephant dung? Queen Alindā replied: "Enough, daughter! Let it be. This is a royal elephant-keeper; he is not to be killed. What can be done? Thus was Sudarśanā consoled by her mother-in-law.

Then, at another time, Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Aliṃdā: "Madam, it would be dear to me to see King Kuśa’s cavalry. Queen Aliṃdā said: "Very well, daughter; tomorrow go out to see King Kuśa’s horse-escort. Then she...

Queen Alindā, having summoned the chief groomsmen, gave them this command: "Tomorrow, Princess Sudarśanā, together with the women of the inner court, will go out to view the royal horse-stables. Now, you must decorate all sixty thousand horses and have the stable-yard sprinkled, swept, and strewn with loose flowers. Upon hearing Queen Alindā’s command, those horse-guards decorated all sixty thousand horses with every kind of ornament, and they had the stable-yard sprinkled, swept, and strewn with loose flowers. Then Queen Alindā informed King Kuśa: "My son Kuśa, you should know that Princess Sudarśanā, together with the women of the inner court, will go out to view the royal horse-stables. If you wish to see her, then go to the stable-yard in plain clothes and stand in such a place that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa. King Kuśa, having assented to his mother’s words, waited for the night to pass. At dawn, he disguised himself as a horse-guard, scattered fodder for the horses, and sat there waiting for Sudarśanā. Then Princess Sudarśanā, together with her mother-in-law, Queen Alindā, and all the women of the inner court, ascended a jeweled palanquin and set out for the stable-yard. There, Princess Sudarśanā descended from the palanquin and, surrounded by hundreds of queens, entered the stable-yard. King Kuśa stood behind the horses, gazing intently at Sudarśanā. After wandering and strolling through the stable-yard with the other women of the inner court, when it was time for Sudarśanā to turn back and go toward the palace, King Kuśa struck her on the back with a fresh, steaming piece of horse-dung. Her royal garments were ruined by the horse-dung. Then Princess Sudarśanā said to her mother-in-law, Queen Alindā: "Madam, punishment must be given to this horse-guard. Can he even receive [favor] from King Kuśa?"
"In order to strike the chief queen with horse-dung. Queen Mahādevī Āliṇḍā said: "Daughter, forgive them; these royal horse-guards are not to be killed. What can be done?"

Then, at another time, Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā: "Madam, it is my desire to see King Kuśa’s chariot-army. I have heard that King Kuśa’s chariot-army is vast, consisting of sixty thousand chariots. Queen Alindā said, "Very well, daughter. Tomorrow, go out to see King Kuśa’s chariot-army. Then Queen Alindā summoned the chariot-guards of King Kuśa and gave them this command: "Tomorrow, Princess Sudarśanā, together with the women of the inner apartments, will go out to see King Kuśa’s chariot-army."

Then those charioteers, having heard the words of Mahādevī, on the following day prepared sixty thousand chariots. They were yoked, covered with lion skins, leopard skins, and tiger skins, draped with white woolen blankets (*pāṇḍukambala*), making a joyful sound, adorned with victory banners (*vaijayantī*), fitted with beautiful coral, and with flags and pennants raised high. Then Mahādevī Alindā informed King Kuśa: "My son, you should know that tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā, together with the women of the harem, will go out to view the royal chariot-division. If you wish to see her, then go early to the chariot-house and stand in such a place that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa. Then Princess Sudarśanā, together with Mahādevī Alindā and the entire harem, mounted the royal chariots and set out for the chariot-house. King Kuśa, having promised his mother, went to the chariot-house early at dawn; disguised as a charioteer, he sat at the front of the chariots, waiting for Sudarśanā. Then Princess Sudarśanā, having alighted from her horse-chariot and surrounded by many hundreds of queens, entered the chariot-house. After Princess Sudarśanā had walked about the chariot-house with the other queens, at the moment she turned back thinking, "I am going to the palace," King Kuśa [struck her] with a fresh lump of cow dung that was steaming.

She struck them on their backs; those royal garments were ruined by the lump of cow dung. Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, said to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Aliṃdā: "Madam, punishment must be meted out to this charioteer Rathapāla. He ought not to have been able to strike the chief queen of King Kuśa with a lump of cow dung! The chief queen Aliṃdā said: "Daughter, forgive him. This Rathapāla belongs to the royal family; he is the king’s charioteer and keeper of the chariot-treasury. What can be done? Then Sudarśanā was thus appeased by the chief queen Aliṃdā.

Then, at another time, a fire was set in the royal elephant stable, and a great conflagration blazed up. Thousands of elephant-keepers, high officials, and a great multitude of people gathered, thinking, "We shall extinguish the elephant stable," yet they were unable to extinguish that conflagration. The entire harem also became terrified and panicked by the fear of that fire, fearing, "It might burn down this royal palace as well. All those women of the harem were running out from where the elephant stable was; who would dare to extinguish this fire among the elephants? The great multitude grew exhausted, unable to extinguish that conflagration, nor could they bring down the thick, massive roofs of the elephant stable, even though many people had pulled them up. In the meantime, King Kuśa was wandering and strolling about outside the city. Then a man, a minister of the king, informed him: "Great King, you should know that a fire has broken out in the royal elephant stable. Upon hearing this, King Kuśa, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, arrived at that elephant stable with speed and his retinue. As the king was approaching, all the women of the harem saw him. By the king’s sudden exertion as he approached, those flaming roofs—[he tore them away] along with their supports.

Then he threw the iron thorny spikes from the elephant stable out through the front gate. Indeed, those excellent chains with which the elephants were bound, he snapped with his hand with a crackling sound. And those noble elephants that were seized by fire, having lifted them up, he cast them aside away from the danger of the flames. Thus, in an instant, King Kuśa extinguished the entire elephant stable; the whole elephant army was rescued from the conflagration, and not even a single elephant was burned or harmed. Thereupon, many hundreds of thousands of millions of people, seeing such heroic prowess of King Kuśa, raised thousands of shouts of acclaim. Even the women of the royal harem, seeing such manly valor of King Kuśa, were all joyful and delighted, exclaiming, "Oh, the strength of King Kuśa! Oh, his prowess! Then another hunchbacked woman, filled with joy and impelled by excitement, cried out for King Kuśa, "King! King!"
The powerful, vast, and great lion-throne shines brilliantly;
it appears like the moon in the sky, perfectly circular on all sides.
With eyes as long and copper-red as those of a cakora bird, he shines like the god of love;
the king, a bull among men endowed with power, has released the elephants.
Now King Kuśa, being pleased with that hunchbacked woman, gave her a gift, entertained her, and granted her a boon.
"Truly, this hunchback is fortunate who praises the king;
I shall give you four garments from Kāśī."
Then, having heard that hunchback woman speaking in praise of Kuśa, it occurred to Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter: "This must be King Kuśa."

She whose complexion this hunchback describes—then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, having seen such a complexion and form of King Kuśa, her mind was struck with revulsion and she became filled with pain and dejection: "How can such a man be my husband? He is so ill-colored and hideous; he has thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, and a large belly; he is black, the color of a heap of soot; there is no difference at all between him and this *piśāca*. Then Queen Sudarśanā, enraged at the hunchback, said:
Truly, there is no one who can cut out the tongue of this hunchback,
even with a very sharp weapon, she who praises the king.
Then that hunchbacked woman exhorted Queen Sudarśanā with a verse:
Kings threaten with imprisonment or execution;
therefore, I speak in praise of this [practice], guarding my own life.

Then Queen Sudarśanā, seeing King Kuśa in such a state—discolored and hideous—found no pleasure there in that royal palace, which was so delightful as to resemble the abode of the gods and a mine of endless jewels. She had no desire for food or drink and said: "I will neither eat nor drink; what is the use of my life, since I must dwell with a Piśāca? Then the princess Sudarśanā made this request to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Aliṃdā: "Madam, release me! I shall go to Kanyakubja to be with my parents. If you do not let me go, I will take my own life this very moment. Then it occurred to the chief queen Aliṃdā: "It is better that this princess lives than that she dies. So the chief queen Aliṃdā said: "Daughter, go wherever you wish."

Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, accompanied by a hunchbacked woman, mounted a horse-chariot and departed from Vārāṇasī. Traveling by stages, she arrived at Kanyakubja and went into the presence of her mother and father. Now King Kuśa, having entered his bedchamber late in the evening, did not see Queen Sudarśanā. Although she was searched for throughout the royal palace, she was nowhere to be seen. King Kuśa, unable to find Queen Sudarśanā, became anxious, sorrowful, and consumed with grief; though his harem was so vast, he could not find her. When it became known to him that Queen Sudarśanā had gone to her family home accompanied by a hunchbacked woman, King Kuśa then addressed his mother, Alindā: "Mother, I too shall go to Kanyakubja, to my father-in-law Mahendra, the king of the Madrakas, to bring back Queen Sudarśanā. When Queen Alindā heard her son Kuśa say, "I will go to Kanyakubja," she fainted out of love for her son and thirst for the kingdom. She stumbled, fell broken upon the ground, overcome with grief for her son. "Alas! What misfortune has befallen me, unfortunate as I am! Since I sought this Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendra, the king of the Madrakas of Kanyakubja, and brought her here, I do not know how it will turn out for my son, King Kuśa. Then Queen Alindā spoke to her son Kuśa: "My son, you are a prince of the Ikṣvākus, delicate and raised in luxury. The people there eat only parched grain and wear woolen blankets; their daily work is harsh and their food coarse. How will you endure the journey on the road? King Kuśa said, "Mother, I will travel providing for my own livelihood through dancing, singing, instrumental music, and various other arts and means. Do not be anxious, Mother. Having thus consoled his mother, King Kuśa established his brother Kuśadruma in the kingdom. His brother—

"Exert your sovereignty over these sixty thousand cities, along with their towns and provinces. Here are sixty thousand elephants for you, adorned with every ornament, covered with golden nets, and having beautiful hooves like coral. There are sixty thousand horses, all of them from Sindh, swift of pace, adorned with every ornament.
