There are sixty thousand chariots, covered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins; draped with white woolen blankets; resounding with joyful noise; equipped with victory banners; having beautiful hooves like coral; and with parasols, standards, and flags raised high. These are your vehicles. Rule this kingdom until my return. Then King Kuśa gave instructions to his ministers: "This prince Kuśadruma shall be king in my stead until my return. Know this, and rule the kingdom accordingly; protect the people of the city and the countryside with righteousness. Having thus instructed the ministers and established his brother Kuśadruma on the throne, King Kuśa paid homage to his mother, the Great Queen Alindā, circumambulated her, took up his seven-stringed lute, and set out facing north.

King Kuśa, providing for his livelihood through various means, proceeded toward Kanyakubja, his father-in-law’s domain; traveling by stages, he eventually reached the territory of Kanyakubja. There, he took up residence in a certain village and was granted shelter in an old hall. At that time, a festival was being held in that village. King Kuśa was then addressed by the old woman: "Son, a festival is taking place here in the village; go into the center of the village and you will obtain some food and drink there. Having taken your meal, you may return. Having heard this from the old woman, King Kuśa went into the center of the village. Then, King Kuśa played such a lute and sang such a song that all the people of the village were delighted. Being pleased with him, the villagers gave King Kuśa a full basket of various kinds of snacks, a large bowl of rice, and a jar of curd, along with many other things.

And there were various side dishes. Then King Kuśa brought all the solid and soft foods into the hall. When the old woman saw the abundant solid and soft foods—seeing that a large basket was given full of various kinds of snacks, a large tray was given full of rice, and various side dishes had been brought in by King Kuśa—she became joyful. She thought, "Today this musician will take his single meal and depart in the last watch of the night; the remainder of this solid and soft food will be my sustenance for two or three months. Then, while King Kuśa was conversing with the old woman, he ate half of the basket of snacks as he walked along. The old woman knew it, thinking, "Even now, in just a moment, he will give me the rest of the snacks. But then King Kuśa, being hungry, ate the entire basket of snacks and did not leave even a single morsel behind. The old woman thought, "Now that this musician has eaten the whole large basket of snacks, he must be full. He will not be able to eat any more of this tray of sweetmeats; thus, my food will last for a long time. Then King Kuśa, walking along the path and being hungry, consumed the large tray of sweetmeats, that jar of curd, and those various side dishes—all of it. Not a thing remained for the old woman. The old woman became hopeless and cried out, "Help! Help! Enter! Run! A demon in human form has entered my house and wishes to devour me! King Kuśa said, "Mother, why do you cry out? Why do you run? No wicked people dwell in this village. Do not be afraid, do not cry out. Having stayed here for this one night, I shall depart tomorrow."
Then King Kuśa, having risen at the time of the first light of dawn, set out and proceeded by stages toward Kanyakubja.

Having arrived, he entered the florist’s workshop and approached the chief florist, thinking, "I too shall dwell here; I am skilled in this craft. Now, in that florist’s workshop, royal necklaces, fragrant crests, and garlands were being made. King Kuśa then produced such necklaces, fragrant crests, and garlands—so well-made, perfectly finished, variegated, and beautiful—that when all the florists saw them, they were struck with wonder. "Oh! What a noble master’s son, what a magnificent craftsman, who makes such necklaces, fragrant crests, and garlands—so well-made, so perfectly finished—that we have never seen their like before! And King Kuśa inscribed his own name upon all of them, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of King Kuśa. These necklaces, fragrant crests, and garlands were brought into the palace and presented to Sudarśanā. "Look, Sudarśanā, at these varieties of flowers; how well-made, how variegated, how perfectly finished, and how many-colored they are! Then Sudarśanā took whichever necklace, crest, and excellent garland was most beautiful there, intending to fasten it on, but as soon as she saw Kuśa’s name, this thought occurred to her: "This is the work of Kuśa; King Kuśa must have come here in commoner's guise. Thereupon, Sudarśanā set aside those items made by Kuśa and took others that were ordinary. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her sisters-in-law and the women of the harem: "Sudarśanā, why do you set aside these most beautiful necklaces, crests, and garlands to take others that are ordinary? She said to them, "Enough for me with these; let this [ordinary one] be mine. She did not reveal the secret to anyone.
Now, King Kuśa, having lived at the root of the florist’s [tree], did not obtain his purpose. Then—

"How many stools are being made? How many beds and seats are being made? How many footstools are being made? How many *bhadrapīṭha* chairs are being made? How many *ayakkā* sandals are being made? How many *phelika* boxes are being made? How many *anta-koṭa* (corner-cases) are being made? And what other various kinds of carpenter’s tools are being made? Now King Kuśa produced such carpenter’s tools—well-made, well-finished, and shapely—that when all the carpenters saw them, they were struck with wonder: "Aha! What a fine master’s son, what a splendid craftsman, who makes such carpenter’s tools so well-made and well-finished, the likes of which we have never seen before! And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name as a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of King Kuśa. Then those female slaves of the harem brought those carpenter’s tools into the royal palace. Having selected the most beautiful among them, they were presented to Sudarśanā: "Sudarśanā, look, look at these carpenter’s tools; how beautiful and handsome they are! Take whichever one you prefer. Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whichever is the most beautiful there—whether it be a stool, a couch, a chair, a footrest, a footstool, a *bhadrapīṭha*, an *ayakkā*, an *anta-koṭa*, a box, or a small chest"—looked until she saw the name of Kuśa. Then it occurred to her: "This is the work of Kuśa. She then set that aside and took another, an ordinary one. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, and those women of the harem: "Sudarśanā, why do you reject such beautiful carpenter’s tools as these?"
"Setting aside other ordinary things, you take these. She then said, "Enough for me with those; let these alone be mine. Whatever secret was there, she did not disclose it to anyone.

Now King Kuśa, having lived at the root of a carpenter, did not find his purpose there. So he departed and attached himself to a washerman. There too, clothes were washed for the king’s harem; Sudarśanā’s clothes were also washed right there. King Kuśa recognized Sudarśanā’s garments. He washed Sudarśanā’s clothes in such a way—so well-washed, clean, and spotless—that when all the other washermen saw those washed clothes, they were filled with wonder: "Aha! What a fine master’s son, what a splendid craftsman, who washes these clothes so well-washed, so thoroughly cleansed, so clean and spotless, such as we have never seen before! King Kuśa wrote his own name with *bhallātaka* [markings] as a mere sign, so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of Kuśa. Then those palace maidservants brought those clothes into the royal palace; those which were the queens' clothes were presented to the queens, and those which were the women of the harem's clothes were given to the women of the harem. Now, when those women of the harem saw Sudarśanā’s clothes—white, clean, and spotless—they were struck with wonder: "All these beautiful clothes of Sudarśanā are so well-washed, clean, and spotless; they deserve double or triple the washing fee! Sudarśanā too, seeing those garments pure and spotless, was delighted.

She grew up until, in a certain border region, there was a washerman who, while marking clothes with *bhallātaka* fruit by way of mere signs, would write a name upon a garment. There, seeing the name "Kuśa" written on it, she thought, "This is Kuśa’s work. She did not accept it herself, but had her attendants take it away. All the women of the harem gave their own laundry for washing into the hands of the maidservants; however, Sudarśanā did not wish to give her laundry for washing. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, and the other women of the harem: "Sudarśanā, when all your garments have been well-washed, perfectly clean, and beautifully finished, why do you not give the fee for the washing? Sudarśanā said: "What is your concern? It will be given at another time. She did not disclose that secret to anyone.

Now King Kuśa, having lived at the feet of the washerman, did not obtain his purpose. Thereupon, he departed and attached himself to the chief of the laundrymen. And there, in that laundry shop, the garments of the king’s harem were being washed, as were the garments of Sudarśanā. It was right there that King Kuśa recognized Sudarśanā’s garments. Kuśa dyed those garments of Sudarśanā with such beautiful colors, such exquisite patterns, and such various types of dyeing that they were so well-colored that all the laundrymen were struck with amazement, saying: "Oh, what a fine master’s son! What a splendid craftsman is he who dyes these garments so beautifully colored and so exquisitely patterned, the likes of which we have never seen before! And on every one of them, King Kuśa wrote his own name as a mere mark using *bhallātaka* (myrobalan) juice, so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of Kuśa. Then, by those slave-girls of the harem, whichever garments belonged to the queens were given to the queens, and whichever garments belonged to the women of the harem were given to the women of the harem; [and so too] the garment of Sudarśanā.

The women of the harem, having seen them, were amazed and said, "These garments of Sudarśanā are well-dyed, beautiful, and most variegated; she should be given double or triple the dyeing fee. Then those garments were presented to Sudarśanā. When Sudarśanā saw those garments—well-dyed, beautiful, and most variegated—she became contented and filled with joy and gladness. She looked at the place where the dyer made his mark with *bhallātaka* (myrobalan) and there she saw the name of Kuśa. It occurred to her, "This is Kuśa’s work. She did not accept it herself, but gave it to her attendant. Then the women of the harem each gave the dyeing fee for their own garments into the hands of the maidservants, but Sudarśanā did not wish to give the dyeing fee. Her mother, her sisters, and the other women of the harem said to her, "Sudarśanā, since your garments are so well-dyed, variegated, and beautiful, you ought to give double or triple the dyeing fee; yet you do not wish to give it. Sudarśanā said, "Why are you concerned? He will shine [with glory] at another time."
Whatever secret there was therein, he did not disclose it to anyone.

Now King Kuśa, having lived at the court of Rājaka and finding no benefit there, fled from that place and took refuge with a master goldsmith. There, by the command of King Mahendraka, various kinds of food vessels and drinking vessels made of gold and silver and inlaid with jewels were being fashioned for the sake of the harem. Then King Kuśa made such food and drinking vessels—made of gold, made of jewels, and inlaid with gems—so beautiful and well-proportioned that not even a single other goldsmith was capable of making such vessels. When those goldsmiths saw such things...

They were filled with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh, how wonderful! This son of the virtuous teacher is a master craftsman who fashions such jewel-vessels as these, the likes of which we have never seen before. And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name as a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of Kuśa. When all those royal vessels made of gold and silver were finished, they were presented by the chief of the artisans to King Mahendraka. Upon seeing the vessels fashioned by Kuśa, King Mahendraka was amazed, thinking, "Such are these jewel-inlaid vessels; they must have been made by a truly skillful master. Then King Mahendraka placed those jewel-vessels into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying, "Go, enter the inner apartments. First give them to the Great Queen and my daughter Sudarśanā according to their preference; afterwards, they shall be given to the other queens and the women of the harem. Those eunuchs and chamberlains then entered the inner apartments with the jewel-vessels and presented them to the Great Queen, saying, "Queen, these jewel-vessels have been sent by the King. Let the Queen and your daughter Sudarśanā take what they prefer first; afterwards they will be shown to the other queens and all the women of the harem. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, the women of the harem, the eunuchs, and the chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, these jewel-vessels—drinking vessels—have been sent by your father. You should take what you prefer first; afterwards they will be shown to the other queens and all the women of the harem. Take whatever you desire. Now, Sudarśanā thought, "I shall take whichever among these is the most beautiful, well-made, perfectly finished, and elegant," until she saw the name of Kuśa. It occurred to her, "This is the work of Kuśa. She then set that one aside and took others made by an ordinary craftsman. Then Sudarśanā [spoke] to her mother and her sisters...

And she was addressed by the women of the inner apartments, by the eunuchs, and by the chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why do you discard such beautiful, precious vessels, all so exquisite, and take up others that are common? She then said: "Enough for me with those; let this very thing be mine. Whatever secret was therein, she did not disclose it to anyone.

Now King Kuśa, having stayed with the coppersmith, did not find what he needed. So he departed and attached himself to a master goldsmith. There too, by royal command, various kinds of golden ornaments were being made for the sake of the harem: head-covers were being made, foot-rugs were being made, golden garlands were being made, *kilaṃjakas* were being made, turbans were being made, jeweled earrings were being made, baskets were being made, *mukhaphullakas* were being made, *bimbās* were being made, bracelets were being made, anklets were being made, rings were being made, hip-ornaments were being made, foot-rugs were being made, anklets were being made, and toe-rings were being made. Then King Kuśa made such golden ornaments—noble, beautiful, well-fashioned, well-finished, well-polished, with impurities and dross thoroughly removed, soft, workable, and radiant—such that when all those goldsmiths saw them, they were struck with wonder: "Oh! What a fine master’s son, what a splendid craftsman, who makes such golden ornaments so well-fashioned, well-finished, and shapely, the likes of which have never been seen by us before! And in all of them, King Kuśa wrote his own name as a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of Kuśa. Then, at that time, by those goldsmiths...

The ornaments were finished, and all of them were presented to King Mahendra. When the king saw the ornaments that had been fashioned by King Kuśa, he was filled with wonder, exclaiming, "Aha! How well-made, how perfectly finished, and how beautiful these ornaments are! They have been crafted by the son of a skilled master. Then King Mahendraka sent those ornaments into the hands of the eunuchs and the chamberlains, saying, "Go; first give these ornaments as you please to the Great Queen and Sudarśanā, then to the other queens, and finally to all the women of the inner apartments. Those eunuchs and chamberlains, having entered the royal palace, presented the ornaments to the Great Queen and Sudarśanā, saying, "Queen, these golden ornaments have been sent by the king. You and your daughter Sudarśanā may take whichever you prefer first; afterwards they will be given to the other queens and to all the women of the inner apartments. Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whatever among these golden ornaments is the most beautiful, well-crafted, perfectly finished, and elegant," looked at them and saw the name of Kuśa upon one. It occurred to her, "This is the work of Kuśa. She then set that aside and took others that were ordinary, made by inferior craftsmen. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, the women of the inner apartments, the eunuchs, and the chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why are you so perverse? Why do you reject these golden ornaments—which are the most beautiful of all, well-made, perfectly finished, elegant, and crafted by the son of a skilled master—and instead take others that are ordinary, made by inferior craftsmen? Sudarśanā said, "Enough for me with those; let this very one be mine. She did not reveal the secret to anyone.
Now, King Kuśa, having lived at the goldsmith’s place, did not find what he sought. Thereupon, having departed from there, he approached the head jeweler. Even here, by the king’s command—

For the sake of the city, ornaments of various kinds were being made: necklaces of pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, rock crystal, emeralds, and red corals were being made; half-necklaces were being made; jeweled earrings were being made; jeweled armlets were being made; jeweled head-coverings were being made; bracelets were being made; arm-rings were being made; and jeweled girdles were being made. Now King Kuśa had such well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely jeweled ornaments made that when all those jewelers saw them, they were filled with wonder, saying, "Oh, what a fine master’s son! What a marvelous craftsman he is, who makes such well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely ornaments as we have never seen before! And on every one of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name merely as a sign, so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of Kuśa. When those jewelers had finished the ornaments, they presented them to King Mahendraka. When the king saw the ornaments made by Keśin, he was filled with wonder, saying, "Oh, what a fine master’s son! What a marvelous craftsman! Then King Mahendraka sent those ornaments into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying, "Go, give these ornaments first to the Great Queen and to Sudarśanā according to their preference, and afterwards to the other queens and all the women of the harem. Then those eunuchs and chamberlains, having entered the royal palace, presented the ornaments to the Great Queen and to Sudarśanā, saying, "O Queen, these jeweled ornaments were sent by the king for you and for your daughter Sudarśanā; take whichever you prefer. Afterwards, they will be given to the other queens and all the women of the harem. Then Sudarśanā thought, "I shall take whichever among these jeweled ornaments is the most beautiful, well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely," until she saw the name of Kuśa. It occurred to her, "This is the work of Kuśa."

She, having discarded those, now took up others that were common, poorly crafted, and made by unskilled artisans. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, the women of the inner apartments, the eunuchs, and the chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why have you become so perverse? Why do you discard such jewel ornaments—well-made, well-finished, beautiful in form, and crafted by skilled artisans—to take up others that are common and poorly crafted by unskilled artisans? Then Sudarśanā said: "Enough for me with these; let this alone be mine. She did not disclose the secret concerning that matter to anyone.

Now, King Kuśa, having lived at the workshop of the ivory-carver, found no employment there. So he departed and went to the master craftsman who worked with conch shells. There too, by royal command for the sake of the harem, various kinds of ornaments and vessels made of conch and elephant tusks were being fashioned. They made bracelets from elephant tusks; they made cosmetic boxes; they made ivory caskets; they made *rocanapiśācikās* (perfume containers); they made ivory ewers; they made ivory combs; they made items fashioned from the feet of elephants; they made lion figures; they made conch shells; they made conch beds; they made oil vessels, perfume vessels, and pigment vessels out of conch; they made conch stalks; they made conch caskets; they made conch bracelets; they made conch girdles; they made conch necklaces; they made conch palanquins; and they made conch shields. In this way, he fashioned various kinds of vessels and ornaments made of conch and elephant tusks—well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely—such that all the workers in conch and ivory were filled with wonder upon seeing them. "Oh! What a noble master’s son, what a magnificent artisan, who makes such ornaments and vessels of conch and ivory as we have never seen before! And in all of these, King Kuśa inscribed his own name and mark.

He wrote it on a small slip so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of Kuśa. Then, when those shell- and ivory-workers had completed everything exactly as they were commanded, they presented them to King Mahendraka. Seeing that work of Kuśa—so magnificent, beautiful, well-crafted, and worthy of a king—the king was filled with wonder: "Aha! How wonderful are these things made by Kuśa, the son of a master craftsman! The princes, the ministers, and the royal officers were also struck with amazement upon seeing the shell and ivory articles made by Kuśa; they exclaimed, "These were made by Kuśa, the son of a master craftsman! King Mahendraka sent those ornaments and vessels into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying: "Go, enter the inner apartments and first give them according to their preference to the Great Queen and my daughter Sudarśanā; afterwards, they shall be given to the other queens and the women of the harem. Then those eunuchs and chamberlains took the ornaments and vessels and entered the inner apartments. They were presented to the Great Queen, who said: "Queen, these shell and ivory ornaments and vessels have been sent by the King. You and your daughter Sudarśanā may take them first according to your preference; afterwards they will be given to the other queens and all the women of the harem. When Sudarśanā saw those shell and ivory ornaments and vessels, and perceived how well-made, perfectly finished, auspicious, and beautiful they were—seeing that they were crafted by the son of a master craftsman—she reached out her hand to take them. However, as soon as she saw the name of Kuśa, the thought occurred to her: "This is the work of Kuśa. She then set those aside and took others that were ordinary, made by common craftsmen. Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, the women of the harem, the eunuchs, and the chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why are you acting like this?"

"Abandoning these most beautiful, well-made, well-finished, and shapely [garments] crafted by the son of a master artisan, you take up others that are common and poorly made by an inferior craftsman. Why do you not take these most beautiful ones? Then Sudarśanā said:
Enough for me with these; let this alone be mine: that which is secret therein, he does not disclose to anyone.

Now King Kuśa, having stayed with the ivory-worker, found no distinction [in his work]. Thereupon, leaving him, he went to stay with the puppet-maker. There, by the king’s command, various kinds of mechanical puppets were made for the sake of the harem; various playthings and diverse mechanical puppets were made; even fans were made as mechanical puppets. There were palm-leaf fans, peacock-feather fans, footstools, chairs, and large couches with mechanical puppet-legs; there were bracelets and other ornaments with mechanical puppet-parts. Various kinds of birds were made as mechanical puppets: parrots, mynas, cuckoos, swans, peacocks, woodpeckers, cranes, pheasants, and pheasant-like birds; oil-flasks were also made as mechanical puppets. Various kinds of fruits were made as mechanical puppets: mangoes, pomegranates, citron fruits, *vīrasenaka* fruits, grapevines, mangoes, rose-apples, pepper berries, wood-apples, coconuts, jackfruits, *kṣīrika* fruits, *nīpa* flowers, *kadamba* flowers, and date-palm vines. In this way, various kinds of mechanical puppet-vessels were made. Now, King Kuśa [beheld] such things as these...

He fashioned eight mechanical vessels that were well-crafted, perfectly finished, and beautifully shaped; seeing them, all the machine-makers were struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh, how wonderful! This son of a master craftsman is a truly skilled artisan who makes such vessels—well-crafted, perfectly finished, and beautifully shaped—which we have never seen before. And on every one of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name as a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of Kuśa. When the machine-makers had completed all the vessels, they presented them to the king. King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, was astonished upon seeing those works made by Kuśa and thought, "Oh, how marvelous these mechanical vessels are—so well-crafted, perfectly finished, and beautifully shaped, made by the son of a master craftsman! The king then placed those vessels in the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying, "Go, enter the inner apartments; first give them to the Great Queen and my daughter Sudarśanā, and afterwards to all the other queens and the women of the harem. The eunuchs and chamberlains took the vessels and entered the inner apartments, presenting them to the Great Queen and her daughter Sudarśanā. They said, "Queen, these mechanical vessel-vessels have been sent by the king for you and your daughter Sudarśanā. You and Sudarśanā should take whichever you prefer first; afterwards they will be given to the other queens and all the women of the harem. Then Sudarśanā, having seen which among them was the most beautiful, well-crafted, perfectly finished, and beautifully shaped, reached out her hand to take it. But when she saw the name of Kuśa, the thought occurred to her, "This is the work of Kuśa. She then set that one aside and took others that were ordinary. Sudarśanā was then addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the harem, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why are you perverse? Why do you reject these well-crafted, perfectly finished, and beautifully shaped items made by the son of a master craftsman, and instead take others that are ordinary and made by a poor artisan? Why do you not take the most beautiful ones? She replied: "I am not perverse. I am taking the best, but I do not wish to take the work of Kuśa. They said, "Sudarśanā, what is this? Do not speak thus! Take the best! She replied, "I am not perverse. I am taking the best, but I simply do not wish to take the work of Kuśa. They said, "Sudarśanā, what is this? Do not speak thus! Take the best! She replied, "I am not perverse. I am taking the best, but I simply do not wish to take the work of Kuśa. They said, "Sudarśanā, what is this? Do not speak thus! Take the best! She replied, "I am not perverse. I am taking the best, but I simply do not wish to take the work of Kuśa. They said, "Sudarśanā, what is this? Do not speak thus! Take the best! She replied, "I am not perverse. I am taking the best, but I simply do not wish to take the work of Kuśa. They said, "Sudarśanā, what is this
Darśanā said: "Enough for me of this; let this alone be mine. Whatever secret is therein, no one knows it."

Now King Kuśa, having lived at the root of the machine-maker, did not find his purpose there. So he departed and took refuge with the chief of the reed-workers (*varuṭa*). There, various kinds of royal reed-articles were being made: fans, palm-leaf fans, parasols, parasol-staves, baskets, cane-seats, cane-frames, cane-caskets—such various kinds of reed-articles were being made by royal command for the sake of the inner apartments. There, King Kuśa worked together with those reed-workers on various kinds of reed-articles for the inner apartments, such that not even one among all those reed-workers was able to make anything like them. When all the reed-articles had been completed exactly as ordered, they took those articles and presented them to the king. The king sent them into the inner apartments into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, first offering them to the Great Queen Sudarśanā. [The eunuchs said: "These have been sent by the king; you take them first according to your preference, and afterwards they will be given to the entire inner apartment. The Great Queen took whatever she desired, and Sudarśanā was also told: "Take these excellent reed-articles, whichever you prefer. Then, seeing that those reed-articles were beautiful, magnificent, well-made, noble, worthy of a king, and a source of wonder for many people—and seeing her own name written upon them as a signature by King Kuśa himself—she set those aside, thinking, "These were made by Kuśa," and instead took other ordinary reed-articles. Then she...

She was addressed by her sisters, by the women of the inner apartments, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains: "Sudarśanā, why do you discard these beautiful and magnificent royal ornaments and take up others that are common? She replied: 'Let these be mine; enough with those. Now, they did not know the secret reason why Sudarśanā would not accept those royal ornaments."

Now King Kuśa, having stayed there at the hut of the reed-worker, did not find his purpose. So he departed and entered the kitchen of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, where he approached the chief cook. "I too shall live right here; I will do whatever work you command, for I am skilled in that labor. Then the chief cook stationed King Kuśa in the kitchen and gave him orders: "Perform the work here. King Kuśa then prepared such varieties of meats, sauces, vegetables, and foods—sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, and astringent—in the royal kitchen that none of those employed in the royal service had ever seen such things before, let alone tasted them prepared. Furthermore, since the time Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, was born, he had never before experienced such a supreme flavor. When it was time for the meal, King Mahendraka sat down at the head of the dining hall and began eating those excellent varieties of meats, sauces, vegetables, and foods—sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, and astringent—which had been prepared by King Kuśa; yet he was not satisfied. The king was astonished and asked the chief cook: "Ho, man! By which cook has today's food been prepared? For since my birth, I have never before tasted such a superior flavor with the tip of my tongue. Then the chief cook, joining his palms in reverence, addressed the king: "Your Majesty, another guest cook has arrived and entered the kitchen; by him the meal for the Great King has been prepared."

Then it occurred to the king: "This soup is excellent; it must be gathered from various sources and cherished so that it does not go anywhere. The king then addressed the chief cook: "Ho there, cook! Bring that soup with which my meal today was prepared, so that I may see it. At that time, when the king had sat down at the head of the meal, the chief cook presented King Kuśa, saying: "This is that soup with which the Great King’s meal was prepared. Now, King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, looked upon King Kuśa and saw him to be ill-favored—ill-favored, unpleasant to behold, with thick lips, a thick head and feet, a large belly, dark, and the color of a heap of soot. Upon seeing him, the king was struck with wonder: "Oh, how strange! One who is called 'Beautiful' (*Śobhana*) is actually of such a common appearance, yet possesses such a sense for flavors, such a mastery of taste! The king then consoled him regarding the soup: "The provisions provided are indeed excellent. Having seated him before him and served him foods fit for a king—both hard and soft—the king had him eat and gave him drink. A garland was also offered to him. Then King Mahendraka gave this command: "Let this soup enter the royal palace through an open gate."

Thus, now, he dwelt in that royal household, honored and respected, beloved by the king, and dear, pleasing, and agreeable to all the princes, ministers, and the elite of the army. Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, addressed the eunuchs and chamberlains: "Sirs, let this cook enter the inner apartments with confidence; let him be a source of amusement for the women of the harem. Thereupon King Kuśa entered the royal palace with confidence, thinking: "The women of the harem have been given to me by our king as a plaything. Then those women of the harem played and sported with him in confidence; they climbed onto his back and carried him about in various ways. Then King Kuśa—

As he was being carried away by the women of the inner apartments, he was suddenly seen by Sudarśanā. Upon seeing King Kuśa, Sudarśanā became terrified and agitated; she grew angry with those women of the inner apartments, reviled them, and scolded them, saying, "Is it possible for women to carry a man about? Then those women of the inner apartments said, "Sudarśanā, why are you angry with us, why do you revile us, and why do you scold us? If we are merely carrying this plaything around, and he is your husband, then you should be jealous of him! Sudarśanā said, "Let my jealousy be as it may, but it is not possible for you to carry him about. Whosoever shall carry him, I will no longer be pleasant to her. Then Sudarśanā, having seen King Kuśa in the inner apartments, her face turned pale and distressed with grief, neither approached him nor spoke a word to him. Then King Kuśa said, "Sudarśanā, even now, upon seeing me, you are afraid? Sudarśanā said, "What does it matter that he has come here? It would be a marvel if he were seen coming by day or night! He is not a forest-demon, and you have not been killed by anyone. Your kingdom is vast, your inner apartments are vast; go to your own kingdom, play, enjoy yourself, and take your pleasure there. What will you do here? King Kuśa said, "Sudarśanā, I will not go without you. The directions do not appear to me anymore, since I came here. Sudarśanā said:
What shall I do now, or whom shall I blame?
My heart trembles upon seeing him, like one who has beheld a sea-demon.
What shall I do now, or whom shall I blame?
My heart trembles upon seeing him, like a bewildered doe seeing a hunter.
Without threatening him, following him day and night as he went, [the king said:
"Go, Kuśa, to your own kingdom; I do not desire you, who are ill-favored."
The king said:
O large, dark-complexioned one with beautiful hips and slender waist, being infatuated by your charms, I do not even desire my own kingdom.
I shall not go, O lady with well-rounded thighs;
I do not know the direction from which I have come.
Confused in mind, I wander through the world.
I am intoxicated by desires, O lady with eyes like those of a deer.
The goddess said:
This distraction of your mind is because you desire one who does not desire you; O King, you lust after one who is unwilling—this is not the characteristic of a wise man.
Kuśa said:
Whether she is unwilling or willing, the man who obtains a beloved woman—therein they praise the gain; therein, the lack of gain is wretched.
The goddess said:
You are able to delight even a thousand women in a single night;
yet, through desire for a single woman, you undergo great suffering.
The king said:
"I do not consider this to be suffering, O illustrious one who has gained such beauty;
if you have practiced the holy life well, you shall become my wife."
The goddess said:
Shame on your religious life! Let this evil be yours:
in the next world, you shall desire either a female dog or a female jackal.
Kuśa said:
"Do not speak thus, O blessed lady, fair-hipped one with a slender waist;
we too are ascetics, and it is well that we shine through our holy life."
O noble lady, they too shine here because of their well-practiced conduct;
having been reborn in the heavens among the Thirty-three, they enjoy all their desires at will.
Therefore, O blessed lady, O fair-hipped one of slender waist, I tell you this:
there is no other husband for you than Kuśa, who possesses the voice of a lion.
The goddess said:
If this speech of the fortune-teller should prove true, I will not be your wife; cut me into pieces as you wish!
The king said:
I do not wish to cut you, O fair-hipped one of slender waist;
uncut, O blessed lady, you shall become my wife.
And my kingdom was great, with many horses and many men;
it was of infinite and manifold extent, with abundant clothing and food.
Thus, having abandoned both my kingdom and my realm, I have come here;
deluded by desire for you, I do not even aspire to the kingdom.
The goddess said:
You dig a well in stone and seek a calyx in the *karṇikāra* flower;
you attempt to bind the wind with a net—desiring that which does not desire to be desired.
You desire me who does not desire you, and you seek me who seeks you not;
go back to your own kingdom—why do you weary yourself?
The king said:
"This is no hardship for me; this is my holy life.
But in the future, O blessed lady, you shall indeed become my wife."
The goddess said:
Let this evil celibacy you have undertaken be yours;
I seek rather a female dog, a jackal, or even a female donkey.
Then that heroic prince Kuśa, peerless in battle and possessed of wisdom, having ascended [the chariot], spoke these words:
If, O blessed lady, you of beautiful hips and slender waist, I were to go along and bind you with fetters, what would your kinsmen do for you?
The goddess said:
I am practicing that very same Dharma which was produced long ago;
it is that very same Dharma which you wish to bind me for, even as I remember it.
The king said:
"I am able to adorn you, O noble lady, O mistress of the household; once adorned, you may go wherever you wish. What can your father do?"
I am able to delight even a thousand women in a single night;
you alone are my choice, O blessed one, O lady with pure teeth, mistress of my household.
The goddess said:
I know you, O Great King, that you are powerful, a bull among men;
yet you are ill-colored, difficult to behold, and unpleasant to the touch, O Lord of the Earth.
With thick lips, a thick head, thick limbs, and a large belly, I do not wish to see you; do not weary yourself.
These high-walled enclosures, with their watchtowers and parapets,
are indeed those which ward off the elephants that might otherwise carry them away.
These fight with spears, javelins, and arrows, and with very sharp swords; O Lord of Creatures, may they seize you!
Thus King Kuśa now reviled Sudarśanā in various ways, and no one knew that this was King Kuśa.

Now, the neighboring rival kings—those of great renown, great power, and great armies—heard that Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, who was gracious and beautiful to behold, had fled from King Kuśa and come into her father’s presence; and that King Kuśa did not find her pleasing as a wife because she was fair-complexioned. Then those seven kings, having equipped their fourfold forces—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—gathered together for the sake of Sudarśanā. Among those seven kings, the most noble and excellent one was the king named Durmati, who was the strongest and most powerful of the seven. Then all those seven kings set out with great prosperity and great splendor, and in due course they reached the park of Kanyakubja. Now, Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, sent a messenger to each of those seven kings, saying: "This daughter of mine, Sudarśanā, is the wife of King Kuśa; therefore, I cannot give her to another. When those seven kings heard the reply of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, they became enraged and incensed; they surrounded the city of Kanyakubja on all sides with their respective divisions and remained there. King Mahendraka, too, having entered the city and bolted the gates, remained besieged within. Then it occurred to Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas: "I am indeed held besieged by these seven kings. All these kings are of great renown and great power; I am not capable of giving them battle. Even if I were to give my daughter to one of them, the other six kings would oppose me. What shall I do now? Then King Mahendraka, being angry with his daughter Sudarśanā, rebuked her: "Why have you fled from your husband and come here? Because of you, I am besieged by seven kings..."

"I am held captive. If anyone among these seven should cause me harm, then I shall cut them into seven pieces and give one piece to each of those seven kings. Then Sudarśanā, having heard her father’s words, became afraid, terrified, and filled with grief and dejection; she addressed her mother: "Mother, if these seven kṣatriyas, having fallen into mutual conflict, should have me killed, then after they have been reduced to ashes and their bones collected, you must have a stone monument (elūkā) erected for me. At the entrance of that monument, you must plant a karṇikāra tree. Then, at the end of summer when the first month of the rainy season arrives, that karṇikāra tree will be in full bloom, with a color like the luster of gold. At that time, you will remember me, thinking, 'Such was my daughter Sudarśanā in appearance. Then the Great Queen, having heard her daughter Sudarśanā’s words, became afraid, terrified, and filled with grief and dejection; with a choked throat and a weeping face, she said, "How can there be separation from my daughter? Then it occurred to Sudarśanā: "Just as King Kuśa is endowed with such vigor, strength, and prowess, these seven kings are not capable of giving battle to Kuśa. If King Kuśa should conquer us, I would wish to live."

Then Sudarśanā approached King Kuśa and performed various kinds of flattery and spoke to him: "Great King, my father threatens me thus: 'If these seven kings should cause me any harm, then having cut [my body] into seven pieces, I shall give one piece to each of these seven kings. Now King Kuśa spoke to Sudarśanā in many ways: 'I desire you; I would not inflict such great disrespect upon you, but what would you do for me? Thus King Kuśa remained conversing with Sudarśanā. And Sudarśanā’s mother heard this, and having heard it...

Again, seeing King Kuśa, [Sudarśanā’s mother] thought, "Who is this? Where has he come from? Is he a bamboo-worker, a weaver, a leather-worker, a barber, an outcaste, or a scavenger—one who reviles and threatens my daughter? Then Sudarśanā, placing her hands together in an añjali before her mother, said: "Mother, do not speak thus! He is no bamboo-worker, nor weaver, nor slave, nor leather-worker. This is named Kuśa, the eldest son of King Ikṣvāku and of his five hundred princes; Mother, do not think of him as a slave."
Resembling a conch shell in its whiteness and attended by throngs of women,
this flourishing kṣatriya clan— you indeed consider yourself a slave to them!
Amidst a family of Kṣatriyas, flourishing and filled with throngs of women adorned with golden vessels, you indeed consider yourself a slave.
There are sixty thousand cities, prosperous, flourishing, and free from thorns;
the Kṣatriya clan is thriving, yet you consider yourself a slave.
Sixty thousand elephants, adorned with golden ornaments,
covered in gold, possessing tusks as long as plow-poles, have emerged.
Mounted by village chiefs with swords and javelins in hand,
you consider yourself a slave to this prosperous Kṣatriya clan.
Sixty thousand chariots, adorned with the sound of joy,
made of iron, well-fastened, and covered with leopard skins, [were there].
Mounted by village chiefs, armed with bows and clad in armor—
yet you consider the prosperous clan of a Kṣatriya to be merely your slave.
There were sixty thousand noble steeds, the finest of horses,
wearing golden girths and bits made of precious gems.
Mounted by village chiefs, armed with nooses and clad in armor,
you consider yourself a slave to this prosperous kshatriya clan.
Twenty thousand brahmins constantly eat at the king’s expense,
whether by day or by night, always treated with honor and worshiped;
yet you consider the family of this kṣatriya to be prosperous and think of yourself as a slave.
Five hundred princes, together with their mothers and fathers, belong to a prosperous kshatriya clan; yet you consider yourself a slave.
There are sixty thousand treasures, as well as a father and a grandfather;
there, a king named Kuśa is the lord of men,
and by his complexion and prowess, there is no one equal to him in the world.

Then Queen Mahādevī, the mother of Sudarśanā, having heard these words, became joyful, thinking: "Such is my son-in-law, endowed with all virtues. Then the mother of Sudarśanā, having heard her daughter’s words, informed Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas: "Great King, you should know that your son-in-law, King Kuśa, has arrived here. Upon hearing the queen’s words, the king became afraid, terrified, and agitated, his hair standing on end. The king said: "Queen, have you gone mad? Have you lost your mind, that you speak thus, saying 'King Kuśa has arrived here'? What kind of King Kuśa is he? Where have you seen this King Kuśa? The queen said: "Great King, I am not mad, nor have I lost my mind. Rather, this son-in-law of yours, King Kuśa, is the one who cooks food in your kitchen and is the one who provides entertainment for the women of your inner apartments. Having heard this, the king became even more afraid and terrified.

He became filled with suffering and dejection, thinking: "This is not the suffering for me that seven kings hold me captive; rather, this is my suffering: that King Kuśa has come here out of anger toward Sudarśanā, and in his wrath at being held against his will, he will surely cause some harm within the inner city. Then King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, terrified and trembling, entered his own inner apartments. Joining his palms in reverence to King Kuśa, he asked for forgiveness, saying: "Forgive me, Great King, for whatever offense I have committed. Then King Kuśa comforted his father-in-law: "Do not fear, Great King; there is nothing of mine for which you must ask forgiveness. Thereupon, King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, led King Kuśa into the bathhouse for a moment. After having his hair and beard trimmed by barbers, he was anointed with hundred-fold refined fragrant oils, bathed with royal bathing powders, and rubbed with royal unguents. Having been dressed in royal garments and ornaments and adorned with jewelry, he sat upon a single seat together with his father-in-law, while being entertained by a five-fold musical ensemble.

Now, the loud, great, and tumultuous roar of the military forces of those seven kings was heard. King Kuśa then asked his father-in-law: "Great King, whose sound is this great clamor of a multitude of people that is being heard? The king replied: "For the sake of Sudarśanā, these seven kings have surrounded this city on all sides; I am besieged and must hold my ground. This is the noise of the military forces of those kings. Then King Kuśa reassured his father-in-law: "Do not fear, Great King. I shall act in such a way that these seven kings will bow down and become obedient to my word. King Kuśa then addressed his father-in-law: "Great King, have all these illustrious elephants, all the horses, all the quadrupeds, and the entire populace plug their ears with beeswax, lest they break their own ranks upon hearing my lion’s roar. Then King Kuśa, the illustrious one—

Having mounted an elephant and accompanied by a great multitude of people, he caused the city gate to be opened and rushed out. King Kuśa let out a lion’s roar; as he roared that lion’s roar, all seven kings, along with their armies and their mounts, were broken. Having captured them alive, he bound them with many firm bonds and presented them to his father-in-law, Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas. “Great King, here are those seven kings; they have all prostrated before Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas. ‘Victory to the Great King! We have come for refuge to the Great King. We shall be ready to carry out your every command at the mere word. Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, asked his son-in-law Kuśa: “Son, what do these seven kings please you? What shall we do? “I will do exactly as you command,” [Kuśa replied]. King Kuśa said: “Great King, you have many daughters in your harem; they must certainly be given to their husbands. These seven kings are all Kṣatriyas, possessed of great strength, great mounts, great fortune, and vast kingdoms. Therefore, Great King, having adorned seven of your daughters with a thousand pieces of gold each, give one daughter to each of these kings. These seven kings will become your sons-in-law, and they will become a powerful faction for you. All those neighboring kings—being of great strength, great mounts, and great retinue—will bow down and submit to you, and no rival king will oppose you. Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, said: “Son, very well; I will do exactly as you command. Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, had those seven daughters adorned with gold—each one adorned with a thousand pieces of gold—and gave one daughter to each king with great royal majesty and great royal splendor, establishing a bond of friendship involving sons and grandsons. Then those seven kings were sent back to their respective kingdoms by Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, with great hospitality and honor: “Go, sirs, and rule your own respective kingdoms.”

Now King Kuśa, having stayed for some time after those kings had been dismissed, addressed his father-in-law Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas: "Great King, I take my leave; I too shall go to my own realm. Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, said: "Son, do not go! You have given me my life; you have rescued my entire kingdom from peril. I am old, aged, advanced in years, and my youth has passed. I am the father and you are the son; you must rule the kingdom, do not go! King Kuśa said: "Great King, it has been a long time since I arrived, and my kingdom is unsettled. My mother will be anxious; I take my leave, I must go. Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, said: "If you must go, then you must go. King Kuśa said: "Great King, I must indeed go. Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, summoned his daughter Sudarśanā and instructed her: "Daughter, your husband King Kuśa is endowed with prowess; he is so mighty and powerful that he has rescued both you and me, as well as the entire kingdom, from danger. All kings bow down before him. Daughter Sudarśanā, you ought to serve King Kuśa, your husband, with love and respect. Then Sudarśanā, joining her palms in reverence, promised her father's words, saying, "So be it. Thereupon Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, gave his daughter Sudarśanā to King Kuśa and dismissed him to his own kingdom with great honor and a vast assembly—a fourfold army consisting of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—saying: "Go, my son, to your own kingdom."

Now King Kuśa, while traveling to his own kingdom, stayed in a grove on the outskirts of a city that had a park; there was a great lotus pond there. While bathing in that lotus pond, King Kuśa saw his own reflection in the water, and it was such that he was ill-colored, unsightly, and unpleasant to behold. Having seen his own body thus become unlovely, he said this: "It is possible that Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, will despise me because of my deformed, ill-colored, and unsightly physical form. What if I were now—"

"I shall take my own life. Now, King Kuśa, desiring to kill himself by his own hand, was perceived by Śakra, the lord of the gods, while he was in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. Śakra thought to himself: "This King Kuśa is a Bodhisattva who has set out for the welfare and happiness of all beings. Because he is now ugly and unsightly, he desires to take his own life; if he dies, it will be a great misfortune for the whole world. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, took a divine jewel-gem named Jyotīrasa from the midst of a single-stringed necklace of divine red pearls. Standing in the air, in the sky, he addressed King Kuśa: "Great King, do not take your own life! Instead, fasten this single-stringed necklace with the Jyotīrasa gem upon your head. Once it is fastened, no man in all of Jambudvīpa will be your equal in complexion or form. Furthermore, if you wish to regain your former complexion and form, then cover that single-stringed necklace with the Jyotīrasa gem with a cloth, and your former complexion and form will return. King Kuśa then bathed in that lotus pond, anointed himself with unguents, and put on robes fit for a king. He fastened that single-stringed necklace upon his head. Then, looking at his own face in the lotus pond, he realized there was indeed some distinction. As he examined himself, he saw that he was handsome and beautiful to behold, such as no man in Jambudvīpa had ever seen before in terms of complexion and form. Seeing himself thus endowed with such noble splendor, King Kuśa became joyful and delighted, thinking: "Now Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, will no longer despise me, nor will anyone else think I am ugly."
Then King Kuśa, standing at the foot of his own gate, thought, "I shall enter," and was then [addressed] by the doorkeepers.

"Who are you, man, that seeks to violate the royal palace? Do you not know that King Kuśa is difficult to approach and hard to withstand? Do not fall into misfortune and ruin this very moment! Then King Kuśa said, "I am your master; I am your King Kuśa. The gatekeepers said, "Do we not recognize King Kuśa, such as King Kuśa is? May it be well! If King Kuśa were indeed like this, then we would be favored with the highest grace, and the entire kingdom and the Ikṣvāku clan would be blessed by a king so gracious, handsome, and endowed with such supreme beauty and form. Then it occurred to King Kuśa: "He does not recognize me. Thereupon, King Kuśa covered his single-string necklace and *jyotīrasa* gem with his own garment. When the gatekeeper saw King Kuśa in his true form, he was terrified and trembling and prostrated himself, saying, "Great King, we did not know; Great King, you are truly great! Then King Kuśa entered the royal palace and approached the queen. But the queen stopped him, saying, "Who are you, man, and from where do you come, you who wish to violate the royal palace? You do not know that the inner apartments of King Kuśa are difficult to approach. Do not violate the royal palace, lest you fall into misfortune and ruin! Then King Kuśa said, "Queen, I am your husband; I am King Kuśa, know this! The queen said, "You are not my husband; you are not King Kuśa. What, do I not know what King Kuśa is like in appearance and form? May it be well! If King Kuśa were of such appearance and form, then I would be favored with the highest grace. Then King Kuśa covered that single-string necklace and *jyotīrasa* gem with his garment, and immediately his former appearance and form were restored. Then Sudarśanā said, "Great King, why do you display this illusion? King Kuśa said, "Queen, this is no illusionist at all; rather, I intended to kill myself by my own hand. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me this single—"

"O Great King, do not destroy yourself! Take this single-string necklace, this *jyotīrasa* jewel. Bind it upon your head; then no other man in all of Jambudvīpa will be your equal in complexion and form. If you wish to regain your former complexion and form, then have this single-string necklace, this *jyotīrasa* jewel, covered with a cloth; then your former complexion and form will return. This is a favor granted to me by Śakra, the lord of the gods. Then Queen Sudarśanā said, "I am favored by Śakra, the lord of the gods, since such a complexion and form has been bestowed upon you. The queen said, "Great King, never cover this single-string necklace, this *jyotīrasa* jewel. Let such a noble form as this be yours at all times. You shall be more pleasing to the entire kingdom and to the whole body of people. Thus, King Kuśa proceeded along the road in such a complexion and form, resembling a son of the gods.

Now at that time in Vārāṇasī, all five hundred princes minus one, along with all the ministers and the entire army, heard that King Kuśa was approaching. They all went out to meet King Kuśa. King Kuśa also approached, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant and surrounded by the fourfold army. However, those princes and the army did not recognize King Kuśa. They asked one another, "Who might this be, so handsome, beautiful, and majestic, coming with such sublime complexion and form, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant? King Kuśa himself is not to be seen. It occurred to King Kuśa, "They do not recognize me. Then King Kuśa, while still mounted on the back of the noble elephant, covered his face with his hand, which held a single-string necklace of *jyotirasa* gems. Immediately, his complexion and form returned to how they were before. Then those four hundred and ninety-nine princes, the ministers, and the army, seeing King Kuśa’s own true complexion and form, were terrified and struck with fear; they prostrated themselves at his feet and said to the king, "Victory to you, Great King! We did not [recognize you]."

"Great King, we know that this is he. Then King Kuśa informed his brothers, the ministers, and the army commanders of this matter: "Sirs, Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me this single-string necklace with the *jyotīrasa* jewel. Bind it upon your heads; then no other man will be your equal in complexion and form. Then those princes, the ministers, and the army commanders said this to the king: "We are favored by Śakra, the lord of the gods, since the great king has come to possess such a complexion and form. Thus, with great royal majesty and great royal power, King Kuśa arrived at Vārāṇasī and entered the royal palace. With his sublime complexion and form, he greeted Queen Mahādevī Alindā, bowed at her feet, and stood before her. But Queen Mahādevī Alindā did not recognize King Kuśa. She asked, "Where is my son? Where is King Kuśa? King Kuśa said, "Mother, I am your son; I am King Kuśa. The queen said, "You are not my son! You are not King Kuśa! How is it that I do not recognize King Kuśa? Has King Kuśa been struck down or killed by someone, that he is not seen? Alas, what a helpless death for me, that separation from my only son has occurred! Then the king, seeing his mother lamenting, covered that single-string necklace with the *jyotīrasa* jewel with a cloth, and his complexion and form returned to how they were before. When Queen Mahādevī Alindā saw her son in his own natural complexion and form, she became joyful and asked her son, "Son, how has your complexion and form become like this? King Kuśa said, "Mother, Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me a single-string necklace with the *jyotīrasa* jewel. It was bound upon me; because of this, my complexion and form have become like this. Then Queen Mahādevī Alindā became exceedingly glad, filled with joy and happiness: "I have seen my son with such a sublime complexion and form as I had hoped for. And all the women of the inner apartments, seeing the king’s sublime complexion and form, became joyful, filled with happiness and gladness. The jewel of flavor was given by Śakra, the lord of the gods; it binds that time during which the divine state prevails. At whatever time one covers that jewel with the hand, at that time it returns to its former color and form. In this way, King Kuśa, having struck down his adversaries and destroyed his enemies in Vārāṇasī, now rules his kingdom with noble enjoyments and luxuries.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses in the presence of the fourfold assembly and a great multitude of people:
Thus, for one who possesses merit, all matters become favorable,
just as King Kuśa was reunited with his wife and his kinsmen.

"Monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the king named Kuśa was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way. At that time, on that occasion, I was the king Kuśa. That Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way; he was this Śākya Mahānāma. That great queen named Alindā was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way; she was Queen Māyā. That Sudarśanā was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way; she was Yaśodharā. "Monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the eldest among those seven kings, named Durmati, was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way; he was Māra the Evil One. Those other kings were the retinue of Māra. Even then, by the sound of my clearing my throat, this Māra the Evil One, together with his army and his mounts, was defeated by me. And now, monks, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, by the sound of my clearing my throat, this Māra the Evil One, together with his army and his mounts, has been defeated by me."
